1. Introduction

When Jean Tirole famously described economics as moving from the “hedgehogs” who 
know one big thing to the “foxes” who know many things, he articulated a widespread 
perception: the age of a unified, monistic economics has ended (Tirole 2017). At first 
sight, this diagnosis resonates with earlier claims by David Colander, John B. Davis, or 
Alessandro Roncaglia that the “neoclassical synthesis” had lost its grip, leaving the dis
cipline fragmented into a plurality of models, styles, or research programs (Cedrini and 
Fontana 2018; Colander 2000; Colander et al. 2004; Davis 2019, 2006; Roncaglia 2019). 
A majority of economists perceive an increasing lack of orientation (Bachmann 2019; 
Falk and Andre 2021; Weimann 2019). Nevertheless, empirical investigations into pub
lication patterns tell a different story. Bibliometric studies point to a remarkable con
centration of journals, institutions, and keywords, suggesting that economics remains 
more centralised than its practitioners often believe (Aigner, Greenspon, and Rodrik

2025; Aistleitner, Kapeller, and Kronberger 2023; Beyer et al. 2018; Fontana and Iori 
2023; Fourcade, Ollion, and Algan 2015; Glo€tzl and Aigner 2019). This tension between 
perceived fragmentation and observable concentration has fuelled a so far unresolved 
debate over what, if anything, still unites the discipline.

The central claim of this paper is that an important level of analysis has so far 
been omitted. The alleged “unity” of economics has usually been defined in theoret
ical terms, through the prevalence of “neoclassical” assumptions such as rationality, 
self-interest, and equilibrium, or through the dominance of specific keywords trace
able in publication databases (Ambrosino et al. 2018). However, this approach misses 
the deeper level on which disciplinary unity historically operated. Throughout much 
of the twentieth century, economics was held together by a shared methodological 
vision that crystallised into a specific methodological basic type. Its hallmark was the 
pursuit of pure, universal, axiomatic theory as the foundation of positive economic 
knowledge. Empirical work was subordinated to theory, and normative reasoning was 
reduced to welfare criteria derived from positive models. This basic type defined what 
counted as “scientific” economics, stabilised the discipline across diverse subfields, 
and shaped economics education as well as internal critique.

This paper does not argue that mainstream economics has dissolved, nor that its 
policy influence or institutional structures have fundamentally weakened. On the con
trary, many core assumptions, teaching practices, and policy frames remain remark
ably resilient. The argument advanced here is narrower and more specific: it concerns 
the erosion of a shared methodological ordering principle that once structured the 
relation between theory, empirics, and normativity.

In its place, at least three methodological orientations have gained prominence and 
now coexist: a model portfolio orientation that treats models as context-sensitive tools 
(Gru€ne-Yanoff and Marchionni 2018; Rodrik 2015); an experimental paradigm that 
grants primacy to empirical identification (Angrist et al. 2017; Backhouse and Cherrier 
2017; Banerjee and Duflo 2019); and a normative turn that employs theory with the per
formative ambition to design markets, institutions, and behavioural interventions 
(J. Davis 2017). These orientations should not be understood as mutually exclusive 
camps, nor as entirely novel inventions. Taken together, these orientations can no longer 
be fully accommodated within the traditional methodological basic type. They point 
towards a new methodological attitude but at the same time still embody incompatible 
assumptions about the relation between theory, empirics, and normativity.

Therefore, the current transformation of economics should not be interpreted as a 
harmonious opening towards pluralism. Rather, contemporary economics is charac
terised by persistent methodological tensions among prevailing research trends. The 
paper argues that these tensions are best understood as paradoxical: economics has 
become more plural and more performative, yet it lacks a shared methodological 
ground. Articulating these paradoxes, rather than prematurely resolving them, is a 
necessary step towards a broader methodological horizon capable of accommodating 
the discipline’s ongoing transformation. This paper cannot deliver a corresponding 
new methodology, but it aims to prepare the ground for future methodological reflec
tion beyond the diagnosis of the “end of economics as we know it” and towards the 
articulation of a new methodological basic type.



THE EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF THE HISTORY OF ECONOMIC THOUGHT 3

Section 1 points out that the debate on the fragmentation vs. concentration of eco
nomics assumed some version of the neoclassical doctrine as historical unity, and 
why this can be misleading. Section 2 reconstructs the methodological constitution 
that historically unified economics, which I call Economics 1.0. It shows how the disci
pline’s coherence evolved on a basic methodological vision linking theory, empirics, and 
normativity. Section 3 analyses the erosion of this framework through theoretical impos
sibility results, empirical revolutions, and design-oriented practices. Section 4 identifies 
three new methodological orientations that have gained prominence in recent decades 
and examines how they jointly transcend but also contradict the old framework. Section 
5 distils these contradictions into two paradoxes, concerning the status of economic 
knowledge and the performativity of theory. A concluding section reflects on what these 
paradoxes imply for the future of the discipline: the end of economics as we knew it, but 
also the beginning of a more reflexive and pluralist science.

2. Focusing on theoretical unity may hide the fragmentation of economics

The recent debate on whether economics is fragmenting or remaining concentrated 
presupposes that the discipline once possessed a unifying centre. Studies that judge or 
measure the variety or concentration of the discipline must assume a baseline of 
unity: only if there was once a coherent frame can we now speak of fragmentation or 
persistence. What, then, was this unity?

The contemporary debate was prominently initiated by David Colander. In his presi
dential address to the History of Economics Society in 1999, delivered with a sympa
thetic touch of self-irony, he declared the term “neoclassical” effectively dead (Colander 
2000). He observed that most economists no longer actively used the label to describe 
themselves or their assumptions. Instead, a more eclectic configuration had emerged in 
which methods appeared to matter more than adherence to central dogmas. Even among 
historians of economics, Colander argued, the term was ambiguous. For some, it referred 
to the marginalist revolution of the late nineteenth century; for others, it captured post- 
war mathematical economics more broadly. Originally coined by Veblen to criticise 
Marshall’s economics, “neoclassicism” only later came to be used as a self-description in 
the writings of Hicks and Stigler, and was consolidated in Samuelson’s neoclassical syn
thesis (1955). For Colander, the concept faded gradually between roughly 1935 and 2000
– “a slow transition rather than a sudden epiphany” (Colander 2000, 133).

To illustrate this transformation, Colander pointed to researchers such as David 
Romer, Richard Thaler, George Akerlof, Amartya Sen, and Paul Krugman, who 
appeared to move beyond strict commitments to rationality, self-interest, and equilib
rium. He later extended this observation to emerging fields such as behavioural eco
nomics, agent-based modelling, evolutionary game theory, and experimental 
economics (Colander et al. 2004). John B. Davis characterised this shift as a form of 
“mainstream pluralism,” to distinguish it from prior heterodox pluralism, and charac
terised it as a reverse imperialism in which economics increasingly imported methods 
and topics from neighbouring disciplines (J. B. Davis 2006).

Since then, the thesis of increasing fragmentation has been articulated in various 
forms. Roncaglia (2019) offered a detailed intellectual history of major research 



4 F. BALLY-ROMMEL

programmes culminating in what he described as an “age of fragmentation.” 
Empirical evidence appeared to support this view. Since the 1970s, the number of 
specialised journals, research fields, and publications has grown dramatically from 
roughly 1,000 articles annually in 1950 to over 20,000 since 2015 (Claveau and 
Gingras 2016; Glo€tzl and Aigner 2019). Co-authorship increased markedly (Jones, 
Reedy, and Weinberg 2014; Kosnik and Lea-Rachel 2014; Laband 2013; Cedrini and 
Fontana 2018; Davis 2019), articles became longer and more technically sophisticated 
(Ellison 2002) and the JEL classification system required major revision in 1991 to 
accommodate new categories (Cherrier 2017). Prestigious awards such as the Clark 
Medal increasingly recognised applied and empirically oriented work (Backhouse and 
Cherrier 2017; Cherrier and Svoren�c�ık 2018). Cedrini and Fontana (2018) further 
documented a diversification of methods within the top 8 journal publications.

At the same time, bibliometric studies focusing on citation structures and keyword 
frequencies told a more complex story. Despite surface-level diversification, structural 
concentration persisted across several dimensions. The “Top 5” journals (AER, QJE, 
JPE, Econometrica, and Review of Economic Studies) retained disproportionate influ
ence, with a small share of journals accounting for a large proportion of citations 
(Card and DellaVigna 2013). Geographic and institutional concentration remained 
pronounced: a majority of highly cited articles originated from a limited number of 
Anglophone institutions, particularly in the United States (Harvard, MIT, Stanford, 
Chicago, Berkeley) (Aigner 2017; Aigner et al. 2018; Glo€tzl and Aigner 2019). Studies 
by Kapeller, Beyer, Pu€hringer, and Grimm, based on comprehensive surveys of pro
fessorships in Germany and the United States, found that a large majority of econo
mists could still be classified within a broadly neoclassical orthodoxy, while explicitly 
heterodox positions remained marginal and the so-called “Colander’s Edge” or the 
new mainstream pluralism accounted for ruffly 5% of professorships even though 
these are located at prestigious universities in Germany (Reinke 2024). Fontana, who 
had initially supported the fragmentation thesis, later revised this assessment in light 
of evidence indicating the persistent centrality of typical neoclassical concepts 
(Fontana and Iori 2023).

The result is a seemingly paradoxical picture. While the proliferation of fields, 
methods, and empirical approaches suggests fragmentation, institutional hierarchies 
and conceptual core elements remain strikingly stable. Bibliometric research, much of 
it inspired by Colander’s provocation, attempted to measure pluralism through the 
frequency of theoretical signal words. Yet even if no new comprehensive theory has 
replaced neoclassicism, many economists report a growing sense of fragmentation 
and a loss of orientation (Bachmann 2019; Falk and Andre 2021; Weimann 2019).

This tension indicates that theoretical labels and citation structures may not fully 
capture the relevant dimension of unity and change. The discipline may indeed be 
diversifying, but this diversification appears to operate primarily at a methodological 
rather than a purely theoretical level. This is also suggested by further bibliometrical 
evidence (Biddle and Hamermesh 2017; Hamermesh 2013; Joshua Angrist et al. 
2017). Economics has not fractured into mutually exclusive paradigms; rather, it has 
developed diverging methodological programs that continue to share important his
torical roots. The verdict on fragmentation versus concentration therefore depends on 



THE EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF THE HISTORY OF ECONOMIC THOUGHT 5

the dimension under examination. Theoretically and institutionally, economics 
remains highly concentrated. Methodologically, however, a more substantive trans
formation may be underway. To understand this shift, it is necessary to revisit the 
form of methodological unity that previously structured the discipline.

3. The methodological basic type - Economics 1.0

The idea that economics once possessed a relatively strong internal unity is widely 
shared among historians of economic thought. In retrospect, the interwar period is 
often described as comparatively pluralistic (Morgan and Rutherford 1998), whereas 
the decades following the Second World War are characterised as a period of consoli
dation, during which a common epistemic horizon structured the discipline. 
Although assumptions, mathematical techniques, and specific theoretical commit
ments evolved from Marshallian partial equilibrium to various strands of rational 
choice and general equilibrium theory (Herfeld 2013). This horizon rested on a 
shared methodological vision.

I argue that what held economics together throughout much of the twentieth cen
tury was not merely a set of core assumptions but a methodological vision that led to 
a methodological basic type. This continuity is often associated with “neoclassical” 
economics. To avoid terminological ambiguity, I refer to the methodological basic 
type here as Economics 1.0, to distinguish it from earlier political economy. At its 
core lay the conviction that economics should approximate the epistemic standards of 
the natural sciences by grounding itself in a universal, axiomatic theory. Theory was 
not one domain among others; it functioned as the constitutive foundation of scien
tific legitimacy. Empirical work gained prestige insofar as it calibrated, operational
ised, or illustrated theoretical constructions. Normative reasoning was considered 
acceptable when presented as a formal extension of positive analysis, for instance, 
through welfare criteria such as Pareto optimality or the Kaldor–Hicks compensation 
principle. In this constellation, Economics 1.0 provided something akin to a disciplin
ary constitution: it defined standards of legitimacy, structured the division of labour, 
framed economics education, and shaped even the terms of internal critique.

3.1. From political economy to pure economics

The emergence of this basic type was itself the result of a historical transformation. 
Nineteenth-century political economy remained explicitly entangled with moral phil
osophy, governance, and practical reasoning. Adam Smith held the chair of moral 
philosophy; John Stuart Mill openly acknowledged the abstract character of economic 
reasoning and emphasised the corrective role of “practical men” (Mill 1836). 
Economic analysis was closely connected to normative questions concerning good 
government and social organisation.

By the late nineteenth century, however, a reorientation occurred. Authors such as 
William Stanley Jevons, L�eon Walras, Carl Menger, Alfred Marshall, and Vilfredo 
Pareto re-defined economics as a science aspiring to the rigour of mechanical physics. 
Walras, in his E�l�ements d’�economie politique pure (1874), explicitly described 



6 F. BALLY-ROMMEL

economics as a “pure science,” analogous to mechanics. Empirical observation was 
understood as the starting point for abstraction, but the primary scientific task was 
the construction of an internally consistent theoretical system. Marshall’s Principles of 
Economics (1890) symbolically marked this shift by omitting the “political” of earlier 
textbooks, thereby projecting a more autonomous discipline. Pareto further formal
ised this orientation through ordinal utility and the concept of Pareto efficiency, 
refining the formal apparatus while simultaneously reshaping the presentation of nor
mative claims.

This epistemic reorientation did not eliminate normative concerns, but it relocated 
them within a formal framework. Economics increasingly defined itself less by its 
subject matter, wealth, markets, or the economy, than by its method. Mathematical 
deduction and universal modelling came to serve as markers of scientific status. 
These developments, among others, laid the foundations for the methodological basic 
type that would later crystallise more fully.

3.2. The “high theory” constellation

By the mid-twentieth century, this orientation had crystallised in the grand project of 
general equilibrium theory. John Hicks’s Value and Capital (1939) and Paul 
Samuelson’s Foundations of Economic Analysis (1947) became canonical, combining 
mathematical formalism with broad ambitions to unify micro- and macroeconomics. 
The work of Kenneth Arrow and G�erard Debreu (1954) provided the crowning 
achievement: a complete existence proof for a general competitive equilibrium, using 
the tools of convex analysis and topology. Many historians of economics have inter
preted this moment as the apex of theoretical unification, the point at which econom
ics seemed to have attained the status of a “hard” science.

Methodologically, the Arrow–Debreu framework exemplified the aspiration 
towards a universal, axiomatic structure. Formal coherence became a central criterion 
of scientific achievement. Empirical considerations did not disappear, but the evalu
ation of theoretical work increasingly focused on internal consistency, generality, and 
deductive clarity. Even the welfare theorems were presented as logical implications 
within this formal system.

This configuration may be described as the methodological subtype of monistic the
ory. Its purpose was the systematic exploration of a model world: extending the 
framework to new domains, refining assumptions, and analysing special cases. The 
expansion of growth theory, trade models, and labour market models in the 1950s 
and 1960s illustrates this dynamic. Success was often measured in terms of theoretical 
integration and analytical tractability, the exploration of a new formal model world 
(Hands 2001; Morgan 2012).

Alongside this theoretical core, a theory-oriented empirical methodological subtype 
developed, closely linked to it. Institutions such as the Cowles Commission sought to 
integrate theory and econometrics by specifying structural models and estimating 
parameters. Empirical work was thus embedded within the theoretical framework, 
aiming to operationalise and quantify its structures. Rather than challenging the core 



THE EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF THE HISTORY OF ECONOMIC THOUGHT 7

models directly, econometric practice was typically oriented towards their specifica
tion and refinement (Backhouse and Cherrier 2017; Boumans 2004).

Friedman’s essay “The Methodology of Positive Economics” Friedman (1953) 
expressed a related view: theories were to be evaluated by the accuracy of their pre
dictions rather than the realism of their assumptions. This stance reinforced the pri
macy of theoretical structure while granting empirical testing a defined, though not 
autonomous, role.

Normative reasoning was likewise framed within this architecture. Welfare eco
nomics presented criteria such as Pareto efficiency and the Kaldor–Hicks principle as 
formal implications of positive models. In this way, normative claims could be articu
lated as extensions of analytically derived results, allowing economists to present pol
icy-relevant conclusions within a self-consciously scientific framework. This may be 
described as the formal-normative methodological subtype of Economics 1.0.

Taken together, the monistic theory subtype, the theory-oriented empirical subtype, 
and the formally embedded normative subtype constituted the methodological basic type 
of Economics 1.0. They structured the discipline’s intellectual order: defining legitimate 
problems, shaping graduate training, and influencing the allocation of prestige and 
resources (Backhouse and Cherrier 2017; Colander 1992; Hoaas 1993; Mankiw 2014; 
Milton Friedman 1953). Even internal critics such as Keynesians, monetarists, behav
ioural economists, and other dissenters often engaged with this horizon, situating their 
contributions in relation to the methodological aspiration of positive economics.

For this reason, the mid-twentieth century is often remembered as the era of “high 
theory.” Substantive disagreements were significant and sometimes intense. Yet these 
disputes unfolded within a shared methodological commitment: the belief that eco
nomics should rest on a general, axiomatic framework capable of organising theory, 
empirical analysis, and normative reasoning within a unified structure.

4. The transformation of the methodological base type

If the post-war decades saw the consolidation of a methodological basic type, the sub
sequent period witnessed a gradual transformation of its epistemic self-understanding. 
This transformation was neither sudden nor uniform. The axiomatic program 
remained influential, and continues to do so in many domains. What changed was 
not the immediate disappearance of the framework, but the growing awareness of its 
limits and scope conditions.

A series of theoretical results, empirical developments, and shifts in research prac
tice generated pressures that were interpreted in different ways by different groups of 
economists. Some saw these results as reasons to modify or extend the axiomatic 
core. Others interpreted them as signals that the original ambition of a universal and 
unified theoretical foundation had reached its boundaries. Still others regarded them 
as confirmations of the robustness of the core model, albeit within a more clearly 
delimited domain.

The key point is not that the methodological basic type necessarily “failed,” but 
that it became increasingly contested, interpreted in divergent ways, and also inspired 
new methodological ventures, as we will investigate in the next chapter.



8 F. BALLY-ROMMEL

4.1. Internal theoretical tensions

Several of the most important challenges emerged from within the formal program 
itself. The Cambridge capital controversy, associated with Piero Sraffa and Joan 
Robinson, raised fundamental questions about the measurability and independence of 
capital as a factor of production. If capital could not be defined independently of dis
tributional variables such as the rate of profit, the marginal productivity theory of dis
tribution appeared less secure (Robinson 1971, 1953; Sraffa 1960). For some, this 
suggested deep conceptual problems. For others, the issue could be treated as a tech
nical complication with limited practical relevance. Regardless of interpretation, the 
controversy demonstrated that core theoretical components were not beyond dispute 
(Harcourt 1986; Salvadori and Signorino 2007; Schefold 2020, 2022; Sent 2006a; 
Stiglitz 1974).

Similarly, the Sonnenschein–Mantel–Debreu results showed that even when indi
vidual preferences satisfy standard rationality assumptions, aggregate excess demand 
functions can take almost arbitrary shapes (Debreu 1974; Mantel 1974; Rizvi 2006; 
Sonnenschein 1972). The implications of these results have been interpreted in differ
ent ways. Some regarded them as undermining hopes for uniqueness and stability of 
equilibrium. Others saw them as clarifying that general equilibrium theory should be 
understood as an existence framework rather than a predictive macro theory. The 
results did not abolish general equilibrium theory, but they limited its unifying 
explanatory ambition (Kirman 2010, 1989, 1992).

Kenneth Arrow’s impossibility theorem likewise did not invalidate welfare eco
nomics, but it demonstrated that the aggregation of individual preferences into a 
coherent social ordering cannot satisfy a minimal set of desirable conditions simul
taneously. In addition, Richard Lipsey and Kelvin Lancaster undermined the founda
tions of welfare economics with their Theory of the Second Best (1956). They showed 
that if one condition for a Pareto optimum is violated, the fulfilment of the other 
conditions does not necessarily increase welfare. Again, interpretations diverged. For 
some, this signalled a need for explicit normative commitments beyond formal aggre
gation. For others, it reinforced scepticism towards collective decision-making and 
strengthened arguments in favour of decentralised markets (Gibbard 2014; Hammond 
1987; Sen 2014).

In each case, the results did not compel a single conclusion. Rather, they widened 
the interpretative space. The methodological basic type could still be maintained, but 
its claim to offer a universally valid and internally complete architecture became 
more difficult to sustain without qualification.

4.2. From “the economy” to “economies”

The cumulative effect of these theoretical developments was not the immediate aban
donment of the axiomatic framework, but a gradual clarification of its scope condi
tions. Attempts to preserve theoretical unity often relied on increasingly restrictive 
assumptions. One prominent strategy was the consolidation of the representative 
agent. Faced with aggregation difficulties and the limitations of social welfare func
tions, modelling moved towards the assumption of identical or effectively 



THE EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF THE HISTORY OF ECONOMIC THOUGHT 9

homogeneous agents. As Samuelson himself suggested, this device allowed economists 
to retain formal coherence without committing to the narrative of an economy inhab
ited by identical agents (Gordon 1955; Keen 2011; Samuelson 1956).

Yet the representative agent came at a conceptual price. If all agents are identical, 
differences of opinion vanish. As Sent (2006a, 2006b) notes: such a “monistic” config
uration eliminates disagreement, speculation, and ultimately exchange itself. This 
insight was reinforced by a series of so-called no-trade theorems (Hakansson, Kunkel, 
and Ohlson 1982; Milgrom and Stokey 1982; Sent 2006b, Tirole 1982; Varian 1989), 
which showed that under common knowledge of rationality and information, mutu
ally beneficial trade cannot arise. These results did not refute equilibrium theory; 
rather, they demonstrated that certain canonical assumptions imply a surprisingly 
narrow class of economies or, as Sent concludes the debate: “With one representative 
agent, there clearly can be no difference of opinion, which we call a situation of mon
ism in economies.” (Sent 2006a, 2006b, 90). The ambition of a universal model 
increasingly required either homogeneity or highly specific informational structures.

One attempt to circumvent this homogeneity was a shift towards game theory, 
which allows for a further set of different agent constellations (A. Kirman 1989; A. P. 
Kirman 1992; Rizvi 1994). While strategic interaction enabled richer constellations of 
agents, standard assumptions about rationality and common knowledge again con
strained the diversity of possible outcomes. Agents in canonical models could not 
“agree to disagree,” (Sent 2006a, 2006b, 93) and speculative trade remained difficult 
to justify within fully rational frameworks. The theoretical architecture could be 
maintained, but often only by restricting the variety of agents and institutional envi
ronments considered.

At the same time, developments in information economics, contract theory, and 
behavioural research reintroduced heterogeneity systematically. Asymmetric informa
tion, bounded rationality, incomplete contracts, and institutional variation became 
central analytical themes (Akerlof 1970; Simon 1997). In these domains, markets were 
no longer treated as frictionless coordination devices but as institutional arrangements 
whose functioning depends on specific informational and behavioural conditions.

In their retrospective assessment of Walrasian economics, Bowles and Gintis argue 
that once strong assumptions about complete contracting and purely self-regarding 
preferences are relaxed, economic analysis must incorporate norms, institutions, and 
power relations. This does not entail a rejection of formal modelling. Rather, it 
broadens the ontological horizon: different institutional settings generate different 
behavioural regularities and distributive outcomes. Economic theory thus shifts from 
modelling “the economy” as a single abstract system towards analysing a plurality of 
economies structured by distinct rules, norms, and informational environments 
(Bowles and Gintis 2000). In fact, this is not just a theoretical insight but also a mani
fest research trend, backed by bibliometric evidence (Bowles and Carlin 2026).

Under these conditions, theoretical unity persists primarily at the level of shared 
analytical tools, not at the level of a single, universally valid representation of eco
nomic life. The discipline continues to speak the language of equilibrium, optimisa
tion, and incentives, but these concepts are increasingly embedded in context-specific 
model worlds. The methodological basic type remains recognisable, yet its aspiration 



10 F. BALLY-ROMMEL

to describe one coherent economy gives way to the analysis of multiple, structurally 
differentiated economies. 

4.3. Diverging reactions

These developments did not generate a uniform response. Some economists inter
preted the new results as a reason to intensify empirical identification strategies, 
shifting attention from universal theory to context-sensitive causal inference. Others 
treated the growing diversity of models as a toolbox from which context-appropri
ate instruments could be selected. Yet another group regarded the formal frame
work as sufficiently robust and turned towards its practical implementation in 
institutional design and policy engineering. Thus, the transformation of the meth
odological basic type has not yet reached a definitive conclusion. It generated a 
branching of trajectories. The shared origin remained visible, but the relation 
between theory, empirics, and normativity began to be configured differently in 
each emerging orientation.

5. Methodological fragmentation in economics research

Building on the developments discussed in Section 3, contemporary economics can 
be described as structured by at least three methodological orientations that have 
gained prominence over recent decades. These orientations do not constitute empiric
ally disjoint camps. They are best understood as analytical ideal types that highlight 
different ways of configuring the relation between theory, empirics, and normativity. 
Hybrids, overlaps, and transitions are common, and many research projects combine 
elements of more than one orientation.

The purpose of this section is therefore not to claim that these orientations are his
torically unprecedented. Rather, the claim is that their simultaneous prominence and 
institutionalisation have altered the discipline’s methodological landscape in ways that 
can no longer be fully accommodated within the former methodological basic type 
(Economics 1.0). Section 4.1 examines the evolving status of empirical work and the 
rise of identification-first strategies. Section 4.2 presents the model-portfolio orienta
tion, in which models are treated as context-sensitive instruments rather than ele
ments of a single coherent “model world.” Section 4.3 discusses a normative– 
performative orientation in which models are increasingly employed with explicit 
design ambitions. Section 5 will then show why the coexistence of these orientations 
produces systematic tensions rather than a harmonious pluralism.

5.1. From theory-guided empiricism to identification-first strategies

Economics in the United States already had strong empirical traditions in the inter
war period (Backhouse and Cherrier 2017). During the decades in which Economics 
1.0 was consolidated, however, the highest prestige within the discipline was largely 
attached to contributions in high theory and to empirically oriented work insofar as 
it operationalised theory. The frequently discussed “empirical turn” is therefore best 



THE EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF THE HISTORY OF ECONOMIC THOUGHT 11

understood not as the invention of empiricism, but as a shift in the disciplinary hier
archy: empirical work related to theory gained greater autonomy and, in many fields, 
became the primary source of epistemic authority.

This development can be described in three stages through which empirical 
research gradually moved from a theory-guided, structural orientation to an identifi
cation-first orientation in which causal inference in specific contexts is central.

Stage I: Theory-driven empiricism

The first stage was already identified as the empirical methodological subtype of 
Economics 1.0, as discussed above. Here, empirical work was primarily organised as 
an extension of theory: a model was specified first, and empirical methods served to 
estimate parameters, calibrate relationships, or assess predictive fit. In the 1950s and 
1960s, the Cowles Commission epitomised this orientation through its ambition to 
integrate theory and econometrics by specifying structural models and validating 
them empirically (Dimand and Rivot 2021). Colander succinctly sums up:

“[ … ] when Arrow/Debreu proved the existence of a general equilibrium in 1957, 
there was hope that the pure science of economics would progress in tandem with 
the practical application of that science.” (Colander 2000, 139).

In this context, empirical work was considered a subordinate instrument, a form 
of application rather than a means of producing knowledge. This approach became 
firmly established in econometric textbooks (Qin 2019).

Stage II: Model diversity and contextualisation

This arrangement became increasingly difficult to sustain in the 1970s, in the wake 
of the theoretical limitations discussed in Section 3 and the growing awareness of 
scope conditions. As Backhouse and Cherrier note, “No longer was it possible to 
hope for a single, all-encompassing general theory [ … ] economists were pushed to 
tailor theories and tools to specific uses” (Backhouse and Cherrier 2017, 27). 
Colander similarly interprets this period as enabling economists to work with models 
that were not fully consistent with general equilibrium theory, without abandoning 
formal modelling as such (Colander 2000, 139). In this context, new theoretical devel
opments, such as “new growth theory” or “new trade theory,” gained prominence, 
and the relation between theory and evidence became more explicitly context-sensi
tive. Solow’s notion of a “loose-fitting positivism” captures this shift: theory remained 
central, but its claims were increasingly framed as partial and situational rather than 
universal. This reconfiguration also prepared the ground for the model-portfolio 
orientation discussed in Section 4.2.

Stage III: The credibility revolution—experimental and quasi-experimental designs

The third stage represents a more pronounced departure from Economics 1.0. 
Panhans and Singleton speak of a transition “from models to methods,” and 
Herrmann-Pillath describes the emergence of an experimental paradigm (Herrmann- 
Pillath 2013; Panhans and Singleton 2017). What is distinctive here is not the 



12 F. BALLY-ROMMEL

complete absence of theory, but the methodological prioritisation of identification: 
research designs are organised around establishing credible causal effects in specific 
contexts, while theory plays a thinner and more optional role, sometimes guiding 
hypotheses, sometimes providing interpretation, and sometimes being deliberately 
bracketed.

A key impetus for this shift was dissatisfaction with conventional econometric 
practice and model-dependent inference, famously captured in Leamer’s critique that 
empirical results could be made to vary with specification choices (Leamer 1983). In 
response, laboratory and field experiments, randomised evaluations, and a range of 
quasi-experimental strategies (such as instrumental variables, regression discontinuity, 
and difference-in-differences designs) gained prominence. Methodologically, these 
approaches are oriented towards identifying causal effects without relying on an over
arching structural theory. As Biddle and Hamermesh put it, “Instead, the posing of 
questions to be answered or hypotheses to be tested is more likely to occur through 
informal discussions of earlier models, perhaps mixed with the conjectures of other 
social scientists or commonsense opinions of participants in policy debates” (Biddle 
and Hamermesh 2017, 2).

Raj Chetty’s work on taxation provides a prominent illustration: rather than using 
empirical work primarily to validate a given theory of taxation, it often uses empirical 
evidence to reveal limitations of standard theoretical assumptions under specific insti
tutional and behavioural conditions (Chetty 2009; Chetty et al. 2009). Bibliometric 
evidence documents the disciplinary significance of this identification-first orienta
tion. In areas such as labour economics, it accounts for most top-journal publications; 
in macroeconomics, its share has also been increasing. Overall, estimates place it at 
roughly 30% to 40% of current research output (Angrist et al. 2020, 2017; 
Hamermesh 2013; Biddle and Hamermesh 2017). This development is further 
reflected in widely used textbooks (Angrist and Pischke 2017, 2014).1

5.2. From a consistent model world to a mixed model portfolio
“ … the strength of economics lay precisely in small-scale theorising, the kind of 
contextual thinking that clarifies cause and effect and sheds light – even if partial – on 
social reality. [ … ] is more likely to be useful than a search for universal theories … ” 
(Rodrik 2015, xi)

The model-portfolio methodological subtype is both a legacy of Economics 1.0 and a 
departure from its unifying ambition. It remains committed to deductive modelling 
and formal reasoning, but it abandons the idea that the discipline should converge on 
a single coherent theoretical architecture with universal scope. Models are treated as 
context-sensitive tools designed for particular explanatory tasks, rather than as ele
ments of one overarching representation of “the economy.” Progress consists less in 
unification than in expanding, refining, and selecting among a repertoire of models.

1 Backhouse and Cherrier (2017) still question what proportion of empirical work is truly no longer theory 
driven. In the meantime, however, this has been precisely quantified, also in contrast to the other theory-world 
relationships described. Biddle and Hamermesh (2018) show that the “a-theoretical style”, i.e., work without 
formal theory, has overtaken the classic “measurement with theory” style in many fields of economics.



THE EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF THE HISTORY OF ECONOMIC THOUGHT 13

Rodrik describes economics as working with a “model portfolio,” like a large 
library from which the appropriate model must be selected for the problem at hand: 
“Older models remain useful; we add to them” (Rodrik 2015, 71). Gru€ne-Yanoff and 
Marchionni and others (Gilboa et al. 2014; Gru€ne-Yanoff and Marchionni 2018; 
Rodrik 2015; Sugden 2000) observe a similar stance and note that empirical confron
tation no longer functions primarily as universal confirmation or falsification, but as 
guidance for model selection relative to a target and purpose: “Consequently, con
fronting a model with empirical evidence no longer confirms or falsifies it in any uni
versal sense, but rather facilitates the selection of the appropriate model for a specific 
target T for a particular purpose P” (Gru€ne-Yanoff 2018, 54).

The strength of this orientation lies in its flexibility. Its vulnerability lies in the cri
teria of selection: without explicit methodological rules for relating assumptions, 
mechanisms, and contexts, a portfolio can become internally inconsistent or be used 
in ways that make systematic critique more difficult (Kapeller 2013; Kapeller and 
Ferschli 2019). This tension will matter for the paradoxes discussed in Section 5. In 
terms of disciplinary presence, this methodological type is particularly widespread in 
applied work and corresponds to the applied turn (Backhouse and Cherrier 2017). 
Depending on the definition, its share in top journals can be estimated at 30–40% of 
publications.2

5.3. Economic theory as an instrument of design

In the textbook self-understanding associated with Economics 1.0, positive economics 
describes how economic processes work, while normative economics adds evaluative 
criteria and policy implications. In recent decades, however, an increasingly visible 
strand of research has treated economic theory not only as a descriptive or explana
tory instrument, but also as a tool for shaping institutions and behaviour. John B. 
Davis has described this as a “normative turn” (Davis 2017).3

It is important to stress at the outset that normative or policy-oriented uses of 
models are not new in the history of economics. What appears distinctive in the con
temporary constellation is the explicit methodological articulation and institutionalisa
tion of design ambitions within mainstream research fields. In these domains, models 
are often employed not merely to analyse existing arrangements, but to propose,

significantly higher than that of Rodrik’s proposed empirical approach, which seeks to find a fit. It is possible 
that Rodrik is expressing a more widespread attitude towards models that is not so strongly reflected in presti
gious publications. Davis is not concerned with the question of whether economics successfully shapes the 
world, but instead with the transformation of ambition, thereby sidestepping M€aki’s criticism (M€aki 2013).

choice is always linked to a norm, a point already recognised by early proponents such as Savage (Sugden, 
1991). Herfeld demonstrates this shift in the thinking of other pioneers of the theory in the context of the

fully shapes the world, but instead with the transformation of ambition, thereby sidestepping M€aki’s criticism

14 F. BALLY-ROMMEL

construct, and stabilise specific institutional mechanisms under the presumption that 
certain theoretical properties should be realised in practice.

Davis identifies three prominent strands in which this orientation has developed, 
especially since the 1980s.

5.3.1. Game theory and the design of interaction
Game theory was initially developed within Economics 1.0 as part of the aspiration 
towards axiomatic foundations (Von Neumann et al. 1955). Over time, it became 
increasingly associated with the analysis and, in many cases, the design of strategic 
environments. In auctions, matching markets, and reputation systems, game-theoretic 
models not only describe strategic behaviour; they are often used to engineer inter
action rules that generate desired outcomes. In this sense, game theory can function 
as a design tool for institutional environments rather than merely as a descriptive 
framework (Alexandrova 2006; Nik-Khah 2008).

5.3.2. Behavioural economics and the design of decision contexts
While early behavioural research focused on identifying anomalies relative to stand
ard predictions, a growing share of behavioural economics has addressed the active 
design of choice environments. Here the emphasis shifts from describing how people 
do behave to shaping how they will behave under alternative “choice architectures.” 
The economist becomes, in Thaler’s and Sunstein’s language, a decision architect 
(Binmore and Shaked 2007; Binmore 2007; Davis 2017; Heukelom 2014; Thaler 
2016). Guala distinguishes between a mode of theory-testing in which experiments 
probe theoretical claims and a mode of institution-building in which behavioural rou
tines and decision environments are deliberately constructed (Guala et al. 2007).

5.3.3. Mechanism and market design
In mechanism and market design, the central objective is often not to explain existing 
markets but to construct allocation procedures and institutional rules. In the wake of 
information economics, markets are no longer treated as spontaneously efficient 
arrangements; they are understood as designs that can succeed or fail depending on 
informational and institutional conditions. Mechanism design and related fields pro
pose auctions, matching systems, certification schemes, and other institutional devices 
intended to achieve specified goals under clearly defined constraints (Backhouse and 
Cherrier 2017; Breslau 2013; Hurwicz 1973; Mackenzie 2008; Nik-Khah 2008).

Across these strands, the common feature is not “normativity” in the broad sense, 
but a performative orientation: theory is increasingly used as a means of shaping the 
world. This does not imply that the explanatory ambition disappears; rather, explan
ation and design become more tightly coupled. The methodological tension arises 
because the design stance can be presented as technically neutral while embedding 
normative commitments about desirable outcomes and legitimate institutional forms. 
Making these commitments explicit becomes part of the broader methodological 
challenge.



THE EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF THE HISTORY OF ECONOMIC THOUGHT 15

Davis warns that, without explicit methodological reflection, a design orientation 
may drift towards the maxim: “If one’s theory does not fit the world, work to remake 
the world fit one’s theory!” (Davis 2017, 5).4

Quantifying this orientation is difficult, since design ambitions are not always 
explicitly stated. Bibliometric evidence nonetheless indicates the growing prominence 
of market design and related fields (Fontana and Iori 2023). Together with behav
ioural and game-theoretic contributions that are explicitly oriented towards institu
tional design, the share of this performative–normative orientation can be 
conservatively estimated at roughly 15% to 25% of current research output.

6. Convergence and divergence in economic research

The three methodological orientations described above indicate a shift in the disci
pline’s self-understanding. Rather than converging on a single universal theory, eco
nomics increasingly operates with multiple forms of knowledge about different 
economic contexts. However, this development should not be mistaken for a smooth 
transition towards harmonious pluralism. The three orientations reconfigure the rela
tion between theory, empirics, and normativity in distinct ways, and their coexistence 
generates systematic tensions.

This chapter first identifies elements of a shared departure from the traditional 
methodological basic type (5.1). It then analyses the tensions between the three orien
tations (5.2) and finally condenses these tensions into two methodological paradoxes 
(5.3). The aim is not to declare the end of one paradigm and the arrival of another, 
but to clarify the structure of the current constellation.

6.1. A shared shift in methodological orientation

Taken together, the three orientations account for a substantial share of contempor
ary research output, as indicated by various bibliometric studies. While precise meas
urement remains difficult and dependent on classification choices, their institutional 
visibility and disciplinary recognition suggest that they can no longer be regarded as 
marginal developments.

More importantly than quantitative estimates is their shared departure from key 
features of the former methodological basic type:

� All three orientations qualify or abandon the claim of universal validity associated 
with Economics 1.0 and proceed in more context-sensitive ways.

� Design considerations enter research more directly, either as an explicit goal (in 
the performative–normative orientation) or as an implicit feature of empirical and 
modelling practices.

4 This observation is not only found among methodologists such as Davis, but also programmatically, for 
example, among the central pioneers of mechanism design: ‘the design problem is the “inverse” of traditional 
economic theory, which is typically devoted to the analysis of the performance of a given mechanism’ 
(Hurwicz and Reiter 2006, 3). In fact, the democratic legitimacy of mechanism design, for example, is also dis
cussed in economic journals and must be considered in detail in political processes.



16 F. BALLY-ROMMEL

� Multiple criteria of validity coexist, including internal consistency, empirical 
robustness, contextual relevance, and goal achievement.

� Issues such as inequality, institutional effectiveness, and behavioural feasibility 
increasingly stand alongside efficiency as central evaluative dimensions.

The most visible contrast to the traditional basic type appears in the identification- 
first orientation. Here, empirical credibility and causal inference take precedence over 
systematic theoretical integration. As Biddle and Hamermesh observe, “It is much 
less important today [ … ] to have one’s applied research grounded in economic the
ory and more important that one can demonstrate an explicit causal relation [ … ] 
Modelling the behaviour itself is no longer an essential part of many empirical articles 
in top journals” (Biddle and Hamermesh 2017, 25).

The performative–normative orientation, by contrast, often remains closely con
nected to classical theoretical tools. Yet it diverges from the former basic type by inte
grating institutional shaping and behavioural design into the research process itself. 
The focus on implementation implicitly recognises that economic arrangements can 
take multiple forms and that models may guide their construction. Importantly, this 
orientation does not uniformly implement a single theoretical ideal; in practice, it 
incorporates diverse objectives and institutional designs (Banerjee and Duflo 2019; 
Hurwicz and Reiter 2006; Roth 2002).

Across these orientations, elements of the former methodological type persist. Yet 
the aspiration towards a single, universally binding theoretical architecture no longer 
structures the discipline in the comprehensive way it once did. What emerges instead 
is a shared movement towards plural economic realities and multiple methodological 
commitments. However, this shared shift has not yet crystallised into a new, explicitly 
articulated methodological foundation. The orientations are linked in practice but are 
largely reflected upon in isolation from one another (Banerjee and Duflo 2019; Roth 
2002).

6.2. Methodological tensions

The model-portfolio, identification-first, and performative–normative orientations 
cannot be reduced to mere specialisations within a single framework. They rest on 
partly divergent assumptions about how knowledge is generated, what counts as valid, 
and how economics relates to normative goals. Their tensions can be described in 
terms of three relationships.

6.3. Relationship I: model selection vs model suspension

A first tension arises between the model-portfolio and identification-first orientations.
Proponents of the model portfolio treat theory as a flexible toolbox: different mod

els for different contexts, evaluated by contextual fit and explanatory usefulness. 
Empirical work serves primarily to guide model selection rather than to establish 
independent generalisations (Rodrik 2015). Positive knowledge becomes an expanding 
repertoire of models rather than a unified theoretical system.



THE EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF THE HISTORY OF ECONOMIC THOUGHT 17

Identification-first researchers, by contrast, prioritise causal inference through 
research design. Their work aims at credible estimation of specific effects, often with
out committing to a comprehensive structural model. Theory may inform hypotheses 
or interpretation, but it is not necessarily the organising core of the inquiry. This 
orientation, however, raises questions of external validity: findings may be robust 
within specific settings yet difficult to generalise across contexts.

Each orientation therefore raises questions about the epistemic standards of the other. 
Model-oriented scholars may regard highly localised findings as insufficiently integrated 
(Spiegler 2019), while identification-first researchers may regard flexible model use as 
insufficiently constrained by empirical discipline. The tension concerns not the legitimacy 
of either approach, but the relative priority of theoretical coherence versus empirical cred
ibility (Banerjee and Duflo 2019; Bowles and Gintis 2000; Matthews 2019; Rodrik 2015).

6.4. Relationship II: model flexibility vs normative embedding

A second tension appears between the model-portfolio and performative–normative 
orientations.

Both rely on formal modelling, but they differ in purpose. The model portfolio 
treats models primarily as explanatory instruments. Once a model clarifies mecha
nisms within a given context, normative implications may be discussed, but the posi
tive–normative distinction is typically maintained.

The performative–normative orientation, by contrast, employs models more dir
ectly in institutional design. Mechanism design, behavioural interventions, and stra
tegic architecture translate theoretical structures into institutional arrangements. In 
doing so, they inevitably embody normative assumptions about desirable outcomes, 
coordination, or behavioural standards.

This does not imply that design-oriented work is methodologically flawed. Rather, 
it highlights a difference in stance: explanatory flexibility versus intentional institu
tional embedding. The tension arises when normative commitments remain implicit 
while design practices are presented as purely technical.5 Clarifying these commit
ments becomes part of the broader methodological task.

6.5. Relationship III: empirical neutrality vs. performative effects

A third tension concerns the relation between empirical neutrality and performative 
intervention.

The identification-first orientation upholds an ideal of methodological neutrality 
grounded in credible identification and reproducibility. Yet empirical research often 
intervenes in the settings it studies. Randomised trials, natural experiments, and pol
icy evaluations may alter behaviour and institutions even as they observe them.

The performative–normative orientation acknowledges such intervention more expli
citly. Auctions, matching systems, incentive schemes, and behavioural architectures are 

5 For instance Rodrik’s (2015) call for pluralism contests the image of economics as inherently neoliberal 
(Rodrik 2017).



18 F. BALLY-ROMMEL

intentionally constructed. However, once implemented, these designs generate new 
empirical realities that reshape the conditions under which further research takes place.

From the standpoint of a strict positive–normative distinction, this complicates the 
ideal of detached observation. Even attempts at purely descriptive analysis can have 
performative effects insofar as they frame categories, incentives, and policy options. 
The object of economics is not independent of the theories and methods applied to 
it. This reflexive dimension has long been recognised in philosophy of science 
(Austin 1962) but has rarely been systematically integrated into economic method
ology (J. B. Davis and Klaes 2003).

6.6. Two methodological paradoxes

The coexistence of these orientations reveals deeper tensions that can be understood 
as paradoxes rather than simple contradictions. A contradiction implies mutual exclu
sion. A paradox expresses the coexistence of justified but opposing principles that 
cannot easily be reduced to one another. Two such paradoxes emerge in the current 
constellation: one epistemic and one performative.

6.6.1. The epistemic paradox: What counts as economic knowledge?
Under Economics 1.0, positive knowledge was ideally conceived as a coherent body 
of theory claiming universal scope. The newer orientations jointly qualify this aspir
ation. However, they do not replace it with a new shared definition of positive 
knowledge.

� The model portfolio expands the repertoire of models but does not provide a clear 
ordering principle among them.

� Identification-first research generates robust empirical findings, yet their context
ual nature raises questions about generalisation and theoretical integration.

� Performative–normative research selectively mobilises theoretical insights for 
design, thereby altering the institutional environments in which those insights 
operate.

The expansion of models, results, and design practices increases the volume of 
available knowledge, yet it raises new questions about its organisation, scope, and 
cumulative status. When does an empirical finding become part of economic know
ledge? How should context-bound models relate to one another? How can normative 
commitments be integrated without dissolving positive inquiry?

The discipline therefore faces not a shortage of knowledge, but a lack of explicit 
criteria for its systematic coordination.

6.6.2. The performative paradox: description and intervention
The second paradox concerns the relation between describing economic processes 
and shaping them.



THE EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF THE HISTORY OF ECONOMIC THOUGHT 19

Within the traditional self-understanding of Economics 1.0, economics explained 
mechanisms and informed normative debate. In the current constellation, explanation 
and intervention are more closely intertwined.

� Model selection frames economic problems in particular ways.
� Empirical research designs alter institutional settings while generating evidence or 

suggests to intervene in other contexts by establishing causalities.
� Performative–normative work explicitly constructs markets and behavioural 

architectures.

Science both describes and shapes its object. The more economics succeeds in 
influencing institutions and policy, the more it modifies the environments that future 
research will analyse. This reflexive dynamic cannot be eliminated. It can only be 
acknowledged and addressed.

6.6.3. Towards methodological reflexivity
The epistemic and performative paradoxes suggest that a simple return to a unified 
theoretical paradigm is neither feasible nor desirable. At the same time, unstructured 
pluralism risks incoherence.

What may be required is not a new universal theory, but a more reflexive meth
odological framework: one that integrates empirical precision, contextual modelling, 
and normative transparency. Such a framework would not suppress diversity but 
would make explicit the assumptions, scope conditions, and value commitments 
embedded in different research practices.

Recognising the performative dimension of economic inquiry does not undermine 
its scientific character. Rather, it invites a clearer articulation of how empirical evi
dence, modelling choices, and institutional design interact. In this sense, the current 
methodological fragmentation can be interpreted not merely as disintegration, but as 
a transitional constellation that opens space for renewed methodological reflection.

7. Conclusion

Economics is increasingly described as pluralistic or fragmented. At the same time, 
empirical studies of publication patterns continue to reveal strong institutional and con
ceptual concentration. This article has argued that this apparent contradiction can be 
resolved by shifting the level of analysis. The unity of the discipline in the post-war deca
des rested less on a fixed set of theoretical assumptions than on a shared methodological 
basic type that structured the relation between theory, empirics, and normativity.

Since the 1980s, this basic type has not disappeared; rather, it has been reinter
preted, qualified, and supplemented in various ways. The identification-first, model- 
portfolio, and performative-normative orientations cannot be fully accommodated 
within the former methodological architecture. Together, they signal a transformation 
at the methodological level.

This transformation does not amount to a simple and harmonious pluralisation. 
As Section 5 has shown, the coexistence of these orientations generates systematic 



20 F. BALLY-ROMMEL

tensions concerning the organisation of economic knowledge and the relation 
between description and intervention. These tensions are not merely institutional or 
sociological; they are methodological in nature.

At the same time, the parallel development of economic realities and economic 
research is striking. As economic institutions diversify and become increasingly 
shaped by informational, behavioural, and institutional design, economic theory 
and empirical practice respond with greater contextual sensitivity and performa
tive awareness. The pluralisation of economies and the pluralisation of economic 
methodology appear intertwined. The discipline no longer studies a single abstract 
“economy,” but a range of institutional configurations whose functioning depends 
on historically and socially specific conditions. This raises a question that goes 
beyond the diagnosis of fragmentation:

Can a new methodological basic type be articulated that acknowledges contextual 
plurality, empirical identification, and institutional design without collapsing into 
either theoretical monism or unstructured pluralism?

Such a framework would not replace diversity with a new universal theory. Rather, 
it would provide explicit criteria for coordinating different forms of knowledge and 
for reflecting on the performative effects of economic research itself. In this sense, the 
challenge is not to restore the unity of Economics 1.0, nor to celebrate fragmentation, 
but to develop a reflexive methodological orientation capable of integrating empirical 
precision, contextual modelling, and normative transparency. This could build on 
research focused on the reflexivity of economic agents (Davis 2024; Davis and Hands 
2018; Davis and Klaes 2003).

Whether such a framework will emerge remains an open question. What can be 
observed, however, is that the current constellation cannot be adequately described 
either as simple continuity or as complete rupture. It represents a transitional 
moment in which the discipline confronts its own plurality and its own performative 
power. Recognising the end of economics as we know it may be the first step towards 
a more self-aware and methodologically explicit economics as we want it.

Robust Portfolio Optimization with Respect to Spectral Risk
Measures Under Correlation Uncertainty

Man Yiu Tsang1 · Tony Sit1 · Hoi Ying Wong1

Accepted: 31 January 2022 / Published online: 7 June 2022
© The Author(s) 2022

Abstract
This paper proposes a distributionally robust multi-period portfolio model with ambi-
guity on asset correlations with fixed individual asset return mean and variance. The
correlation matrix bounds can be quantified via corresponding confidence intervals
based on historical data. We employ a general class of coherent risk measures namely
the spectral riskmeasure,which includes the popularmeasure conditional value-at-risk
(CVaR) as a particular case, as our objective function. Specific choices of spectral risk
measure permit flexibility for capturing risk preferences of different investors. A semi-
analytical solution is derived for our model. The prominent stochastic dual dynamic
programming (SDDP) algorithm adapted with intricate modifications is developed as
a numerical method under the discrete distribution setting. In particular, our new for-
mulation accounts for the unknownworst-case distribution in each iteration.We verify
the convergence property of this algorithm under the setting of finite scenarios. Our
results show that the optimal solution favours a certain degree of anti-diversification
due to dependence ambiguity and exhibits its protection ability during the financial
crisis period.

Keywords Investment analysis · Portfolio optimization · Correlation uncertainty ·
SDDP

Mathematics Subject Classification 91G10 · 90C15 · 62H20

1 Introduction

Markowitz’s [40] portfolio optimization model which advocates the idea of mean-risk
models in modern portfolio theory in 1952 and has received tremendous attention
since its proposal. This neat idea is influential upon which many subsequent and

B Tony Sit
tony.sit@cuhk.edu.hk

1 Department of Statistics, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shatin, N.T., Hong Kong

123



8 Page 2 of 29 Applied Mathematics & Optimization (2022) 86: 8

more sophisticated models are established, including models that incorporate various
practical constraints. For instance, constraints on transaction costs are imposed to
capture the costs in buying and selling the assets and constraints on maximum holding
proportion for each asset to cover the investor perference on risk diversification. A
summary of portfolio optimization models can be found in [6], for example. The role
of numerical optimization methods to solve these models has also been an active
research area. Instead of considering single-period models, a more realistic class of
multi-period models are studied as they take the complete investment horizon into
consideration with the possibility of adjusting one’s investment position at certain
times regularly. Under some specific settings, the multi-period problem can be solved
analytically (see, for example, [31] and [18]).

Risk measures and related theories have undergone rapid development in recent
years as attempts to incorporate the effect due to risk aversion on investment decision.
This consideration of risk measures has become more crucial after the 2008 financial
crisis, afterwhich investors have developed preference for robust portfolios. In addition
to the prevalent riskmeasure conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) discussed in [52], which
has been widely adopted in financial sector as required in Basel Accord III, a more
general class of riskmeasures, namely, the spectral riskmeasure, is proposed in [1] and
further discussed in [11] and [7] amongst others. This class includes some novel risk
measures in the literature such as second-order superquantile [51] and Gini-shortfall
[17]. Readers may also refer to [46] and [55] for relevant discussion on such risk
measures. In this paper, we focus on this general class of spectral risk measures under
which many different well-known risk measures are covered.

While the mean-variance model is convenient, variance is a symmetric measure of
volatility and it does not provide effective quantification for downside risk. In modern
portfolio theory, rational and prudent investors are cautious about downside losses at
the cost of sacrificing partially the upward potentials of the associated investments.
The use of alternative risk measures for portfolio models has become increasingly
attractive. An extensive amount of research effort has been devoted to construct imple-
mentable risk-averse portfolio models. Fundamental theories for mean-risk model are
developed in [53] and the context under portfolio optimization is discussed in [42].
Consideration of high-order conditional risk measures based upon the scenario gener-
ation method is recently investigated in [24] followed by [2] which extends the scope
to the use of entropic value-at-risk.

With the growing concerns for reliability of parameter estimation, distributionally
robust portfolio models are developed to protect investors from suffering tremendous
losses due to misspecification of model parameters (see [15]). Two types of uncer-
tainty set construction prevail in the literature, namely distance-type uncertainty and
moment-type uncertainty. For the former, it can be constructed using the empirical
distribution as the reference probability measure through specific metrics; a thorough
discussion usingWasserstein distance can be found in [5]. For the latter, moment infor-
mation from the observed data is captured. In this paper, we consider a multi-period
problemwith the objective function being theworst-case spectral riskmeasure, charac-
terized bymoment-type uncertainty. To bemore specific, themoment uncertainty set is
quantified by the estimated individual asset’s mean and variance while the correlation
is quantified by a specific interval, say for instance, a relevant confidence interval so

123



Applied Mathematics & Optimization (2022) 86: 8 Page 3 of 29 8

as to capture the model uncertainty. Unlike most of the papers on moment uncertainty
set that focus on an ellipsoidal set on the first two moments (see, for example, [9]),
the construction is relatively straight-forward. Ellipsoidal uncertainty set requires the
choice of the scale and shape parameters that are hard to interpret compared to the use
of confidence intervals. A recent discussion on a deliberate construction appears in
[38], which relies on estimates provided by experts. Moreover, the existing ellipsoidal
set cannot capture the correlation uncertainty between assets. A similar multi-period
portfolio problem with ellipsoidal uncertainty sets is investigated in [35] while the
single-period of the problem using CVaR objective is covered in [38]. In this line of
research, related works also include [30, 33, 34] and [36], amongst others.

The motivation of correlation ambiguity emerges from the concern about accuracy
in estimating correlation coefficients. It is inevitable that correlation affects investment
decisions tremendously. It is well known that obtaining accurate estimation of high-
dimensional correlation matrix is especially challenging. Also, through experiments,
[14] observed a lack of confidence in decision making under correlation uncertainty. It
implies that aversion towards correlation uncertainty inheres in the portfolio selection
process without which the resulting strategies tend to be mistakenly optimistic. Thus,
we are interested in the correlation ambiguity in portfolio models. Fouque et al. [16]
studied the situation with two risky assets and one risk-free asset in continuous-time
economy while the multiple-asset case in mean-variance framework is studied in [28].
[25] considered a single-period setting with normally distributed payoffs.

Multi-stage optimization is typically challenging. In the discrete setting, it is obvi-
ous that the number of scenarios grows exponentially as time proceeds. That is, if
we have N scenarios for each period, we would have NT scenarios over these T
periods, which is computationally intractable in general. Under the stagewise inde-
pendence assumption of the randomness, one can circumvent the problem with the
help of stochastic dual dynamic programming (SDDP) method, pioneered in [43].
The method is summarized and analyzed in [54] for the linear case and the risk averse
version is described in [56]. Recently, [23] proposed a variant for linear stochastic
programs with optimality cut selection steps to enhance computational efficiency. For
robust stochastic linear programs, [20] developed a robust version of SDDP, which
involves both upper and lower linear approximations of the recourse function. Time-
dependent variants could be found in [37] and [4]. The convergence proof of the
method for risk neutral and risk averse case in general convex setting appear in [21]
and [22], respectively.

In this paper, we consider a multi-period distributionally robust portfolio optimiza-
tion problemwith the spectral riskmeasure objective under correlation ambiguity. The
use of spectral risk measure permits flexibility on preferences from different investors.
Our numerical method under discrete setting is considered with historical scenarios.
In this area of active research, [26] investigated the risk neutral case with l∞ uncer-
tainty set while [47] studied the one with l2 uncertainty set. Duque et al. [12] discussed
the use of Wasserstein distance ambiguity set in linear stochastic programs with con-
vergence analysis. To the best of our knowledge, multi-period portfolio optimization
problem with moment-type uncertainty set has not been investigated in the literature.
Moment information crucial to investors, such as the mean and variance of random

123



8 Page 4 of 29 Applied Mathematics & Optimization (2022) 86: 8

returns, can be captured explicitly while it is difficult to capture correlation ambiguity
via distance-type uncertainty set formulations.

The contribution of this paper is three-fold. First, we obtain a semi-analytical solu-
tion for the problem, which exploits the explicit formula of worst-case risk measures
presented in [32]. Different from [35], our model works with general spectral risk
measures and we include the no short-selling constraint in our model. This is a real-
istic assumption since short selling is not always allowed. Moreover, the worst-case
distribution cannot be obtained analytically as in their formulation. Despite all the
complexities, our solution can still be computed efficiently via interior-point meth-
ods. Second, to incorporate the support of return vectors, we apply the scenario-based
approach to our problem and propose a variant of SDDP to solve, which considers
the moment-type uncertainty set in the form of correlation ambiguity. This numerical
method can incorporate lower bounds for the random return vectors via the generated
scenarios. The use of SDDP in distributionally robust optimization using l2 distance
appeared recently in [47] and has been investigated in other contexts. We provide the
convergence proof of our proposed algorithm, which extends the previous works [21]
and [22] to the distributionally robust context. In the numerical experiment, our for-
mulation performs better than the l2 formulation in the 2008 crisis during which the
market experienced structural changes. Our model with correlation uncertainty set can
provide amore secured decision if the correlation structure of the assets changes signif-
icantly. Third, we observe that the use approximation of spectral function introduced
in [57] can be potentially useful under the distributionally robust situation in the sense
that the computational time per iteration would reduce with a reasonable marginal
error in optimal value. It is noteworthy that although formulation is developed under
a portfolio optimization framework, the algorithm and the theoretical results can be
readily extended to a more general setting with linear constraints, which can be read-
ily modified to cover applications such as operation planning problem in [55] and
inventory problem in [3].

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows: Sect. 2 introduces the problem,
including the notion of spectral risk measures and construction of uncertainty set. A
semi-analytic solution is derived in Sect. 3. Section 4 discusses the method to obtain
worst-case distribution under uncertainty based on discrete setting, which would be
used in the numerical SDDPmethod. The convergence of themethodwould be verified
in Sect. 5. Some computational results are demonstrated in Sect. 6 and the paper is
concluded in Sect. 7. All the proofs are provided in the Supplementary material.

3 Semi-analytical Solution

In this section, we derive a semi-analytical solution for problem (1) with uncertainty
set (4). An explicit solution is difficult to obtain due to the constraint xt ≥ 0. The
problem without such a constraint and with a different construction of the uncertainty
set has been studied by [35]. Their uncertainty set formulation as some ellipsoidal
set is not compatible with the one we consider (see Remark 3). Our formulation
explicitly addresses correlation ambiguity,whichnaturally emerges in decisionmaking
processes. Also, our model incorporates the practical no short-selling constraints.
These complicate the analysis but the solution obtained can be efficiently computed.
To obtain the solution, we first derive the worst-case spectral risk measure formula.

4 The Numerical AlgorithmUnder Practical Setting

The solution we obtain from the previous section is based on Ω n
t = R . Although it

is common in the literature (see, for example, [35] and [38]), this may not be realistic
for the following reasons. First, the price ratio vector r t has a natural lower bound of
0. It is natural to impose the constraint of r t ≥ 0 almost surely. In particular, r t = 0
corresponds to a total loss for the investment. Second, it is natural to restrict the support
of the return vector r t on a compact domain. For instance, if r t represents the daily
return, it would be realistic that r t would not deviate a lot from 1. Thus, with a more
confined support, this may avoid over-conservative investment strategy.

However, in the presence of the support information, tractable reformulation of the
worst-case risk measure may not be possible. For instance, in [13], they only provide
an upper bound for a single-period portfolio optimization problem. In particular, for
moment-based ambiguity set, the reformulation of theworst-case expectation typically
results in a semi-infinite program and may require specialized numerical algorithm
such as cutting-plane methods to solve (see, for example, [9, 19, 39] and [41]).

A commonway to handle the situation that we do not have a tractable reformulation,
in distributionally robust optimization literature, is through discrete scenarios and this
has been successfully employed in various applications (see, for example, [8, 27, 44,
47] and [58]). Our work is the first to address the multi-period portfolio optimization
under correlation uncertainty with scenario-based approach and we propose a variant
of SDDP to solve the problem. Specifically, we assume that Ωt = {ω1, . . . , ωNt } and
consider the uncertainty set of the form

{ ∣∣∑N ∑ }
Pd= p ∈ N ∣

R ∣ N ∑N
∣ pi=1, pi r i=μ, Σ ≤ pi (r i−μ)(r i−μ)ᵀ≤Σ ,
i=1 i=1 i=1

(10)

where Σ = σᵀCσ , Σ = σᵀCσ and r i correspond to the return scenarios for i ∈
{1, . . . , N }.

Although it may not be realistic to consider Ωt = n
R , the semi-analytical solution

derived, which could be obtained efficiently, serves as a valid upper bound when we
have support information. It also provides us a way to verify our numerical method
proposed. In the following two sections, we discuss and analyze a numerical method
that can solve the problem under Pd. In Sect. 4.1, we first discuss our methodology
to obtain the worst-case distribution, which will be useful in a part of the proposed
numerical method in Sect. 4.2.
