at the longer horizons especially for the longer maturity bond correlations. 

6. The difference in wavelet-based correlation across sub-periods 

Fig. 2 Panels A.1-A.2 and B.1-B.2 compare the wavelet-based stock and 2-year and 10-year bond returns correlation during con
tractions and expansions for the developed and emerging markets, respectively. Panel A presents the results for developed markets and 
shows that a negative correlation is evident in most of the markets at all the time-scales during recessions. For expansionary periods, 
there is greater evidence of a positive correlation, although for some markets, the evidence is more mixed. This includes for the UK and 
US, for which the predominant evidence is of a negative correlation. These finding are broadly consistent across bond maturity, 
although there is greater evidence of a positive correlation during expansions with the 10-year bond. In contrast, the results in Panel B, 
suggest that correlation are positive for emerging markets in both contractionary and expansionary periods. Although for Greece there 
is notable evidence of a negative correlation during an expansion. 

The evidence of a negative correlation during a recession for most of the developed markets is consistent with a flight-to-safety 
argument. For example, Baele et al. (2020), who use daily stock and bond data, find that flight-to-safety events are country specific 
and tend to coincide with increases in implied volatility, the TED spread and decreases in consumer sentiment indicators. Our evidence 
for a negative correlation in developed, but not emerging markets, appears consistent with this argument. A further explanation is the 
resilience of emerging markets, notably to the global financial crisis, which results in a smaller flight-to-safety, and the higher GDP

7. Portfolio risk management 

Several studies indicate the importance of considering the wavelet decomposition in risk management (see, for example, Fer
nandez, 2005; Rua and Nunes, 2012; Mensi et al., 2018; Meng and Huang, 2019). Following these studies, we use value-at-risk (VaR), 
as a well-known risk management measurement, to examine the performance of stock and bond portfolios across time-scales. Spe
cifically, VaR shows the maximum loss of a portfolio at a pre-determined confidence level over a given period of time. The VaR of a 
portfolio comprising n number of assets at the (1-α) confidence level can be given by: 

VaR = I0ϕ− 1(1 − α)σP (8)  

Where I0 relates to the value of the portfolio, ϕ(.) is the standard normal-based cumulative distribution function and σP is the standard 
deviation of the portfolio return. For a portfolio consisting one stock and one government bond (n = 2), the variance can be calculated 
as follows: 

∑n ∑n
σ2

p = ω2

j + 2.ωiωjcov(ri, rj) (9)

Where ωi and ωj are the weights of the stock and bond in the portfolio respectively, σ2
i and σ2

j are their corresponding estimated return 
variances and cov(ri, rj) is the covariance between the returns of the two assets. 

To illustrate the role of time-scales within risk management, we calculate the portfolio variance and return using a 40/60 (stock/ 
bond) weighting.4 In examining the effect of wavelet analysis on VaR, we follow Meng and Huang (2019) and Mensi et al. (2018), 
among others. Specifically, we first estimate the VaR at a given time-scale assuming no co-movement (i.e., cov(ri, rj) =0) between stock 
and bond returns. Second, we estimate the correlation and thus allow it to take a non-zero value. To examine the effect of co-movement 
at each time-scale, we calculate the ratio of VaR without the zero restriction (henceforth, VaRc) to that with the zero correlation 
restriction, VaRu. Thus, we can test whether estimating the correlation across different time-scales affects the VaR estimate at each 
scale, such that if the VaRc

VaR ratio is less (more) than one, the portfolio incorporating the time-varying corelation improves performance 
u 

over the zero correlation portfolio. 
Table 3 reports the VaR ratios for portfolios comprising the 10-year bonds along with the stock returns.5 Again, the analysis is 

performed over expansionary and contractionary periods. Several interesting observations are revealed in the table. First, the VaR 
deviates from one in almost all markets regardless of the market state meaning that stock-bond co-movement affects the portfolio loss 
both over the sample and across the time-scales. Second, the VaR ratios are generally less during expansions relative to recessions, 
although there are exceptions to this, notably for the emerging markets as well as Australia and Portugal. Third, the VaR ratios decrease 
at longer frequencies and this is clearly evident at time-scales five and six.6 For example, the ratio is smallest at the 64− 128 days 
horizon during expansions for 12 countries (Australia, Austria, Belgium, Ireland, Japan, Spain, Sweden, Norway, Greece, Hungary and 
Czech Republic). Moreover, the VaR ratio is also at the lowest level for the horizon of 32− 64 during expansions for Canada, Denmark, 
Finland, Italy, New Zealand, UK, South Africa and Poland. For recessionary periods, the lowest ratio tends to be found at the 32− 64 
time-scale across the majority of the countries. 

8. Summary and conclusion 

Understanding the nature of the stock and bond correlation is important given the key role it plays in portfolio formation. While this 
relation receives a large degree of attention in the literature, we contribute by, primarily, examining how the correlation varies over 
time-scales using a Wavelet approach. Further, we contribute by considering the correlation for 25 developed and emerging markets 
and using three bond maturities over the period from 1991 to 2016, whereas exiting research typically focuses on a more limited set of 
markets.

recessionary periods, with the difference lower for the correlation involving the 10-year bond return compared with bonds at higher 
maturities. Our analysis for the correlation across time-scales documents that developed market correlations are generally negative at 
the first time-scale but move in a positive direction at longer time-scales (although often insignificantly so). In contrast, for emerging 
markets, the correlation is positive even at the first time-scale. In addition, we find more evidence for flight-to-safety behaviour during 
recessions for developed markets compared to emerging markets. A key element of the correlation relates to portfolio management. 
We, therefore, examine the ability of the wavelet correlations to improve VaR modelling. Our results indicate VaR improvement across 
time-scales with the wavelet correlations, with the decrease in portfolio loss at the highest time-scales of 32− 64 and 64− 128 days. 

The results in this paper should enable both investors and regulators to better understand the interrelation between stock returns 
and government bond return and the changes over different time horizons. Notably the results reveal the nature of changing corre
lations across time-scales and that it can improve portfolio risk performance.

Yuancheng Si* and Saralees Nadarajah

From Close-to-Open to Open-to-Close: 
Multifractal Signatures and Cross-Scale 
Dependence Across International Equity 
Indices
https://doi.org/10.1515/snde-2025-0052
Received April 18, 2025; accepted January 13, 2026; published online February 23, 2026

Abstract: Using daily data for major global equity indices over 2010–2025, this study decomposes close-to-
close price changes into an overnight opening gap (diffrate) and an within-session return (intradayrate), and 
quantifies their multiscale structure using Multifractal Detrended Moving Average analysis (MFDMA) and 
Multifractal Detrended Cross-Correlation Analysis (MF-DCCA). We document three robust patterns. First, the 
overnight component is typically more persistent and more heterogeneous: MFDMA estimates show higher 
h(2) and larger multifractality proxies for diffrate in most markets, consistent with information accumulation 
and cross-market spillovers being compressed into a single opening price-discovery event. Second, intraday 
and overnight dynamics are nontrivially coupled: within-index MF-DCCA yields cross-Hurst exponents centered 
around h xy (2) ≈ 0.49, and the cross-exponent declines monotonically as q increases, indicating tighter coupling 
in calm regimes than during extreme co-movements. Third, international comovement is stronger in opening 
gaps than in intraday returns, suggesting that global information is synchronized primarily at the open, while 
continuous trading reflects more local microstructure and liquidity conditions. Clustering based on multifractal 
signatures further reveals richer regime heterogeneity overnight than intraday.

Keywords: multifractal detrended fluctuation analysis; stock indices; market efficiency

JEL Classification: G15; C50; C02

1 Background Introduction

The overnight price differential rate, also known as overnight return, denoted diffrate, measures the percentage 
gap between today’s opening price and yesterday’s closing price (Cheema et al. 2022; Weißofner and Wessels 
2020; Branch and Ma 2012; Si and Nadarajah 2024). It reflects how markets process information that accumu-
lates outside trading hours, so the sign can flip with the tone of news flow: optimistic developments can push 
the opening print upward as buy-side quotes adjust, while adverse signals can pull it downward as sell-side 
liquidity becomes more concessionary. The same logic applies at the single-stock level, yet aggregation to an 
index produces a broader gauge of cross-sectional repricing and day-to-day market mood. While overnight 
price differentials have been examined from multiple empirical perspectives, much of the existing evidence 
relies on single-scale summaries or treats overnight and intraday returns either in isolation or as mechanically

2 — Y. Si and S. Nadarajah: Multifractal Structure of Overnight and Intraday Returns

linked components of the daily return. This study takes a different perspective by treating the overnight gap 
and the subsequent intraday adjustment as distinct but potentially interacting processes, and by focusing on 
how their statistical properties and interdependence vary across time scales. By adopting a multifractal and 
cross-multifractal framework, the analysis emphasizes scale-dependent structure and coupling mechanisms 
that are not captured by conventional persistence or average-dependence measures (Weißofner and Wessels 
2020; Cheema et al. 2022; Si et al. 2024a, 2024b; Si and Nadarajah 2025).

The Efficient Market Hypothesis (EMH) argues that prices incorporate available information (Fama 1970). 
Within this framework, diffrate is useful as a screening statistic for unusual opening behavior and near-term 
sentiment shifts (Weißofner and Wessels 2020), but interpretation is not always clean because multiple chan-
nels can load onto the same opening gap. The main drivers span macro releases such as policy rates or GDP 
(Jiang and Zhu 2017; Tetlock 2010), firm-specific disclosures such as earnings (Avishay et al. 2024; Tetlock 2010), 
shifts in trading activity (Li et al. 2021), external shocks such as political tension (Chi et al. 2012; Guo et al. 2017), 
and liquidity conditions at the open (Tetlock 2010). A practical identification problem follows naturally: where 
does the boundary lie between gaps that primarily reflect new information and gaps that are largely shaped by 
opening-auction frictions and microstructure noise in the first prints?

Empirical evidence on the link between diffrate and intraday returns is mixed and appears market-
dependent. Using U.S. equities over 1994–2010, larger diffrate is often followed by lower intraday returns (Branch 
and Ma 2012). Related findings and trading implications have been reported for commodities and for the 
Ukrainian market (Plastun et al. 2019; Plastun et al. 2020; Caporale and Plastun 2017). For China, A-share index 
data over 1990–2023 support several mechanisms, and trading tests indicate that diffrate contains predictive con-
tent for intraday returns (Si and Nadarajah 2024). Evidence based on U.S. data also points to lower risk and useful 
trend forecasts in models that exploit the overnight component (Liu and Tse 2017), while other China-based evi-
dence stresses fast post-open reversals and hence limited predictive power in some settings (Cheema et al. 2022). 
At the firm level, diffrate has been linked to sentiment measures constructed from financial and stock variables 
(Weißofner and Wessels 2020).

At the index level, diffrate aggregates sectoral and market-wide conditions, which tends to smooth idiosyn-
cratic moves and yield a steadier signal (Lo 1991). For single stocks, the same statistic can react sharply to firm-
specific news (Si et al. 2024b). This difference matters for forecasting applications: adding diffrate can improve 
volatility forecasts for indices but not necessarily for individual names (Ahoniemi and Lanne 2013). At the same 
time, large constituents can dominate index-level gaps, and index moves can feed back into stock responses 
within sectors, so the interaction between cross-level effects and intraday return formation remains open and 
warrants careful separation of aggregation from mechanism.

The relation between intraday and overnight returns has long been studied in market microstructure, and 
several strands of evidence point to different dynamics across the trading day (Branch and Ma 2012). Work on 
intraday patterns highlights nonlinearity and concentration of volatility near the open and close (Hong and 
Wang 2000), while complementary evidence shows that overnight returns are often reversed by subsequent 
intraday returns, with weaker reversal in the other direction (Stoll and Whaley 1990). One behavioral channel 
that has been proposed is corporate insider selling, which may contribute to these reversals by shaping post-open 
trading pressure (Inci et al. 2010).

Risk-based and behavioral explanations both appear in the literature, and the balance between them is 
still debated. A discontinuity-based view emphasizes compensation for jump-related risk, with evidence of a 
substantial premium associated with discontinuous intraday and overnight returns (Bollerslev et al. 2016). A 
related return-dynamics perspective reports persistent firm-level continuation across intraday and overnight 
periods, together with cross-period reversal that can persist for years (Lou et al. 2015). In settings where val-
uation is difficult, sentiment has also been linked to mispricing, with underperformance for stocks with high 
overnight returns and outperformance for those with low overnight returns (Aboody et al. 2018).

Asset-specific studies further illustrate how the overnight–intraday split can vary across markets. Evi-
dence from the COMEX gold front-month contract and the SPDR Gold Share ETF over 1985–2012 shows strongly 
positive overnight returns and negative intraday returns for the former, with the asymmetry persisting over 
time (Blose et al. 2018). Cross-sectional evidence suggests that about 20 % of examined stocks display positive 
and statistically significant abnormal overnight returns, which is consistent with exploitable pricing biases



Y. Si and S. Nadarajah: Multifractal Structure of Overnight and Intraday Returns — 3

in some cases (Lachance 2015). In the Japanese REIT market, significant positive abnormal intraday returns 
followed by negative overnight reversals have been attributed to investor heterogeneity between domestic and 
overseas traders (Chen and Kawaguchi 2018). Similar reversal patterns have been documented for U.S. ETFs 
and international index futures, together with lower volatility in overnight returns than in intraday returns 
(Liu and Tse 2017).

Not all results point in the same direction. Evidence from U.S. equity indices over January 3, 1994, to January 
3, 2014, finds no pervasive intraday or overnight effects in a statistical sense (Monteiro and Manso 2017). At the 
same time, predictability can be stronger in narrower segments, with enhanced forecasting power reported for 
open-to-open returns in small, high-momentum stocks relative to close-to-close measures (Semenov 2015). Taken 
together, these findings underscore that overnight–intraday dynamics can reflect a mixture of efficiency, risk 
compensation, and trading frictions, and they motivate a design that keeps the two components analytically 
distinct.

Considering sample validity and data availability, this study analyzes opening price differential rates and 
intraday returns for 24 major global stock indices from January 2010 to January 2025, using daily data to capture 
stock market behaviors. The selected indices are: SSE Composite Index (China), DAX (Germany), CAC40 (France), 
Nikkei 225 (Japan), KOSPI (South Korea), Hang Seng Index (Hong Kong, China), DJIA (United States), NASDAQ 
Composite (United States), S&P 500 (United States), SENSEX (India), S&P/ASX 200 (Australia), S&P/TSX Composite 
(Canada), SET Index (Thailand), FTSE MIB (Italy), MOEX Russia Index (Russia), IBEX 35 (Spain), SMI (Switzerland), 
WINDALLA (China,Wind All A Index), CSI 300 (China), SZSE Component Index (China), VN-Index (Vietnam), Rus-
sell 3000 (United States), DFM General Index (United Arab Emirates), and STI (Singapore). These indices cover 
major regions, including Asia-Pacific, Europe, North America, and selected emerging markets, and they reflect 
heterogeneity in market capitalization and trading ecosystems.

The FTSE 100 Index (United Kingdom) is excluded due to microstructural and data considerations that make 
its opening gaps less informative for the present objective. In contrast to indices whose opening prints can 
move sharply in response to overnight information, the FTSE 100, compiled by FTSE Russell, often shows high 
continuity between the daily opening and the prior close because of its calculation and opening-auction setting

relate to intraday returns across venues. The information above reflects statistics as of early 2025 and may

2 Methods

Complex systems typically combine nonlinear deterministic mechanisms with stochastic perturbations, so their 
observed signals are rarely well described by a single-scale, stationary paradigm. In many empirical settings – 
including financial markets, communication networks, and biological regulation – the data exhibit 
scale-dependent fluctuation structures, persistent dependence, intermittent bursts, and pronounced nonsta-
tionarity. These features motivate fractal and multifractal approaches, which provide a principled way to 
characterize scaling regularities while remaining robust to slow trends and structural changes (Cao et al. 2013; 
Alvarez-Ramirez et al. 2009).

In this study, our objective is not only to quantify the multifractal properties of individual return compo-
nents, but also to examine the scale-dependent coupling between intraday and overnight dynamics. To this end, 
we adopt Multifractal Detrended Cross-Correlation Analysis (MFDCCA) to investigate the joint behavior of intra-
dayrate and overnightrate. Unlike single-series multifractal tools, MFDCCA is explicitly designed to detect and 
quantify long-range cross-correlations under nonstationarity across a continuum of scales and moment orders. 
This is essential for financial time series, where the linkage between intraday price discovery and overnight 
revaluation may be weak at one horizon yet pronounced at another, and where co-movement is often driven 
by heterogeneous market participants and intermittent information arrivals. MFDCCA therefore allows us to 
move beyond average correlation measures by providing a multifractal description of cross-dependence, cap-
turing whether extreme co-fluctuations dominate the linkage and how the dependence structure evolves across 
temporal aggregation levels.

For the marginal characterization of each component series, we employ the Multifractal Detrending Moving 
Average (MFDMA) method to estimate generalized Hurst exponents and multifractal spectra for intradayrate and 
overnightrate separately. MFDMA replaces polynomial detrending with a scale-dependent moving-average filter, 
which is advantageous when the underlying trend is not well approximated by low-order polynomials or when 
boundary effects and local regime shifts are prominent. In practice, return series – particularly those derived 
from market open/close mechanisms – may contain sparse extreme realizations, volatility clustering, and slow-
moving background variations; in such circumstances, the moving-average detrending embedded in MFDMA 
can provide a more stable separation between low-frequency components and scale-dependent fluctuations. 
This choice is also consistent with the broader goal of producing estimates that are comparable across indices 
and robust to moderate deviations from idealized assumptions.

We do not rely on Multifractal Detrended Fluctuation Analysis (MFDFA) Method as the primary marginal 
estimator for two considerations. First, the polynomial detrending step in MFDFA introduces an additional 
modelling choice (the polynomial order) that may materially affect estimated scaling when the data contain



6 — Y. Si and S. Nadarajah: Multifractal Structure of Overnight and Intraday Returns

local irregularities, abrupt changes, or complex low-frequency components that are not well represented by a 
fixed-order polynomial across all segments. Second, for return measures that may include discretization effects, 
zero-inflation, or occasional near-constant blocks, the fluctuation aggregation in negative moment orders can 
become numerically fragile under segment-wise variance estimates, potentially amplifying small-scale arti-
facts and obscuring economically meaningful scaling patterns. Against this background, the combined use of 
MFDCCA for cross-series scaling dependence and MFDMA for marginal multifractal characterization offers a 
coherent framework to study both the joint dynamics between intradayrate and overnightrate and the inter-
nal multiscale structure of each series under realistic nonstationarity (Gu and Zhou 2010; Cao et al. 2013; 
Alvarez-Ramirez et al. 2009).

2.1 Multifractal Detrending Moving Average Analysis (MFDMA) Method

The Multifractal Detrending Moving Average (MFDMA) method extends the detrending moving average (DMA) 
framework to quantify multifractal scaling in non-stationary time series by replacing polynomial detrending 
with a scale-dependent moving average (Gu and Zhou 2010). In contrast to MFDFA, which removes trends via 
segment-wise polynomial fits, MFDMA defines the local trend through a sliding-window average controlled by 
a position parameter, thereby providing a flexible detrending mechanism that can incorporate past, centered, 
or future information. Consider a time series {x k , k = 1, 2, … , N} of length N with non-vanishing values on its 
support, i.e. x k = 0 holds only for an empty set.

2.2 Multifractal Detrended Cross-Correlation Analysis (MFDCCA)

To complement the single-series multifractal analysis using MFDFA method, we also apply multifractal 
detrended cross-correlation analysis (MFDCCA) to quantify how multifractal features are shared across time 
series. The method extends the detrended fluctuation framework to a bivariate setting and provides a scale-
dependent measure of cross-correlation. In our application, the two series can represent the Opening Price 
Difference Rate (Diffrate) and Intraday Rate (Intradayrate) for the same index, or intraday returns for two dif-
ferent indices. This design allows us to compare the internal linkage between overnight and intraday dynamics 
with the cross-market linkage among indices.

Step 5: Scaling relation and cross-Hurst exponents 
If the two time series exhibit scale-invariant cross-correlations, the fluctuation function follows a power-law 

relationship with the time scale: 
F x y (q, s) ∼ sh x  y ( q ) for each q. (9)

Taking logarithms yields a linear relation,

log F x y (q, s) = h x y (q) log s + C q , (10)

where C q is a constant depending on q. For each q, the cross-Hurst exponent hx y (q) is estimated as the slope of 
the regression of log F xy (q, s) on log s over the chosen range of scales. A value hx y (q) > 0.5 indicates persistent 
long-range cross-correlation at order q, while hx y (q) < 0.5 suggests anti-persistent cross-correlation.

The exponent at q = 2, denoted hx y (2), is directly comparable to the usual Hurst exponent and plays a 
central role in the empirical analysis. It summarises the strength of cross-correlation in typical fluctuations and 
is reported as the main indicator in the tables and heatmaps. The full function hx y (q), however, is still retained 
to capture the multifractal nature of the interaction, and its dispersion over q is used as a simple measure of 
multifractal strength.

Step 6: Multifractal cross-correlation and spectrum width
For a purely monofractal cross-correlation structure, the cross-Hurst exponent does not vary with q, and 

h xy (q) collapses to a constant. In contrast, a pronounced dependence of hx y (q) on q signals multifractal cross-
correlation, meaning that large and small fluctuations exhibit different scaling properties.

To quantify this behavior in a way that is consistent with the single-series analysis, we compute the width 
of the cross-Hurst spectrum for each pair of series,

Δh x y = max h x y (q) − min h x y (q). (11)
q q

A larger value of Δhx y indicates stronger heterogeneity in the scaling of cross-correlations across fluctuation 
sizes. In the empirical sections, this width is reported alongside h xy (2) for both within-index pairs (Diffrate versus 
Intradayrate of the same index) and cross-index pairs (Intradayrate of two different indices). This choice keeps 
the interpretation aligned with the MFDFA results, where the width of the multifractal spectrum serves as a key 
indicator of multifractality.

In the within-index analysis, {X t } and {Y t } represent the Opening Price Difference Rate and Intraday Rate 
of the same stock index. The resulting hx y (q) curves describe how strongly the overnight revaluation and the 
subsequent intraday adjustment are linked across time scales and fluctuation magnitudes. In the cross-index 
analysis, both series are intraday returns from two different indices. The method then reveals how multifractal 
cross-correlations propagate across markets, and whether extreme co-movements differ from the behavior seen 
in moderate fluctuations.

3 Exploratory Data Analysis

This section presents an exploratory analysis of the opening price difference rates (diffrate) and intraday returns 
(intradayrate) for major global stock indices, spanning from January 2010 to February 2025. The diffrate is 
defined as the percentage change between the opening price of a given trading day and the closing price of 
the previous trading day, calculated as follows:

diffrate = Open Price − Previous Close × 100 (12)
Previous Close 

The intradayrate represents the percentage change from the opening price to the closing price within the 
same trading day, expressed as:

Close Price − Open Price
intradayrate = × 100 (13)

Open Price



10 — Y. Si and S. Nadarajah: Multifractal Structure of Overnight and Intraday Returns

A methodological choice that deserves clarification is our use of simple percentage returns rather than 
logarithmic returns. Log returns are often preferred in asset-pricing settings because they are additive over time 
under continuous compounding and provide a convenient approximation when returns are small. However, 
these advantages are not central to the questions studied here, which focus on the market-open revaluation com-
ponent (diffrate) and the within-session price discovery component (intradayrate) at the daily frequency. Our 
primary objects of interest are economically interpretable price changes that map directly to observed open and 
close prices and that preserve the natural decomposition of a daily move into an overnight gap and an intraday 
adjustment. Using simple percentage returns keeps this decomposition transparent: the quantities correspond 
to the percentage difference that practitioners report and that is directly relevant for trading constraints, margin 
calculations, and loss accounting.

Moreover, the present dataset spans multiple markets with heterogeneous price levels, trading frictions, 
and occasional large moves, for which the transformation ln(1 + r) may not be safe enough. When returns are 
non-negligible, ln(1 + r) compresses positive extremes and amplifies negative outcomes asymmetrically, thereby 
altering tail behavior and potentially changing the relative weight of large versus small fluctuations. Since our 
subsequent multifractal procedures (MFDMA and MF-DCCA) explicitly interrogate how fluctuation magnitudes 
contribute to scaling across q-orders, imposing a nonlinear transformation that reshapes the distribution may 
confound the interpretation of multifractality as an intrinsic property of the market process rather than an 
artefact of the return mapping. This concern is particularly salient when comparing indices with very differ-
ent volatility profiles and when the sample includes stress episodes in which daily percentage moves are not 
uniformly small.

Finally, while log returns are additive across time, the analysis in this paper is not based on long-horizon 
temporal aggregation of single-series returns. Instead, it is organized around a two-component decomposition 
and a cross-series linkage: we examine how the overnight gap co-moves with the subsequent intraday adjust-
ment across scales and fluctuation regimes. For this purpose, the economic meaning of the original percentage 
change is more directly aligned with the mechanism under study, whereas log transformation would introduce 
an additional layer of curvature that is orthogonal to the market microstructure interpretation. For robust-
ness, we verify in supplementary analysis that the main qualitative patterns are not driven by the choice of 
return definition, but we retain simple returns as the baseline specification to maintain interpretability and 
comparability across indices.

Descriptive statistics for intradayrate data, presented in Table 3, show mean intraday returns ranging from 
−0.0860 % (SENSEX) to 0.1053 % (WINDALLA). Most indices exhibit means close to zero, suggesting no strong 
directional bias in intraday price movements on average. Notable exceptions include the SSE Composite Index 
and WINDALLA, with slightly positive means (0.0967 % and 0.1053 %, respectively), and the SENSEX and SET 
Index, with slightly negative means (−0.0860 % and −0.0597 %, respectively). Standard deviations vary from 
0.6560 % (STI) to 1.9669 % (PFTS Index), indicating diverse levels of intraday volatility across markets. Extreme 
values are evident, such as the PFTS Index with a minimum of −18.4651 % and a maximum of 47.3477 %, though 
these are outliers. Missing data are present, with the DFM General Index having the highest number of missing 
observations (959), potentially affecting the reliability of statistics for certain indices.

Descriptive statistics for diffrate data, representing overnight price differentials, are provided in Table 4. 
Mean diffrates are generally small, ranging from −0.0877 % (SSE Composite Index) to 0.1348 % (SENSEX). Inter-
estingly, the SSE Composite Index shows a negative mean (−0.0877 %), suggesting a tendency for overnight price 
declines, whereas the SENSEX exhibits a positive mean (0.1348 %), indicating overnight price increases. Standard 
deviations, ranging from 0.0183 % (FTSE100) to 0.8782 % (IBEX 35), are typically lower than those for intraday 
rates, reflecting reduced volatility during non-trading hours. However, indices like the IBEX 35 and VN-Index 
show higher overnight variability (SDs of 0.8782 % and 0.7020 %, respectively). Missing data remain a concern, 
particularly for the DFM General Index (959) and PFTS Index (569), which may limit the robustness of these 
estimates.

The descriptive statistics reported in Tables 3 and 4 indicate that both intradayrate and diffrate are cen-
tered near zero for most indices, yet they differ markedly in dispersion, tail behavior, and data completeness 
across markets. This heterogeneity suggests that the information embedded in opening gaps and the subsequent 
intraday adjustment are unlikely to be linked through a single, time-invariant dependence measure. From a 
market microstructure perspective, diffrate summarizes the overnight revaluation driven by news arrivals and 
the transmission of foreign-market movements when the local market is closed, whereas intradayrate reflects 
within-session price discovery under evolving liquidity and order-flow conditions. The interaction between 
these two components may therefore be scale-dependent, intermittent, and sensitive to fluctuation magnitudes, 
especially in markets where extremes and missingness are non-negligible. Standard correlation or regression 
diagnostics, which aggregate dependence into a single second-moment quantity and implicitly assume stable 
dependence, are not well suited to this setting. To quantify whether overnight gaps and same-day returns co-
move systematically across temporal scales, and to distinguish the coupling of small fluctuations from that of 
large co-movements, we employ Multifractal Detrended Cross-Correlation Analysis (MF-DCCA) as the core tool 
for assessing the within-index linkage between intradayrate and diffrate. In the subsequent subsection, we imple-
ment MF-DCCA on the overlapping sample for each index and report cross-Hurst exponents that summarize the 
strength and heterogeneity of multiscale cross-correlations.

4 Results and Discussion

4.1 Multifractal Detrended Cross-Correlation Analysis (MF-DCCA)

In the MF-DCCA framework, we compute the fluctuation function F xy (q, s) for a set of moment orders 
q ∈ {−4, −2, 0, 2, 4} and time scales s ∈ {5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 45, 60, 90, 120, 180}. For q ≠ 0, the qth-order fluc-
tuation function is defined as { }

2Ns 
1 ∑

F x y (q, s) = 
|

| |q∕  

| 
2

F ( 
2N | x y 𝜈 s) ,

s 𝜈 =1

where F xy (𝜈, s) denotes the local detrended cross-covariance within the 𝜈 th segment of length s and N s is the 
number of non-overlapping segments in one direction.

For q = 0, the direct application of the above expression is not well-defined, because the power mean 
becomes singular as q → 0. Following the standard multifractal literature, we adopt the continuous extension of 
F xy (q, s) at q = 0 based on the logarithmic average:

{
2Ns 

1 ∑ ( )} 
 

F x y (0, s) = exp ln F 2 ( 𝜈, s) + 𝜀 ,
4N xy 

s 𝜈 =1

where 𝜀 is a small positive constant to avoid numerical issues when F xy (𝜈, s) is close to zero. In our implementa-
tion, this formula is equivalent to taking the exponential of one half of the mean log absolute cross-covariance,



Y. Si and S. Nadarajah: Multifractal Structure of Overnight and Intraday Returns — 13

which is consistent with the log-averaging treatment used in MFDFA/MF-DCCA. The generalized cross-Hurst 
exponent h xy (q) is then obtained by ordinary least squares regression of log F xy (q, s) on log s for each q.

The choice of q-values reflects a trade-off between capturing heterogeneous fluctuation regimes and 
maintaining statistical stability. Negative values (q < 0) put more weight on small-amplitude, quiet-period fluc-
tuations, whereas positive values (q > 0) emphasize large deviations and extreme co-movements. Very large 
|q| may lead to unstable estimates due to finite-sample effects and measurement noise. We therefore restrict q 
to a moderate and symmetric range q ∈ {−4, −2, 0, 2, 4}, which is commonly used in empirical applications of 
MFDFA and MF-DCCA. Although the MF-DCCA procedure is carried out for the full set of q ∈ {−4, −2, 0, 2, 4}, 
the main tables in the paper report only the cross-Hurst exponent at q = 2, denoted by hx y (q = 2). There are 
three reasons for this focus.

First, q = 2 corresponds to the second-order statistics of the underlying processes and is directly compa-
rable to the standard DCCA exponent and the classical Hurst exponent based on variance and covariance. It 
therefore provides a natural benchmark for assessing the strength of multi-scale cross-correlations.

Second, hx y (q = 2) puts more weight on medium-to-large fluctuations, which are of primary interest in our 
context of market co-movements and risk transmission. Very large positive q would be dominated by a small 
number of extreme observations and lead to unstable slope estimates, whereas very negative q would be overly 
sensitive to measurement noise in the quiet periods.

Third, the qualitative ranking of indices and index pairs remains consistent across different q-values. Given 
the similarity of the results, only the cross-Hurst exponent at q = 2 is presented in the main text for brevity. The 
patterns observed for q = 2 are robust across the full range of moment orders, and the results for other q-values 
are qualitatively similar. Therefore, additional detailed results for other q-values are omitted in the main text to 
avoid redundancy but could obtained through our code provided with different choice of q.

As reported in Table 5, the MF-DCCA cross-Hurst exponents hx y (q = 2) between the opening price dif-
ference rate and the intraday return are all strictly above 0.38 for all indices in the sample considered, with 
a median of 0.489. Several emerging or less liquid markets (e.g., DFM General Index, PFTS Index, VN-Index, 
and WINDALLA) display particularly high values (hx y (2) ≥ 0.53), indicating strong multi-scale co-movements 
between overnight gaps and same-day returns. In contrast, large developed markets such as the S&P 500, DJIA, 
and NASDAQ exhibit moderate cross-exponents around 0.46–0.50, suggesting that intraday trading and market 
microstructure partially decouple the opening signal from subsequent intraday dynamics.

Table 6 summarizes the distribution of h xy (q) across the five moment orders considered. On average, the 
cross-exponent declines monotonically from q = −4 to q = 4, with the mean value falling from 1.64 at q = −4 
to 0.418 at q = 4. This pattern implies that small fluctuations (negative q) tend to be more strongly cross-
correlated between opening and intraday returns than large fluctuations (positive q), consistent with the idea 
that extreme intraday moves are more strongly influenced by local order flow and liquidity shocks rather than 
by the overnight information embedded in opening gaps.

Cross-index results for intraday returns are reported in Table 7. The MF-DCCA exponents h xy (q = 2) con-
centrate in a relatively narrow band between 0.42 and 0.54, indicating moderate but systematic multi-scale 
cross-correlations among the core indices. The strongest intraday coupling is observed between KOSPI and DAX 
(h xy (2) = 0.539), followed by several pairs involving DAX, NASDAQ Composite, and Chinese or Hong Kong indices 
(e.g., SZSE Component–NASDAQ, CSI 300–SZSE Component, SSE Composite–SZSE Component). This pattern sug-
gests that intraday co-movements are shaped by both regional integration (e.g., within East Asia or within North 
America) and cross-regional linkages to major global benchmarks such as the DAX and the S&P 500.

Table 8 presents the cross-index MF-DCCA exponents for opening price difference rates. Compared with 
intraday returns, the q = 2 exponents are systematically higher, with many pairs exceeding 0.60. In particular, 
A-share indices (SSE Composite, CSI 300, and SZSE Component) display very strong opening-gap co-movements 
with U.S. blue-chip benchmarks (DJIA and S&P 500) and, to a lesser extent, with the NASDAQ Composite and 
DAX. The spectrum widths for these cross-index diffrate pairs are also much larger than for intraday returns, 
reflecting pronounced multifractality in the way overnight information is transmitted across markets. Overall, 
the results indicate that global markets are more tightly connected at the level of opening gaps than at the level

information clustering dominates the scaling structure.

4.3 Data-Driven Clustering of MFDMA-Based Multifractal Signatures

To characterize cross-market heterogeneity without conflating overnight and within-session mechanisms, we 
conduct two separate unsupervised clustering exercises: one based on the MFDMA estimates for the overnight 
component (diffrate) and the other based on the within-session component (intradayrate). This separation is 
economically motivated because overnight returns embed non-trading information arrival and opening price 
formation, whereas intraday returns are dominated by continuous price discovery under market microstructure 
frictions.

For each index and each component, we construct a three-dimensional feature vector that summarizes per-
sistence, multifractality strength, and spectrum shape. Let h(q) denote the generalized Hurst exponent estimated 
under MFDMA and f (𝛼) the corresponding singularity spectrum.
– Persistence at the benchmark scale: h(2), interpreted as a second-moment benchmark of long-range 

dependence or persistence in the scaling law. Values above 0.5 suggest persistent behavior, while values 
below 0.5 are closer to anti-persistence in the scaling sense.

– Multifractality strength: Δh = maxq  h(q) − minq  h(q), computed over q ∈ [−5, 5] with step 0.5, which 
quantifies the dispersion of scaling exponents across fluctuation orders and is commonly used to summarize 
multifractal intensity.

– Spectrum asymmetry (shape): spec_ = (𝛼 R − 𝛼 0 )∕(𝛼 0 − 𝛼 L ), where 𝛼 0 is the location of the spectral 
maximum and 𝛼 L , 𝛼 R are the left and right spectral endpoints. This statistic captures whether the spectrum 
is relatively left- or right-stretched, i.e. whether extreme fluctuations or mild fluctuations contribute more 
to the heterogeneous scaling pattern.



22 — Y. Si and S. Nadarajah: Multifractal Structure of Overnight and Intraday Returns

The above construction intentionally avoids redundant width-type metrics (e.g., multiple variants of 𝛼-range) 
so that each feature contributes distinct economic content: persistence (h(2)), heterogeneity intensity (Δh), and 
asymmetry of fluctuation contributions (spec_).

We standardize each feature using z-scores across indices within each component and apply agglomera-
tive hierarchical clustering with Ward’s minimum-variance linkage (Ward.D2) under Euclidean distance. The 
number of clusters k is selected by maximizing the average silhouette coefficient subject to a minimum cluster 
size constraint of at least two indices per cluster. This constraint prevents singleton clusters that are difficult to 
interpret economically in a cross-market comparison setting.

4.3.1 Clustering Results: Overnight Component (Diffrate)

Figure 6 visualizes the diffrate clustering in the (h(2), Δh) plane, while Figure 7 reports standardized feature 
profiles by cluster. The algorithm selects k = 3 for diffrate, consistent with the notion that overnight returns 
combine information shocks during non-trading hours and opening price formation frictions, which may gen-
erate multiple market-specific regimes.

Economically, the three diffrate clusters can be summarized as follows. First, a group characterized by 
simultaneously high h(2) and high Δh suggests that overnight dynamics exhibit both stronger persistence and 
stronger multifractal heterogeneity, consistent with a regime in which non-trading information shocks, liquid-
ity gaps, and opening price adjustments jointly shape scaling behavior. Second, a cluster with relatively lower 
Δh indicates weaker multifractality and a more regular scaling structure overnight, which is compatible with 
smoother overnight information absorption and less pronounced mixture of mechanisms. Third, the remaining 
cluster captures the intermediate and most prevalent pattern across markets. Notably, indices with exception-
ally large Δh may be absorbed into the nearest cluster due to the minimum cluster size constraint, and such 
cases should be interpreted as outlier-like markets rather than as evidence against the clustering structure.

axis is h(2) (persistence) and the vertical axis is Δh (multifractality strength). Colors/markers indicate Ward-hierarchical clusters
with silhouette-selected k = 3 under the minimum cluster size constraint.

For intradayrate, Figures 8 and 9 show that the algorithm selects k = 2, indicating a more homogeneous 
cross-market scaling structure during trading hours. This is consistent with intraday returns being governed

by broadly similar continuous price discovery and microstructure frictions (order flow, liquidity, and volatility 
clustering) across markets.

The two intraday clusters can be interpreted as a baseline group capturing the typical within-session scal-
ing regime and a non-typical group featuring unusually strong multifractality and/or pronounced spectrum 
asymmetry. In economic terms, the latter pattern is consistent with markets where intraday dynamics are dispro-
portionately shaped by extreme fluctuation episodes, structural liquidity discontinuities, or stronger behavioral 
heterogeneity in order submission and reaction to price movements.

5 Conclusions

This paper decomposes daily index movements into an overnight revaluation component (opening gap, 
diffrate) and an intraday price-discovery component (open-to-close return, intradayrate), and characterizes both 
marginal multifractality (via MFDMA) and multiscale cross-dependence (via MF-DCCA) under nonstationarity. 
Across markets, the overnight component typically exhibits stronger persistence and greater scale heterogeneity, 
consistent with the economic mechanism that heterogeneous information arrivals, cross-market spillovers, and 
deferred order submission are compressed into a discrete opening price-discovery event, whereas continuous 
intraday trading can attenuate persistence through liquidity replenishment, inventory control, and rapid within-
session incorporation of information. Within-index MF-DCCA further shows that overnight gaps and intraday 
returns are systematically coupled across scales, with cross-Hurst exponents centered around hx y (2) ≈ 0.49 and 
a monotone decline of h xy (q) as q increases, implying that coupling is tighter in calm regimes than during extreme 
co-movements where local order flow and liquidity shocks may partially decouple the session path from the 
opening signal. Cross-index comparisons indicate that international integration is stronger in opening gaps than 
in intraday returns, suggesting that global information is synchronized primarily at the open across time zones 
while intraday dynamics remain more venue-specific; clustering based on multifractal signatures is consistent



Y. Si and S. Nadarajah: Multifractal Structure of Overnight and Intraday Returns — 25

with this view by revealing richer regime stratification in diffrate than in intradayrate. Two limitations follow 
directly from the design: the use of daily open/close data limits the ability to separate information-driven gaps 
from opening-auction frictions and to localize coupling within finer intraday intervals, and cross-country institu-
tional heterogeneity (index methodologies, trading rules, and holiday calendars) together with missingness may 
affect strict comparability despite alignment on common trading days and robustness checks. Future work can 
therefore (i) incorporate high-frequency microstructure and opening-auction order-book measures to identify 
when and how the overnight signal is absorbed or reversed, and (ii) link multifractal coupling to explicit infor-
mation states (macro announcements, policy events, and news/sentiment) and to multi-asset spillover networks 
to clarify time-zone lead–lag structures and nonlinear amplification under stress.

Multifractal Detrended Fluctuation Analysis
(MF-DFA) of Stock Market Indexes. Empirical
Evidence from Seven Central and Eastern
European Markets
Laura Raisa Miloş 1,* , Cornel Haţiegan 2, Marius Cristian Miloş 1, Flavia Mirela Barna 1 and
Claudiu Bot,oc 1

1 Department of Finance, Faculty of Economics and Business Administration, West University of Timis, oara,

2 Departament of Engineering Science, Faculty of Engineering and Management, University “Eftimie Murgu”

* Correspondence: laura.milos@e-uvt.ro



Received: 1 November 2019; Accepted: 9 January 2020; Published: 10 January 2020 

Abstract: In this paper, we present a comparative investigation of the multifractal properties of seven
Central and Eastern European (CEE) stock markets using recent financial data up to August 2018 by
employing seasonal and trend decompositions before applying multifractal detrended fluctuation
analysis. We find that stock indices returns exhibit long-range correlations, supporting the idea that
the stock markets in question are not efficient markets and have not reached a mature stage of market
development. The results of the paper are of interest to investors looking for opportunities in these
stock exchanges and also to policy makers in their endeavour of realizing institutional reforms in order
to increase stock market efficiency and to support the sustainable growth of the financial markets.

Keywords: econophysics; MF-DFA; long-range dependency; generalized Hurst exponent; market
efficiency; sustainable development; stock markets

1. Introduction

In its list of recommendations to accelerate capital market development in emerging economies,
the World Economic Forum suggested stock market efficiency and transparency, with the objective
of creating more liquidity in the market and improving the ability of market participants to assess
market’s costs and benefits [1]. The issue of market efficiency has attracted a lot of academic interest in
the past fifty years, with application to individual or regional stock markets, due to its implications for
both investors and public authorities. Investors looking for fair prices will avoid investing in inefficient
markets, while other investors looking for mispriced assets in equity markets will avoid efficient
markets since they do not provide the opportunity for realizing abnormal profits. Public authorities, on
the other hand, will continue their efforts in realizing reforms, meant to enhance stock market efficiency,
in order to ensure that all financial assets are offering optimal risk-to-reward ratios [2]. Understanding
the behavior of developing stock markets is very important when adopting the right public policies
in order to enhance the role of the stock exchange in the sustainable development of the economy.
The positive influence of the market-based economy on the economic growth is well documented
in the literature [3–6] despite some studies which prove the contrary [7] or suggest that causality
flows in the opposite direction [8,9]. A more efficient financial system will enhance GDP growth.
Consequently, policymakers will make all necessary efforts to minimize market failures by making

Sustainability 2020, 12, 535; doi:10.3390/su12020535 www.mdpi.com/journal/sustainability



Sustainability 2020, 12, 535 2 of 15

transactions and capital allocation easier and exerting corporate governance principles [10,11]. On the
other hand, understanding the current degree of market efficiency of the CEE countries, which are the
latest members of the European Union, becomes more important in the context of their integration
with other developed markets [12].

The efficient market hypothesis (EMH), as defined in the pioneering work by Fama [13], presumes
that all information available on the market will be immediately reflected in the asset prices, making
them fair. An emerging stream of financial literature nowadays criticizes the EMH as this assumption
fails to explain ubiquitous market properties such as fat tails, long-term correlation, volatility clustering,
and multifractality. In this respect, fractal theory has been proposed whereas fractal distribution
was found as applicable to financial markets [14]. Fractal methods consist of single fractal and
multifractal methods, the latter being superior given that they can describe the multi-scale and subtle
sub-structures of fractals in complex systems. Multifractal detrended fluctuation analysis (MF-DFA)
was developed in order to investigate the dynamic resources of multifractality (non-linear temporal
correlation versus fat-tailed distribution) [15]. The application area for MF-DFA is widespread in
several markets described by the random walk hypothesis (RWH). On the one hand, MF-DFA has
been applied to agricultural or commodities markets such as oil or gold [16–18] and suggests that
prices do not follow RWH. On the other hand, it has been adopted in financial markets, mostly capital
markets [19–32], and suggests the existence of fractal properties. Due to the discovery of multifractal
properties of the financial markets in the last decade, interest in financial analysis of stock markets
using MF-DFA has increased. Today, multifractality is one of the most active topics in econophysics.
However, most studies using multifractality rather focus on developed stock markets. The use of
the technique for emerging CEE markets is uncommon [28–32], ignoring the potential to highlight
multifractal properties in these markets.

The purpose of the paper is to assess, using MF-DFA, the degree of market efficiency in the case of
the considered seven CEE countries, new members of the European Union (Bulgaria, Croatia, Czech
Republic, Hungary, Romania, Poland, and Slovenia). Using daily blue-chip index data up to August
2018, our study examines the behavior of these stock markets over the long run. Our paper fills the
existing literature gap in several directions. First, from a theoretical point of view, it brings further
evidence for the efficiency of these markets, testing the weak form of market efficiency for the most
important CEE stock exchanges (in terms of market capitalization). Previous empirical literature on
this topic has failed to provide consistent results. Market efficiency, stock market development, and
economic growth are connected, and the CEE stock exchanges are all developing stock markets, for
which sustainable growth is highly important, as shown in the literature [6]. Second, our methodology
improves previous studies in the sense that this is the first stock market study that employs STL
(seasonal and trend decomposition using loess) decomposition, before applying MF-DFA. Isolating the
remaining components allows us to exclude the seasonal oscillations that could be generated by the
annual and sub-annual trading cycles.

The rest of the paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews the literature and background
of the topic. Section 3 presents data and methodology. Section 4 outlines the empirical results, and
Section 5 concludes.

2. Theoretical Background

The beneficial role of stock exchanges in ensuring long-run economic growth and sustainable
development is well known in both the financial and growth literature. This relationship is mainly
explained by higher domestic capital accumulation and mobilization, capital channelling towards
productive sectors, risk transfer, and sharing and price discovery [3–5]. There are also studies that
outline the reverse causality relationship between financial development and growth [8,9] while others
support the unpopular belief that market-based financial development and economic growth do not
share a causal relationship [7].



Sustainability 2020, 12, 535 3 of 15

However, most empirical research suggests a one-way positive connection between stock market
development and economic growth [3–5]. This positive relationship should persist even if, in the
case of the new member states of European Union, the contribution of the stock markets to economic
growth is limited due to the small financial depth of the markets [6]. However, in these countries, the
potential role that the stock market has for economic development depends on the degree of stock
market development. Stock market development, in turn, has been proven to have, a significant
relationship with the degree of market efficiency, regardless of whether markets are developed, frontier
or emergent, at least in the case of Europe [33]. Younger and less developed markets are usually found
in the empirical literature to be less efficient than their more developed counterparts. Lower degrees of
efficiency imply also higher transaction costs for market participants [24,34].

The efficient market hypothesis [13] divides itself into the well-known categories: (i) the weak form,
which states that no analysis of past stock market behavior (technical or fundamental) would allow
market participants to obtain abnormal returns, due to the fact that all historical and current data about
price and volume would already be accounted on the market price; (ii) the semi-strong form, which can
be differentiated by the latter in the sense that the market value of a financial asset adjusts, almost
immediately, to all new (market and non-market) public information about it, following a random
walk departure from previous prices; (iii) the strong form, which assumes that not even privileged
information (insider information) made public to a certain group would allow a certain investor to
gain abnormal profits.

A comprehensive list of studies which cover stock market efficiency is beyond the purpose of our
study. We provide instead an overview of recent empirical work that focuses on testing the weak form
of efficient markets in the case of several CEE stock markets. A sound empirical literature background
regarding the efficiency of the emerging markets prior to 2011 can be found in Dragotă and T, ilică [35]
or Nurunnabi [36]. These studies aimed at testing the weak form of efficient market theory (the data
necessary for testing strong market efficiency or semi-strong market efficiency being probably in most
cases unavailable [24]) and failed to provide an unequivocal response regarding market efficiency for
the CEE stock markets. There are serious doubts about whether stock markets are efficient in these
countries [35]. This might be since the stock market efficiency is time varying [37]. In this case, using a
rolling regression approach can help in analyzing the efficient markets hypothesis [38]. Furthermore,
there is a long memory property in some CEE stock markets [39] that is not consistent with efficiency.

We will further discuss recent empirical tests of the weak form of efficiency in CEE stock markets
(starting with 2011), which also failed in providing a unanimous response. The methodology of these
tests was based on one or more of the following traditional techniques: the Jarque–Bera (JB) test (which
measures the normality of the distribution), the parametric autocorrelation test (which measures the
dependency of successive returns), the non-parametric runs test (which tests the randomness of a
sequence of returns), the variance ratio test (which determines whether there are any uncorrelated
changes in the series), unit root tests (meant to assess the stationarity of time series data), or GARCH
and its variations (for the analysis of seasonality patterns: January effects, day of the month, turn of
the month, day of the week or other).

Smith [34] found evidence for the weak form of efficiency when testing the Martingale hypothesis
for 15 European emerging stock markets over a period of almost 9 years (February 2000–December
2009). The author used a rolling window variance ratio to capture changes in efficiency and to rank
markets according to their relative inefficiency, reaching the conclusion that return predictability varies
widely between the countries. The most efficient markets he studied were the Hungarian and the
Polish markets, while Estonia was less efficient.

Guidi et al. [2] used autocorrelation analysis, the runs test, the variance ratio test, and GARCH-M
for a period of ten years (1999–2009) to empirically prove that the seven CEE stock markets taken into
consideration did not follow a random walk process. However, the authors found that since 2004, the
year of accession to the European Union, CEE countries have improved their stock market efficiency.



Sustainability 2020, 12, 535 4 of 15

The random walk hypothesis was rejected for two of the seven considered stock markets (the Bulgarian
and Slovak markets).

Karadagli and Omay [40] investigated the weak form of market efficiency for emerging economies
(including some of the countries taken into consideration in our analysis) using linear and nonlinear
unit root tests, which provided contradictory results, while using monthly data for the period 2002–2010.
The results provided by nonlinear unit root tests suggested that the Romanian market and the Polish
market were not weak-form efficient, while the linear tests suggested they were, alongside other CEE
stock markets such as Bulgarian, Hungarian, and Slovenian markets. As a group, however, the authors
found that the considered countries were not efficient.

Dragotă and Tilică [35] investigated the degree of market efficiency in the case of 20 East European
former communist countries for the period 2008–2010, posing some doubts about market efficiency
for all the considered countries, regardless of the type of methodology used (unit root tests, runs test,
variance ratio test, filter rules test, or the January effect). They also suggested that the established
degree of efficiency could serve as a method of selection between active and passive strategies on the
market. This hypothesis was stated in Kroha and Skoula [41], who developed a new technical indicator
for trading strategies (for buying and selling signals), called Moving Hurst (MF).

Bot,oc [12] examined the weak form of market efficiency for five CEE stock markets in the
timeframe of 1997–2014 (Croatia, Czech Republic, Hungary, Romania, and Poland), using unit root
tests, a non-parametric runs test, and joint variance tests and found, with the exception of Poland,
Hungary, and Croatia, that the CEE markets did not exhibit weak-form market efficiency.

Tokić et al. [24] analysed financial markets in four CEE countries (Croatia, Serbia, Slovenia, and
Slovakia) for a significant timeframe (2006–2016) and show that all analysed indices, with the exception
of Serbia, exhibited weak-form market efficiency. These results, in contrast with other empirical papers
on the same markets, were justified by the authors by the possibility that market efficiency evolves
positively over time with the level of stock market development.

As a response of econophysics literature to both EMH and RWH, the fractal theory was proposed
by Benoit Mandelbrot and further developed [14,42]. The theory, originating from mathematics,
present fractals as fragmented geometric shapes that when broken into parts, are similar in shape to
the whole. It has started to be used as an alternative to standard tools and methods previously used in
the world of finance in general and financial markets in particular. This is due to the shortcomings
of GARCH processes or Brownian motion, which failed to model all relevant features of financial
markets [42]. The fractal theory, also known as the theory of “roughness and self-similarity” was
applied to the behavior of financial markets in connection with market efficiency, as a non-linear
approach. Kantelhardt et al. [15,43] suggested MF-DFA in analyzing non-stationary time series.

The empirical literature investigating financial market behavior has concluded that there are main
two factors leading to multifractal properties of financial time series: non-linear time correlations
between past and current events and heavy-tailed probability distributions [18]. A large body of
empirical research has proven that multifractality exists in stock market indices, the Hurst exponent
being generally used to monitor the highest volatility periods in financial time series [44] or to measure
the short and long-term memory of the stock market depicting the degree of market efficiency [28,45,46].

Given the rich literature related to using detrended fluctuation analysis (DFA) and its variations
in financial markets (mostly developed ones), we will further limit our empirical literature review to
those studies that have used MF-DFA with application to one or more of the CEE stock markets taken
into consideration in our analysis.

Jagric et al. [28] used wavelet analysis and estimated the Hurst exponent on a sliding time window
to test the existence of long-range dependence (LRD) in six transition economies. They divided their
results into two groups: markets with strong LRD (Czech Republic, Hungary, Russia, and Slovenia)
and markets with a weak form of LRD (Poland, Slovakia) while also finding evidence for the time
dependence of the Hurst coefficient.



Sustainability 2020, 12, 535 5 of 15

Domino [29] analyzed a large number of stocks from the Warsaw Stock Exchange (126 companies)
during the period 1991–2008 and computed the Hurst exponent in order to search for the moment
when changes in the long-term return rate of an investment were more likely to occur, in a way that
could be used in an investment strategy. He concluded that a dropping Hurst exponent could be
regarded as a signal for a potential change in the trend or in the return.

The informational efficiency of the Romanian stock market was analysed using MF-DFA by
Ples, oianu et al. [30] in the case of the blue-chip Bucharest Exchange Trading (BET) and the composite
BET-C index, as well as ten different stocks listed on the Bucharest Stock Exchange. Using daily
time series from January 2001 until May 2012, as well as intradaily time series that ranged from
January 2011 until December 2011, they confirmed the multifractal nature of this market, as well as its
predictable nature.

Caraiani [31] tested for the presence of multifractality in three important CEE stock markets
(Polish, Czech, and Hungarian) using MF-DFA. Using both original return time-series for the blue-chip
indexes WIG, BUX, and PX (up to December 2010) and reordered (reshuffled) time series, he indicated
the long-run dependence of these markets. He also tested whether the degree of multifractality
changed during the financial crisis period. During this period, he found no evidence of an increase of
multifractality spectrum strength, but rather of its shape.

Ferreira [32] investigated the behavior of 18 Eastern European stock markets using a sliding
window DFA (with data ending in March 2017) and found that most of the considered markets were
long-range dependent, suggesting a market inefficiency. One important conclusion of their paper has
to do with the evolution in time of the dependence levels observed for the Czech, Hungarian, and
Polish stock markets. These dependence levels were descending, even better than the benchmark
indexes for the developed markets. The markets were ranked, with the help of an efficiency index,
modeled after the one proposed by Kristoufek and Vosvrda [45]. The most efficient markets were
Czech Republic, Hungary, and Poland.

To conclude, we can say that most of the studies applying MF-DFA, but also other traditional tools
in order to test weak-form market efficiency in the case of CEE stock markets, suggest that these stock
exchanges are inefficient, with some exceptions. These exceptions might be caused either by the type
of methodology used or by the time horizon. However, these empirical results must be treated with
caution, since market efficiency could increase or decrease over time (time-varying market efficiency)
due to various factors including the level of stock market development [47]. Moreover, although
MF-DFA is a well-known methodology, it is not that widely applied in the case of the CEE countries,
so there is still a basis for rigorous testing in order to understand better the market behavior.

3. Data and Methodology

Data regarding the daily values of CEE stock market indices (up to August 2018) as well as data
regarding market capitalization were obtained from Investing.com, CEIC, and the World Federation of
Exchanges (Table 1). The seven CEE stock markets included in our analysis were the top ones in term
of market capitalization when considering the new member states of the European Union.

The time-series analysis of stock market returns consists of three stages. In the first step, we
calculate stock market returns. In the second step, we apply seasonal and trend decompositions (STL)
to isolate deterministic components. Finally, we apply multifractal detrended fluctuation analysis
(MF-DFA) to the stochastic component of the financial return series.

3.1. Stage 1: Calculating Stock Market Returns

Let Pt be the index price at the end of period t. The simple return on that index over period t, rt, is
given by:

The log-return on that index over period t, rL, is given by:

t = log t

Pt−1

In our study, we use daily simple returns. Because of the daily frequency of our data, the results
of the analysis based on simple and log returns are very close. For coarser data, the use of log-returns
is advised because simple returns do not additively compound over time.

3.2. Stage 2: STL Decomposition

Using the Wold representation theorem [48], stock returns can be decomposed into deterministic
and stochastic components. Because we are interested in the behavior of the stochastic component,
we first decompose the time series of calculated stock returns (1) into deterministic and stochastic
components. For this purpose, we use an STL (seasonal and trend decomposition using loess)
decomposition based on the loess smoother, proposed by [49]. The STL method additively decomposes
each stock return time series into a deterministic trend (Ti), seasonal (Si) components, and stochastic
remainder (Ri) component, as in [50]:

rt = Ti + Si + Ri (3)

The STL decomposition consists of three steps. In the first step, the trend component is initialized.
The next two steps are two recursive procedures: an inner loop as well as an outer loop. The outer loop
calculates robustness weights according to the remainder component. These weights are subsequently
used in the next iteration of the inner loop. The outer loop role is reducing (or, in some instances,
eliminating) outliers and extreme values in the time series. The inner loop corrects the trend and
seasonal components [50]. The time series is then partitioned into cycle subseries which are loess
(LOcalregrESSion) smoothed and then passed through a low-pass filter. The resulting seasonal
components are subtracted from the raw data. The residual is loess smoothed, and the trend is
re-initialized. What is left is the remainder that subsequently enters the outer loop.

To our knowledge, this is the first stock market study that employs STL decomposition before
applying the MF-DFA. Isolating the remaining components allows us to exclude the seasonal oscillations
that could be generated by the annual and sub-annual trading cycles. We have applied the STL
decomposition with the scope of removing the seasonal components and benefiting from more reliable
results but also to have information on the inner dynamics of stock market returns, as suggested by [51].
STL has several important advantages compared to other time series decomposition methods, such as
TRAMO/SEATS [52] and X11 [53]. First, STL can handle any type of seasonality (not only monthly
and quarterly data). Second, its seasonal component is allowed to change over time. Third, the user
can specify both the rate of change in the seasonal component and the smoothness of the trend cycle.
Finally, the method is more robust to outliers.

In this study, the STL decomposition is implemented in the R statistical package using the stl
function of the stats library [51,54]. We set the function parameters as follows: (i) the span of the
loess window for seasonal extraction (s.window) is set to 21 (i.e., the number of trading days in a



Sustainability 2020, 12, 535 7 of 15

calendar month); (ii) the number of backfitting iterations (inner) is set to 1; (iii), the number of outer
iterations (outer) is set to 15; (iv) the degree of locally-fitted polynomial in seasonal extraction (s.degree)
is set to 1; the other parameters are left as default. The parameter choices in (ii) and (iii) are robust
iteration options necessary to minimize effects of outliers, and (iv) is necessary for better handling of
seasonal effects.

3.3. Stage 3: MF-DFA

The multifractal detrended fluctuation analysis (MF-DFA) is the strongest technique for detecting
multifractality in a time series [51]. It takes the average volatility of the time series in each interval as a
statistical point that is subsequently used to calculate volatility functions. It then determines generalized
Hurst exponents based on the power law of volatility functions [55]. The important advantage of
MF-DFA over other approaches is its ability to detect long-term correlations in non-stationary time
series. Below we outline the key steps and formulas underlying the analysis.

Let R(i) for i = 1,· · · ,N be a possibly non-stationary time series of the remainder component
resulting from the STL decomposition of stock market returns (2), where N indicates series length.
The first step of the MF-DFA is to construct the “profile”, Y(j), by integration after subtracting from the
time series, R(i) its average, R [51]:

∑j
Y( j) ≡ (R(i) −R), i = 1, . . . , N (4)

i=1

The second step of the MF-DFA is to divide the profile Y(j) into Ns ≡ int (N/s) non-overlapping
segments of equal length s. Observe that time scale N is not usually an integer multiple of length s.
Therefore, one can disregard a short part of the profile Y(j) at the end, and the sub-division is also
realized starting from the opposite end. As a result, a total of 2 Ns segments is obtained.

In the third step of MF-DFA, we compute the local trend for each of the 2Ns segments by a
least-squares fit of the series. This involves fitting a polynomial of degree m to approximate the profile
in each of the 2Ns windows. The variance is then calculated using the following formulas:

The parameter q helps distinguishing between segments with small and large fluctuations. The
negative value of the q parameter enhances the small fluctuations, whereas a positive one enhances the



Sustainability 2020, 12, 535 8 of 15

large fluctuations. For q = 2, we have a special case of a well-known detrended fluctuation analysis [56].
Observe that Fq(s) is an increasing function of s.

In the final step we determine the scaling exponent of the fluctuation function for any fixed q and
obtain the relationship between Fq(s) and s. If Fq(s) is a power law, the series are in the log-log scale for
that particular q:

Fq(s) ∝ shq (9)

The exponent hq is called a generalized Hurst exponent. In the special case of stationary series, h2
becomes the well known Hurst exponent [57]. One can use the Hurst exponents in order to measure
market efficiency [23,45,46,58]. A Hurst exponent value that ranges between 0.5 and 1 would imply a
positive autocorrelation (a persistent behavior), characterized by long memory effects, which occur
regardless of the time scale. Values closer to 1 indicate the presence of large and abrupt changes.
A Hurst exponent value that ranges between 0 and 0.5 indicates negative autocorrelation—a change of
the trend (an anti-persistent behavior) [41]. Antipersistence means to cover less distance, by reverting
itself more frequent than a random process. According to Peters [59], a value of H equal to 0.5 (q = 0)
reflects a Brownian time series or otherwise, a classical random walk.

Generally speaking, the series is characterised by multifractality if the exponent hq depends on q,
and it monotonically decreases as q increases. The series is mono-fractal when hq does not depend
on q [51].

The hq resulting from MF-DFA can also be expressed as a function of the Renyi exponent, τ(q):

τ(q) = qhq − 1 (10)

Another illustrative way to analyze whether the time series is mono- or multifractal is by the
multifractal spectrum:

f (α) = qα− τ(q) (11)

where α is the Hölder exponent:
∂hq

α = hq + q − τ(q) (12)
∂q

The multifractal spectrum shows the importance of each of the various fractal exponents in the
series. Finally, the range of generalized Hurst exponents, ∆h = max(hq) −min(hq), is another helpful
measure of the degree of multifractality. A higher ∆h indicates a more multifractal series.

4. Results

Figure 1 presents, by way of illustration, the three constituent elements for the Romanian stock
market index, BET: the seasonal (Figure 1b), trend (Figure 1c), and remainder (Figure 1d). The results of
STL decomposition of other stock returns time series are similar and are available in the Supplementary
Materials (due to space constraints). In Figure 1, there can be noticed the annual oscillation that
characterizes the seasonal component, which is consistent with earlier findings that stock market
returns have a clear seasonal pattern [60]. On the contrary, the trend component does not show a large
temporal evolution of stock index returns, and the range of variability is very small (i.e., its coefficient
of variation is close to zero). The remainder does not follow a regular pattern, experiencing high
frequency fluctuations, that could be explained by other macroeconomic determinants, such as, e.g.,
the financial crisis of 2008–2009 [61,62]. The remaining component presents a noisy character which is
not, however, a pure random noise. As we show below, the application of MF-DFA to the remainder
ensures capturing the dynamic characteristics of the inner fluctuations of the stock returns.

comFpigounreen2t.b indicates the dependence of the generalized Hurst exponent with q. One can observe
that the function is decreasing, which proves the existence of patterns of multifractality in the time
fluctuations of the remainder. Figure 2c shows the Renyi exponent, τ(q). For monofractal series,
τ(q) is linear, while for multifractal series, it is nonlinear. We see that τ(q) has an exponential shape,
which indicates multifractality. Figure 2d shows the multifractal spectrum obtained from Equations
(11) and (12). Consistent with other indicators, the multifractal spectrum exhibits a single-humped
shape, usually describing the multifractal series. Finally, we calculate the range of generalized Hurst
exponents, ∆h. The range ∆h measures the level of multifractality, being known the fact that the larger
this range the more multifractality resides in the series [15]. For the Romanian stock market index, we
found ∆h = 0.22. Thus, the remainder of the stock market index is characterized by high multifractality,
the time dynamics being mostly governed by large volatility.
