Jung and Chang (2016) note that due to conditioning on general market index returns,
partial correlation coefficients tend to be smaller than Pearson correlation coefficients of the
same stock returns. In addition, not accounting for common factors that have an influence
on stock returns can result in biased Pearson correlation estimates, which are not useful
for investors seeking to diversify risk away from their portfolios. Furthermore, when the
common factor in partial correlation estimates is chosen to be the general market index, the
partial correlation coefficient resembles the CAPM.

4. Results: Clustering of Stock Market Returns
Jung and Chang (2016) were among the first to propose the use of partial correlation

coefficients for clustering stock returns using an agglomerative hierarchical clustering
procedure. In this section, we extend these clustering applications by proposing the use
of a wavelet-based partial correlation dissimilarity measure in the context of the k-means
clustering algorithm to identify groups of stocks that exhibit distinct market movement
characteristics.

In addition to being useful for portfolio diversification purposes (Cuthbertson and
Nitzsche 2004), such an analysis enables the exploration of differences between stocks
on a time scale basis, such as variations over short-term, medium-term, and long-term
cycles, and it is therefore particularly well suited for investors that differ in terms of their
investment horizon orientations.

Can the partial correlation coefficient be used to cluster stock market returns from
different economic activity sectors and over different time scales?

For the clustering applications of this section, we will use the following partial correla-
tion dissimilarity measure between stocks xt and yt, which is based on the wavelet partial
correlation coefficient formula presented in[ Section 3: ]

δx,y:z(λj) = 1− ρx,y:z(λj) /2 (2)

This measure resembles the Pearson correlation dissimilarity measure that is frequently
used for clustering continuous data observations (Everitt et al. 2011, p. 50). However, it
differs in two important aspects: (i) it is based on the partial correlation coefficient that
measures the association between two stocks (xt and yt), while controlling for the effect of
a third variable (the stock market index), and (ii) it can be calculated and used in clustering
applications separately for each time scale.

Consequently, using the dissimilarity measure δx,y:z(λj), the k-means clustering al-
gorithm can be applied separately for each time scale. To see this, first consider a p-
dimensional dataset consisting of the level j wavelet coefficient vectors generated from
the returns series of p separate stocks, as described in Section 3.1. If there are K separate
clusters inherent in the data, total dispersion is provided by the following matrix:

To evaluate the consistency of the resulting cluster formations for time scales 3, 6, 
and 8, we performed a silhouette analysis, which is a frequently used method for validat-
ing cluster formations. For each object, an index is defined that compares the object’s sep-
aration from its cluster against the heterogeneity of the cluster (Everitt et al. 2011). Conse-
quently, it provides an indication of how similar an observation is with the cluster to 
which it has been assigned relative to other clusters.  

Values of the index close to 1 suggest that the object is well classified since the clus-
ter’s heterogeneity is smaller than its separation, while values close to −1 suggest misclas-
sification. Borderline cases where the object is not clearly assigned between two neigh-
bouring clusters are indicated with values close to zero.  

In silhouette plots, the values of the index for each cluster are displayed with hori-
zontal bars, as shown in Figure 3 for the three clusters of time scale 8. Kaufman and 
Rousseeuw (1990), who first proposed the silhouette method, consider silhouette width 
values higher than 0.5 to be indicative of a good cluster formation, as is the case with the 
results of time scale 8. However, more useful in applied work is the average silhouette 
width curve for different cluster sizes, since it enables identification of the optimal group 
sizes that maximize silhouette width.

by time scale, which entails different implications for investors wishing to diversify risk
away from their portfolios but differ in terms of their investment horizon orientation.

Similarly to Kenett et al. (2015), our findings also suggest that stocks can be correlated
outside their primary sector classification and the correlation levels vary by time scale.
These findings have implications for the stock selection strategies of investors relying on
sectoral diversification in their efforts to diversify risk away from their portfolios. The
degree of comovement between the different economic activity sectors is higher when
considering long-term cycles. Therefore, diversification is less important in the long-run,
a finding also reported by Rua and Nunes (2009). In contrast, more clusters were found
to exist over short-term cycles, suggesting the existence of sectors with distinct market
movements and therefore more opportunities for diversification.

Furthermore, accounting for movements in the general stock market index changes
the correlation levels between the different economic activity sectors, which suggests that
relying on simple Pearson correlation estimates might not be adequate for constructing
well-diversified portfolios. Our proposed method can therefore be used as a supplementary
tool that can reveal previously unobserved correlations between stocks, not dominated by
movements in the general stock market index.

Our research can be extended in several directions that can improve some of the
limitations associated with our proposed method. First, it would be useful to consider
the incorporation of alternative wavelet-based dissimilarity measures in the clustering
algorithm that can potentially improve the within-cluster dispersions when working with
stock market returns. Moreover, the areas of application can be extended to include
additional asset classes such as fixed-income securities. Second, it is worth considering
the use of alternative wavelet transforms for calculating the partial correlations between
stock market returns, such as the discreet wavelet transform and the maximal overlap
discreet wavelet packet transform (Percival and Walden 2000). Similarly, using alternative
wavelet families can potentially improve the resolutions of stock market returns at higher
frequencies. These are fruitful areas for further research, particularly with the aid of
simulation studies that can evaluate the performance of the different methods with varying
sample sizes.

Third, financial markets constitute complex environments influenced by the activities
of multiple agents interacting over different cycles. In such environments, it is highly likely
that correlations between stock market returns are influenced by many common factors
and not just the general stock market index. Developing alternative methods for clustering
stock returns over different time scales, while conditioning for multiple common factors in
the analysis, is an interesting area for further research.

Finally, the partial correlation coefficient between stock returns, much like the Pearson
correlation coefficient, is not static and could change periodically, particularly during times
of extreme market volatility. Therefore, it is important to update the estimated coefficients
frequently and in line with changes in the market conditions, especially when working with
individual stock returns, which are more directly influenced by changes in the individual
strategies of companies.

The Global Transmission of Stock Market: A Spatial Analysis

Hong Zhang,1 Xiaojie Gao,2 and Keqiang Dong 2

1Basic Courses Department, Tianjin Sino-German University of Applied Sciences, Tianjin, China

e stock markets, exhibiting complex self-correlation or cross-correlation over a broad range of time scales, are correlated not
only in time but also in space. e conventional spatial weight matrix in the econometric analysis is short of economic relation
between nonadjacent economic entities. erefore, this paper applies the detrended cross-correlation analysis coecient and
partial correlation coecient to analyze the global spatial interaction. is study computes the spatial Moran’s I value by the two
types of weight matrix for the 15 typical stock indices around the world, to explore the spatial agglomeration phenomenon. en,
the Spatial Durbin Model is applied to investigate the transmission of the stock market. e result from the Moran’s I value
indicates that the 15 typical stock indices are spatially correlated. e result of the Spatial Durbin Model gives the relationship
among the closing price, the opening price, the highest price, and the lowest price.

1. Introduction
With the increasing complexity of the securities market, the uncertainty of securities 
investment is increasing, it is very common for investors to use security portfolio 
investment strategies to obtain returns and control risks, which underscores the clear 
application value of studying the optimization of portfolio models (Kaplan 2017; Li et al.  
2021). Meanwhile, since Markowitz initiated the mean-variance portfolio (M-V) model, 
the research on the optimization of portfolio model has promoted the development and 
improvement of modern portfolio theory, further highlighting the important theoretical 
value of this research (Markowitz 1952; Chun et al. 2020).

The importance of portfolio model optimization makes a large number of scholars 
cultivate in the MV model. Their studies mainly include seven sectors: First, some 
optimizations of portfolio model are put under the constraint of trading and capital 
(Lam et al. 2019; Wu et al. 2021); second, from the perspectives of optimizing risk and 
measuring returns, the value-at-risk, conditional value-at-risk, expected loss, and similar 
measures are used to replace the Expectation and Variance of M-V model (Aboulaich 

CONTACT Xu Wu wuxuphd@foxmail.com School of Business, Chengdu University of Technology, Chengdu, 
China

with their consent.



MATHEMATICAL AND COMPUTER MODELLING OF DYNAMICAL SYSTEMS 737

et al. 2010; Guo et al. 2019); third, some optimized models are studied from the 
perspective of behavioural deviations and background risk (Xu et al. 2015; Reichlin  
2016); fourth, the multi-objective portfolio selection models are developed based on 
expanding the goal of maximizing the profit and minimizing the risk (Garcia et al. 2020; 
Petchrompo et al. 2022); fifth, the M-V model concentrates on the stochastic uncertainty 
existed in the investment issues, in order to optimize this kind of portfolio, the portfolio 
model based on fuzzy decision theory is raised (Mehlawat et al. 2020; Gupta et al. 2020; 
Garcia et al. 2020); sixth, bringing the selective process of investment and dynamic 
adjustment of stocks into model optimization is necessary, the multi-period dynamic 
model is constructed (Narang et al. 2022, Gupta et al. 2020; Li et al. 2023); seventh, some 
non-investment applications such as gardening, insurance and credit are also taken into 
account in the portfolio models (Wang et al. 2022; Gupta et al. 2023).

Through the literature review of some scholars’ research on portfolio models, it can be 
seen that the return, risk, and correlation measures used by early people in the study of 
portfolio model optimization are mainly based on statistical characteristics such as 
expectation, variance, and covariance in the Gaussian statistical methods, which implied 
that the premise of return rates on assets obeying normal distribution (Huang et al. 2017; 
Zhang et al. 2018).

With the deepening of research, people find that the capital market is a fractal complex 
system, and the return rates on assets obeys the fractal distribution and has the char
acteristics of multifractal correlation. Compared with the normal distribution, the fractal 
distribution has ‘heavy peak’ and ‘thick tail’ characteristics, and the multifractal correla
tion includes the multifractal autocorrelation of the return rate sequence on assets itself 
and the multifractal correlation among different return rates sequences on assets 
(Bouoiyour et al. 2018; Zhang et al. 2021). Because the rate of returns follow the fractal 
distribution, fractal measurements such as fractal expectation and fractal variance have 
been developed. And investment portfolio model based on fractal statistical analysis is 
constructed, which aims to improve the M-V model under the constraint of the fractal 
distribution (Xu et al. 2016; Feng et al. 2023). The multi-fractal correlation exists in 
different return rates, meaning that the autocorrelation of the return rate sequence on 
assets itself and the correlation between different return rates sequences on assets will be 
different with the different of the investors’ attention to the size of the fluctuation 
amplitudes and the length of the time scales. The statistical characteristics such as 
expectation, variance, and covariance in the Gaussian statistical methods are faced with 
the defects that they cannot accurately measure asset returns, risks and correlations, 
much less accurately capture volatility and correlations at different volatility ranges and 
on different time scales, thus affecting portfolio effectiveness (Stoyanov et al. 2010; Zhang 
et al. 2021).

Since the accurate measurement of the correlation of return rate on assets is an 
important condition to ensure the effectiveness of the portfolio model, it is difficult to 
ensure the effectiveness of the portfolio model by using the measurement of return, risk 
and correlation based on the Gaussian statistical methods (Becker et al. 2015; Yousefi 
et al. 2018). In order to make up for the defects, some scholars use the q-order detrended 
covariance under s-scale in multifractal detrended cross-correlation analysis (MF-DCCA 
or MF-DXA) or q-dependent detrended cross-correlation instead of covariance or 
variance as the correlation or the fluctuation measure of return rate on assets, and the 



738 H. LI ET AL.

corresponding fractal optimal portfolio models are constructed under a single fluctuation 
magnitude importance situation (the order q is a certain fixed constant) and a single time 
scale attention situation (the scale s is a certain fixed constant) (Tang and Zhu 2018; Zhao 
et al. 2018; Jiang et al. 2019). In essence, this treatment borrows from the idea of the 
DCCA cross-correlation coefficient, which can effectively measure mono-fractal correla
tions between non-stationary series (Zebende 2011; Kristoufek 2014a). As the DCCA 
cross-correlation coefficient becomes more and more useful for measuring correlation, 
for use in regression, etc., and the development of estimation methods for related 
parameters, it lays a foundation for further consideration of the measurement of multi
fractal correlation (Zebende et al. 2013; Kristoufek 2014b, 2015). Subsequently, some 
scholars constructed Mean-MF-DCCA(M-D) model of dualistic assets by using q-order 
detrended covariance under s-scale in multiple fluctuation magnitude importance situa
tions (order q can take multiple constants variably) and multiple time scale attention 
situations (scale s can take multiple constants variably) (Li et al. 2021).

Obviously, M-D model is beneficial to promote the theoretical model to adapt to the 
actual situation. However, it should be noted that when people conduct investment 
practices, investors not only have diversified fluctuation magnitude importance situa
tions and time scale attention situations, also face the problem on portfolio of multi-risk 
assets, that is, investors often allocate their money not only between two risky assets, but 
in multiple risk assets. Therefore, the above-mentioned M-D model of dualistic risk 
assets needs to be extended to the M-D model of multi-risk assets, and empirical testing 
of its effectiveness is carried out to provide a reliable decision-making basis for investors 
to solve the problem of multi-risk asset portfolios. Meanwhile, some given researchers 
optimize the M-V model on account of the mono-fractal correlation between each rate of 
returns, and the mean-detrended cross-correlation analysis model is created (Zhang et al.  
2022). Notably, the mono-fractal correlation is a special case of multi-fractal correlation 
between different assets, so the mean-detrended cross-correlation analysis portfolio 
model cannot deal with the improved issue that multi-fractal correlation in assets.

In view of the above analysis, the main aim of this article is incorporating the multi
fractal correlation into the optimization of the multi-risk asset portfolio model, which 
can be shown in mathematical language is that on the basis of using q-order detrended 
covariance under s-scale to measure the multifractal correlation of multi-risk assets, the 
M-D model of multi-risk assets, and an empirical test of its effectiveness is carried out. 
Obviously, the M-D model of multi-risk assets should also consider investors’ diversified 
fluctuation magnitude importance situations and time scale attention situations. Both the 
order q and the scale s can take multiple constants variably. For the convenience of 
expression and highlighting the variable features of order and scale, q-order detrended 
covariance under s-scale is called ‘variable detrended covariance’.

Compared with the existing achievements, the contribution of this paper lies in the 
construction of the M-D portfolio model of multi-risk assets by using variable detrended 
covariance from the perspective of multifractal correlation of multi-risk assets, which can 
provide the strategical suggestions for the market participators faced with the multi- 
fractal correlation laid in assets, both contribute to the deepening of portfolio modelling 
research and the application of multi-fractal correlation. Thus, this paper contributes to 
the deepening and expansion of both modern portfolio theory and fractal market theory 
from a theoretical perspective. This is what makes the M-D model unique relative to 



MATHEMATICAL AND COMPUTER MODELLING OF DYNAMICAL SYSTEMS 739

existing portfolio models. So, this research is not only beneficial for mixing the portfolio 
theory and fractal market theory but also helps the enhancement of the portfolio model. 
The rest of the paper is organized as follows: Section 2 is the construction of M-D model 
of multi-risk assets, Section 3 is an empirical analysis of the effectiveness of the 
M-D model of multi-risk assets, and Section 4 is the conclusion.

2. Model building
Due to construct multi-risk assets of the M-D model need to use variable detrended 
covariance to measure multifractal correlation of return rates on assets, specifically 
including measuring multifractal autocorrelation of each asset return series (multifractal 
variance measurement) and correlation between different asset return series (multifractal 
covariance measurement), and embed them into the modern portfolio theory return-risk 
criterion to solve the investment weights of each asset. Therefore, it is necessary to give 
a proper interpretation of the return-risk criterion and variable detrended covariance. To 
this end, the following firstly explains the reward-risk criterion. Secondly, expounds the 
variable detrended covariance. And lastly, the M-D model of multi-risk assets is con
structed based on the return-risk criterion and variable detrended covariance measure.

2.1. Return-risk criterion

When constructing the optimal investment portfolio of risky assets, the reward-risk 
criterion (RRC) plays a crucial role. It can be known from modern portfolio theory 
that the optimal portfolio of risky assets is derived from the efficiency frontier of 
investment portfolio, which must meet RRC, namely the constructed investment portfo
lio should realize risk minimization when the return is fixed or return maximization 
when the risk is fixed (Markowitz 1952; Merton 1972; Giorgi et al. 2011). Because the 
reward-risk criterion is often used to measure the returns and risks of securities based on 
expectations and variances, it is often referred to as the mean-variance criterion (Levy 
and Sarnat 1971; Ismail and Pham 2019).

According to RRC, if portfolio P is composed of m types of risk assets fY m

It can be seen from Eq. (2.2) that, when covariance, variance and expectation are used 

to measure the correlations, risks and expected returns of risky assets, RRC is the mean- 
variance criterion. At this point, the optimal weight of risk assets is affected by covar
iances, variances, and expected returns. Therefore, when the covariances, variances, and 
expected returns are not measured accurately, the calculated optimal weights will also be 
wrong, which ultimately affect the effectiveness of the model. Because the autocorrela
tions (measure volatility risk) and the correlations have the most obvious impact on the 
effect of the portfolio, which directly affects the effect of risk diversification. Therefore, it 
is particularly important to accurately measure the correlations and autocorrelations 
when building a portfolio. It is precisely because of this that, in the actual situation of 
returns on assets are multifractal correlated, variance and covariance are difficult to 
accurately measure the risks and the correlations. And it is necessary to use measures that 
can accurately measure multifractal correlations and autocorrelations, then embed the 
measures into RRC to replace covariance and variance to optimize the M-V model of 
multi-risk assets.

2.2. Variable detrended covariance

In order to accurately capture the multifractal correlations of returns on assets, the 
MF-DCCA method has been proposed (Zhao et al. 2018). Moreover, a large number 
of scholars have shown that,  variable detrended covariance or called q-order 
detrended covariance under s-scale in MF-DCCA can accurately measure the multi
fractal correlation between time series (Shahzad et al. 2017; Cai and Ren 2019). The 
multi-fractal correlation can be understood to mean that for the series of correlation 
coefficients fxtg formed by the series of asset returns in different subintervals, if there 
has a smooth increment and holds for all moments t and orders q,

Based on Eq. (2.5), when there is a multifractal correlation between returns on assets 
series, the power law relationship Fijðq; sÞ,shijðqÞ must be hold, and the generalized scale 
index hijðqÞ will change with the order q. Then ln Fijðq; sÞ and ln s can be used as double 
logarithms coordinates using the regression method to find the generalized scale index, 
and judge whether the returns on assets series have multifractal correlations by observing 
the relationship between hijðqÞ and q. Meanwhile, Fijðq; sÞ ¼ Fjiðq; sÞ is established. In 
addition, when friðt n

Þgt¼1 ¼ frjðt n
Þgt¼1, Ff ðsÞ in Eq. (2.4) will become the variance or 

autocorrelation of measuring each subsequence after removing trend, and Fijðq; sÞ in Eq. 
(2.5) will become Fiiðq; sÞ or Fjjðq; sÞ, used to measure the fluctuations of the return rate 
sequences under q and s. In fact, the calculation steps of calculating the variable 
detrended covariance, together with this step, are the MF-DCCA method.

From the calculation steps, it can be found that the q-order detrended covariance 
under s-scale Fijðq; sÞ will change with the change of q and s. Therefore, it is possible to 
measure the correlation between risk assets Yi and Yj under different fluctuation ranges 
and different scales by adjusting q and s. At the same time, since q and s can take any 
value from the interval ½qmin; qmax� (the subsequent analysis shows the value of qmin and 
qmax are −20 and 20 seperately.) and ½3; intð0:25nÞ� respectively, order q and scale s can be 
changed to take multiple values in the interval when considering investors’ diversifica
tion fluctuation amplitude importance situations and diversification time scale attention 
situations, so the q-order detrended covariance under s-scale can also be called the 
variable detrended covariance.

The variable detrended covariance is used to measure the multi-fractal correlations 
between different assets, which facilitates one to analyse the fine-grained structure of 
correlations between assets at different volatilities and at different scales. It will be 
more complex to consider multifractal correlations between assets as opposed to 
mono-fractal correlations between assets. Compared with using the DCCA cross- 
correlation coefficient to measure the mono-fractal correlation, the variable detrended 
covariance continues to consider the influence of different fluctuation amplitude. 
When considering mono-fractal correlations, the methodology used is usually 
a special case of MF-DCCA, which only considers the change in correlation triggered 
by a change in scale swhen order q is taken to be 2 and does not consider the change 
in correlation that occurs when both order q and scale sare changed. Without taking 



MATHEMATICAL AND COMPUTER MODELLING OF DYNAMICAL SYSTEMS 743

into account the importance that investors attach to volatility, this does not ade
quately depict the structure of the information about correlations between assets. 
Consequently, using the variable detrended covariance to measure the multifractal 
correlation between assets and optimizing the portfolio model accordingly is an 
extension, which can be more adaptable to market environments where there is 
a multifractal correlation between assets than constructing portfolios by considering 
the unifractal correlation between assets.

As can be seen from the above that, when there are multifractal correlations between 
returns on risk assets, the correlations between risk assets will be different under different 
degrees of importance of fluctuation ranges and different scales observation intervals. 
The variable detrended covariance Fijðq; sÞ in MF-DCCA can precisely measure the 
multifractal correlations under different fluctuation ranges and time scales by adjusting 
the degree of importance of fluctuation range q and time scale observation interval s, so 
as to make up for the imperfections of the M-V model and other existing portfolio 
models that do not take into account multifractal correlations of multi-risk assets. 
Therefore, the variable detrended covariance Fijðq; sÞ can be used as a measure of multi
fractal correlation into RRC to optimize the M-V model of multi-risk assets.

2.3. Construction of M-D model of multi-risk assets

On the basis of the previous analysis of RRC and variable detrended covariance, the 
variable detrended covariance Fijðq; sÞ can be embedded into RRC to construct 
a M-D model of multi-risk assets, to make up for the defect that existing researches fail 
to consider the multifractal correlations of the returns on assets. In order to correspond 
to the M-V model of multi-risk assets built by Eq. (2.1), it is still assumed that the 
investment portfolio P is composed of m types of risk assets fY m

of risk assets Yi, ωiðq; sÞ is the investment weight of risky asset Yi under the order q and 
scales. At this time, the expected return EP ðq; sÞ of the P can be calculated by Eq. (2.6).

According to Eq. (2.9) and Eq. (2.10), the M-D model constructed in this paper 
is applicable to multivariate asset portfolios with multiple fractal correlations. 
Because of the rise in the number of assets, it exceeds in difficulty the existing 
research results that only consider the multiple fractal correlations between two 
assets (Li et al. 2021). Meanwhile, unlike the mean-detrended cross-correlation 
analysis portfolio model constructed in the existing literature that targets mono- 
fractal correlations between asset returns, the M-D model targets multifractal 
correlations between assets, which is more conducive to incorporating investors’ 
emphasis on different volatility magnitudes into portfolio construction (Zhang et al.  
2022). Besides, compared with existing results that consider mono-fractal and 
multifractal correlations between assets (Li et al. 2023), the M-D model in this 
paper makes numerous scales s and orders q go ahead by Eq. (2.10), the investment 
cost issue brought by remixing the mean-detrended cross-correlation analysis port
folio modes.

To sum up, the multifractal correlations of the returns on assets can be measured by 
using the variable detrended covariance Fijðq; sÞ in MF-DCCA, the M-D model of multi- 
risk assets can better capture the multifractal correlations of the returns on assets than 
that of the M-V model of multi-risk assets by considering multiple scales and multiple 
orders. Thus, from an economic perspective, the M-D model is more advantageous for 
investors as it facilitates risk diversification through diversified or portfolio investments. 
At the same time, the optimal weight ωiðQ; SÞ under the M-D model of multi-risk assets 
comprehensively considers multiple scales and multiple orders, which is more refined 
than the M-V model of multi-risk assets, and easier to adapt to the realistic environment 
of the capital market. Therefore, the M-D model of multi-risk assets overcomes the 
defects of the M-V model of multi-risk assets and is beneficial to enhance the effect of 
the portfolio. In addition, since the M-D model is mainly constructed creatively for the 
multi-fractal correlations between assets, it is applicable when the market is a fractal 
market with multi-fractal characteristics between assets. The fractal market is an expan
sion of the efficient market, that is to say the efficient market is only a special case of the 
fractal market, so the M-D model will have a broader scope of application compared to 
existing models such as M-V model.

3. Empirical analysis
The foregoing theoretically discusses shows that the M-D model of multi-risk assets can 
make up for the imperfections of the M-V model of multi-risk assets and is beneficial to 
improving the performance. The following empirically test is further carried out to verify 
the effectiveness of the M-D model of multi-risk assets. In the empirical analysis, this 
paper takes the daily closing prices of industrial index, commercial index, real estate 
index, utility index, composite index and financial index in the Shanghai Stock Exchange 
as samples. And the sample interval is from 1 January 2004 to 1 January 2020. Because the 
industry indexes still have unsystematic risks, it is reasonable to use the industry indexes 
as samples. At the same time, the sample interval contains complete market quotation, 
which can fully reflect the effectiveness of the portfolio model under different market 
quotation, so the selection of the sample interval is representative.

3.1. Empirical test of multifractal correlations

Since the purpose of constructing the M-D model of multi-risk assets is to overcome the 
defects that the M-V model of multi-risk assets and other related studies have not 
considered the multifractal correlations, it is necessary to verify the existence of the 
multifractal correlations of the returns on assets first. Then, the solid foundation of using 
M-D model in practice can be laid. At can be seen from the above that the MF-DCCA can 
be used for testing. For this purpose, the descriptive statistics on the sequences of the 
daily returns on six industry indexes are first conducted in Table 1.

Table 1 shows that the kurtosis of the sequences of the daily returns on each industry 
index is obviously greater than the kurtosis value zero of the Gaussian distribution, which 
has the characteristic of ‘high peak’. Meanwhile, the skewness of six sequences is not zero, 
which reflects the asymmetry and ‘heavy tail’ characteristics of the return rate distribu
tion. And in addition to financial indices, the distribution of the other five industry 
indexes return rate sequences is negative skew. Therefore, from the descriptive statistics 
in Table 1, it can be inferred that the daily returns on industry indexes have the 
characteristics of ‘high peak and heavy tails’, which are inconsistent with the assumption 
that return rates follow the normal distribution in an efficient market. Thus, it can be 
concluded that the capital market is not an efficient market, and there may be multi
fractal correlations, which can be further tested. In view of this, according to the above 
introduction of MF-XA method, a total of 21 kinds of correlations between the six 
industry indexes can be obtained by analysing the correlation between the six industry 
indexes. Among them, there are six kinds of correlations between the industry index itself 
and itself, which are special multifractal correlation, namely the multifractal

autocorrelation or fluctuation of the industry indexes. The relationship between order q 
and generalized scale index hijðqÞ in 21 cases are shown in Figure 1.

As can be seen from Figure 1 that when using MF-DCCA to analyse the correlation 
between the six industry indexes, the generalized scale index hijðqÞ of 21 cases will change 
with the change of the order q. Thus, Figure 1 shows that the capital market is not an 
efficient market and is a multifractal market, there are multifractal correlations of the 
industry indexes. This research sits comfortably with some scholar’ views that the 
security market has multi-fractal characters and the multi-fractal correlations exist in 
assets (Shahzad et al. 2017; Bouoiyour et al. 2018). Compared with some current research 
that mono-fractal correlation lies in assets (Zhang et al. 2022), this paper pay more 
attention to explore multi-fractal correlations between different asset, and the recogni
tion of complicated correlations about assets are improved. As a matter of fact, if the 
capital markets are efficient, the generalized scale index hijðqÞ is a constant (its value is 
o.5) that cannot change as the order qchanges. Meanwhile, Figure 1 also shows that when 
jqj> 20, the generalized scale index hijðqÞ gradually becomes stationary, that is, when 
jqj> 20, Fijðq; sÞ will tend to be stable with respect to the change of q, so q can be valued 
between −20 and 20 in practice.

It can be seen from the above that the capital market has multifractal features, and 
industry indexes have multifractal correlations. Since the M-V model of multi-risk assets 
does not consider the multifractal correlations of the risk assets, it is difficult to adapt to the 



748 H. LI ET AL.

real environment of the capital market. Thus, it is necessary to consider the multifractal 
correlations of the risk assets when optimizing the portfolio, and the construction of the 
M-D model of multi-risk assets has empirical support. In practice, the market environment 
of using M-D model is authentic and utilizing M-D model is feasible to do investment.

3.2. Effectiveness test of M-D model of multi-risk assets

On the basis of verifying that the capital market has multifractal features, the 
following is an empirical analysis of the actual effect of the M-D model of multi- 
risk assets by comparing and analysing the performance of the six industry indexes 
under the M-D and M-V models. There are two ingredients for choosing the 
M-V model as a benchmark: First, the structured M-D model is the improvement 
of the M-V model. Adopting the M-V model as the benchmark can examine 
whether the validity of the M-D model in practical application improves or not. 
Second, the M-V model plays a significant role in modern portfolio models. Using 
this model as a benchmark can help reflect the improvement of the M-D model in 
theory and practice. In order to ensure the rigour of the analysis process and the 
reliability of the results obtained, the following three points will be followed in the 
specific empirical analysis.

First, due to the merits and demerits of the portfolio model are mainly depend on the 
out of sample test results, so the whole sample interval is divided into 16 subintervals 
according to natural year in this paper, the data of each year is used as the ‘forming 
period’ to form the M-D and M-V, and the data of the following year is used as the 
‘testing period’ to test the effects of the previously built portfolios. There are 15 forming 
periods and 15 testing periods. The 15 forming periods and 15 testing periods are 
essentially subintervals of the entire sample interval. This treatment not only satisfies 
the extrapolation of the sample but also facilitates obtaining the performance of each 
testing period and the performance sequence of the entire sample interval, laying the 
groundwork for the back-testing test using different performance measures in the later 
section. At the same time, M-D model and M-V model have the same forming period and 
testing period, which means that the number of transactions under the two models are 
exactly the same, so when comparing and analysing the investment performance of 
M-D model and M-V model, whether to consider the transaction cost issue does not 
affect the relative merits of the two.

Second, when Eq. (2.2) and (2.10) are respectively used to construct the M-V model 
and the M-D model of six industry indexes, in order to fully explore the performance 
differences of the two portfolio models under different established returns, this article 
combines the established returns u commonly used by portfolio investors, and sets 
u 2 f0:05; 0:10; 0:15; 0:20; 0:25; 0:30; 0:35; 0:40g to analyse the performance of the two 
kinds of portfolios under eight types of established returns.

Third, when building the M-D model according to Eq. (2.10), it is necessary to set the 
investor’s degree of preference αiðq; sÞ for the order q and scale s. In practice, due to the 
portfolio investors usually have longer investment periods, they usually tend to prefer 
a longer time scale. At the same time, because the frequency of small fluctuations in 
security prices is much higher than that of large fluctuations, people tend to pay more 
attention to frequently occurring situations under the influence of cognitive biases, then

longer scales and small fluctuation ranges (Type 3, T-3). For the three types of relative 
preferences, taking into account the number of trading days in a year, that’s about 242

survivor bias, but rather a performance enhancement of the M-D model that 
compensates for the shortcomings of the M-V model that fails to take into account 
the multiple fractal correlations that actually exist between assets. It shows that

under the three preference types of T-1, T-2 and T-3, the M-D model is superior to 
the M-V model in general. In Tables 2 to 4, the performance of M-D is not as good 
as that of M-V for the years 2005, 2008, 2009, 2011, and 2012. This is due to the 
fact that the prices of the stock market indices in these years show a homogeneous 
peer-to-peer trend of unilateral upward or unilateral downward movement, resulting 
in the weak multi-fractal correlation between different indices, which is not able to 
satisfy the prerequisites of the M-D model in terms of the existence of multi-fractal 
correlation among the assets, which, on the contrary, implies the superiority of the 
use of the M-D model in the case of the existence of the multi-fractal correlation 
among the assets. Thereby, Tables 2 and 4 provide empirical support for the 
performance optimization of the M-D model from a yield perspective.

Thus, from the view of return rates, Tables 2 to 4 have proved that the 
M-D model is better than the M-V model on the whole, which improves invest
ment performance and achieves the goal of optimization. From a practical invest
ment perspective, as long as the return of M-D model is better than that of 
M-V model in most of the time, even if the difference is not significant each 
time, the performance of M-D model will be better than that of M-V model under 
multiple transactions. At the same time, by taking cumulative excess return rates 
of the M-D under T-3 type as an example, it can be found that the performance of 
M-D model is significantly better than that of M-V model at the 1% significance 
level. Due to the return rate is a performance measurement index without risk 
adjustment, which cannot fully reflect the effect of the portfolio model in diversi
fying risks while obtaining returns, namely it is impossible to judge the advantages 
and disadvantages of the portfolio model in implementing RRC.

Common risk-adjusted performance measures used in the selection of evaluation 
metrics are the Sharpe ratio, Treynor ratio, and return-risk ratio. In practice, portfolio 
models tend to contain a certain amount of unsystematic risk, but the Treynor ratio 
measures risk in terms of Beta which only measures systematic risk, which may result 
in a large bias. Meanwhile, the return-risk ratio and Sharpe ratio measure the return 
that can be obtained by taking a unit of risk. But the Sharpe ratio differs from the 
return-risk ratio in that the risk-free return is deducted from the return obtained by 
taking a unit of risk, which does not make a fundamental difference in measuring the 
return obtained by taking a unit of risk. Although the returns on short-term treasury 
bonds, interest on short-term bank deposits, etc., are usually regarded as risk-free 
returns, strictly speaking, risk-free returns do not exist in practice, and they should 
theoretically be constants. If the Sharpe ratio is chosen as the performance measure, it 
may be biased by the selection of the risk-free return. So it is more reasonable to 
choose the return-risk ratio in verifying whether the M-D model satisfies the RRC 
better than the benchmark model.

Therefore, in order to further verify that the M-D model is better than the 
M-V model in RRC realization, the following uses the return-risk ratio as the risk- 
adjusted performance measurement indicator to analyse the effectiveness of the 
M-D model. For brevity, the following only gives a comparative analysis of the return- 
risk ratio of M-D and M-V under T-3 type preference. The differences of the return- 
risk ratio between the 120 M-D under T-3 type preference and the 120 M-V are shown 
in Table 5.



752 H. LI ET AL.

According to Table 5, there are 65 cases in which the differences between the 
return-risk ratio of the M-D than that of them M-V are greater than zero, account
ing for 54.17%. Since the return-risk ratio measures the cumulative return rates 
obtained by the unit risk taken, a higher return-risk ratio means that the investment 
portfolio is better at maximizing returns and minimizing risks, and is more in line 
with RRC. Thus, Table 5 shows that the M-D model is more compliant with RRC 
than the M-V model, and the M-D model is still effective under the risk-adjusted 
performance measurement indicator. As a result, under the risk-adjusted perfor
mance measures, the empirical results also reflect the improved performance of the 
M-D model in compensating for the shortcomings of the M-V model, providing 
evidence to support the improvement of the M-D model.

Tables 2 to 5 use the return rates and the return-risk ratio as performance 
measures, which from the unadjusted and risk-adjusted views verify the effective
ness of the M-D model relative to the M-V model respectively. Although Tables 2 
to 5 set the investor’s preference for the time s and the orderq when verifying the 
effectiveness of the M-D, it should be pointed out that when investors’ preference 
for scale and order as other values, similar results can be obtained. Moreover, 
when investing according to the M-D model and the M-V model respectively for 
a long time, the superiority of the M-D will be more obvious. For this reason, take 
the scale and order of investors’ preference as S ¼ f50; � � � ; 60g and 
Q ¼ f␀ 20; � � � ; ␀ 10g respectively as an example for illustration, that is, when 
there are s 2 S and q 2 Q, take αiðq; sÞ¼121␀ 1, otherwise take αiðq; sÞ¼0. For the 
sake of intuition and simplicity, the following Figure 2 only shows the cumulative 
return sequences of the M-D and M-V in the sample range under eight kinds of 
established returns.

Figure 2 shows that under the eight kinds of established returns, there are 94 
cases where the cumulative return rates of the M-D are greater than that of the 
M-V, accounting for 78.33% of the total 120 cases. As can be seen that the 
cumulative return rates of the M-D are higher than that of the M-V in most 
cases. Thus, it not only verifies that long-term use of the M-D model can improve 
the superiority of the model, but also verifies the effectiveness of the M-D model 
under other preference conditions.

In summary, under the reality cases that the returns on assets have multifractal 
correlations, whether from the view of yields, the view of return-risk ratio, or the 
view of cumulative yields, the M-D model under any preference, is generally better 
than the M-V model and more in line with RRC. Therefore, the empirical results 
are consistent with the theoretical analysis, and the M-D model that takes into 
account the multifractal correlations of the returns on assets is effective and can 
overcome the defects of the M-V model. In actual investment, investors using the 
M-D model can obtain better investment performance, better diversification of risk 
while obtaining returns, and improve the effectiveness of portfolio investment 
management.

Figure 2. The cumulative return sequences of M-D and M-V.

4. Conclusion
In view of the existing portfolio model studies have not considered the defect of multi
fractal correlations of the returns on assets, this paper incorporates the multifractal 
correlations of the returns on assets into the portfolio model of multi-risk assets. On 
the basis of using variable detrended covariance to measure multifractal correlations of 
the returns on assets, the variable detrended covariance are embedded into the reward- 
risk criterion, the M-D model of multi-risk assets is constructed, and the analytical 
solution of the model is given. The theoretical analysis shows that the M-D model 



754 H. LI ET AL.

comprehensively considers multiple scales and multiple orders, which is more refined 
than the M-V model of multi-risk assets, and overcomes the defects of M-V model.

In addition to completing the theoretical construction of the M-D model, this 
paper confirms that the real securities market is a fractal market with multi-fractal 
correlations between assets, indicating the feasibility for investors to use the 
M-D model in their investment practice. Additionally, because investors prefer 
a longer scale or pay more attention to a smaller fluctuation range in practice, the 
investors can be divided into three parts: investors only prefer longer scales (T-1), 
investors only prefer small fluctuation ranges (T-2), and investors prefer both 
longer scales and small fluctuation ranges (T-3). Investors with different prefer
ences can invest using the M-D model by adjusting the order qand scale 
saccording to their preferred type of investment. Besides, the empirical results 
show that under the T-1, T-2, and T-3 type preferences, the proportions in which 
the return rates of the M-D are higher than that of the M-V are 60.00%, 53.33% 
and 53.33%, respectively. When investing in accordance with the M-D model and 
the M-V model respectively for a long time, evaluation indicators based on 
cumulative rates of return show the superiority of the M-D will be more obvious. 
So, compared to the M-V model, the M-D model not only can help investors to 
improve the return rates, but also help investors to better realize RRC, providing 
an empirical basis for the theoretical analysis results.

The research results of this paper provide a better decision-making basis for 
market participants seeking higher performance in practice. Furthermore, in 
theory, this paper helps promote the effective integration of modern portfolio 
theory and fractal theory, advancing both portfolio theory and fractal market 
theory. Notably, the model in this paper presupposes the existence of multi
fractal correlations in asset returns and is therefore mainly applicable to fractal 
markets. If the securities market developed into the desired efficient market, 
then the M-D portfolio model would face limitations. Fortunately, existing 
research results show that the existence of feedback traders in real markets 
and the adoption of feedback trading behaviour by investors leads to the exis
tence of multi-fractal features in securities markets (Wu et al. 2015). Therefore, 
as long as there are feedback traders in the securities market, there will be 
a suitable environment for the use of the M-D model. In addition, since the 
calculation of the variable detrended covariance when using the M-D model 
requires the use of software such as Matlab or Python, this does not dispropor
tionately affect institutional investors with specialized knowledge, but it may 
limit the use of some individual investors who lack programming knowledge. At 
the same time, since it takes more than 5 min to calculate the investment weights 
of the M-D model by using an ordinary computer, there will be a limitation on 
high-frequency trading under 5 min.

The unique contribution of this paper is to incorporate multiple fractal correla
tions among assets into the research framework of portfolio model optimization 
and construct the M-D portfolio model of multi-risk assets. Based on the research 
in this paper, in the future, the M-D model constructed in this paper can be 



MATHEMATICAL AND COMPUTER MODELLING OF DYNAMICAL SYSTEMS 755

embedded into cross-sectional momentum or inverse rotation investment strate
gies to further optimize the feedback in behavioural finance of trading strategies, 
the M-D model can also be extended to multi-objective and multi-stage portfolio 
models. Meanwhile, the variable detrended covariance extracted from the MF- 
DCCA in the construction of the M-D model in this paper can measure the multi- 
fractal correlation between time series, so we can refer to scholars’ ideas on the 
application of the mono-fractal correlation measure, the DCCA cross-correlation 
coefficient (Zebende 2011; Kristoufek 2015), and consider its further use in the 
regression of multifractal correlated time series.

Network-Based Identification of Risk Contagion Pathways Between U.S. Credit 
and Equity Markets During Stress Periods 
Jiahui Han 
Master of Finance, MIT Sloan School of Management, MA, USA 

DOI: 10.69987/JACS.2026.60204 

   

K e y w o r d s   A b s t r a c t  

Financial contagion,  This paper investigates risk contagion pathways between U.S. credit and equity 
Network topology, markets during periods of financial stress through network-based 
Granger causality, methodologies. The study constructs both correlation- and Granger-causality-
Systemic risk based networks to identify transmission channels and quantify contagion 

intensity across market segments from 2008 to 2024. Using daily credit default 
swap (CDS) spreads and equity sector indices, we analyze the evolution of 
network topology during three major stress episodes: the 2008 financial crisis, 
the 2020 COVID-19 market turbulence, and the 2023 regional banking stress. 
Network centrality measures reveal systemically important transmission 
nodes, while time-varying connectivity patterns demonstrate significant 
amplification of cross-market linkages during stress periods. The empirical 
findings indicate that financial sector stocks serve as primary transmission 
channels from credit to equity markets, with contagion strength increasing 
sharply (more than threefold) during crisis periods compared to normal times. 
The research provides quantitative evidence for regulatory frameworks 
focused on systemic risk monitoring and contributes methodological insights 
for identifying vulnerable transmission pathways in interconnected financial 
systems.

The Multifractal Nature of Cross‑Correlations 
between Emerging Market Equities and Financial Assets: 
An Econophysics Perspective

Turker Acikgoz1 

Accepted: 7 May 2025 / Published online: 26 May 2025 
© The Author(s) 2025

Abstract
Emerging markets have achieved significant economic milestones, garnering 
increased attention from international investors and academics. However, these 
markets present numerous economic, political, and social risks that significantly 
influence the performance of equities. Consequently, effective risk management for 
investments in emerging markets has become a critical issue requiring resolution. To 
this end, this paper examines the multifractal cross-correlations between emerging 
economy stock markets and various financial instruments—including bonds, com-
modities, energy commodities, cryptocurrencies, and developed market equities—to 
illustrate the nonlinear dynamics and interconnectedness. This analysis aims to facil-
itate effective risk management for investments in emerging markets. Unlike previ-
ous studies, which predominantly utilized linear and bivariate analyses, this study 
contributes by offering a comprehensive multifractal perspective on asset intercon-
nectedness, significantly enhancing the effectiveness over conventional econometric 
approaches. By employing the MFDCCA (Multifractal Detrended Cross-Correla-
tion Analysis) method, we analyze the return and volatility series of these finan-
cial assets, revealing strong, complex, and nonlinear dynamics. Our results indicate 
significant and persistent cross-correlations, particularly between emerging market 
equities and developed equities, commodities, and energy commodities, with these 
correlations strengthening over larger time scales. Cryptocurrencies, however, show 
significantly weaker correlations with emerging markets. In this context, the pres-
ence of multifractality suggests that these assets operate within a complex, adaptive 
system, potentially challenging the applicability of the Efficient Market Hypothe-
sis. The economic implications are significant; these findings suggest that equities 
from emerging markets might be effectively diversified or hedged with assets from 
developed markets. The persistence in these cross-correlations can offer valuable 
insights for investors concerning optimal portfolio allocation during both stable and 
volatile market periods. For policymakers, these insights could prove beneficial in 

Extended author information available on the last page of the article

Vol.:(0123456789)



	3608 T. Acikgoz 

anticipating systemic risks and advancing financial stability, given that emerging 
market equities are shown to be interconnected with global financial assets.

Keywords  Multifractality · Nonlinear Dynamics · Complex Systems · Risk 
Management · Emerging Markets

1  Introduction

Emerging markets have been increasingly garnered attention from international 
investors and academics. This heightened interest stems from the fact that these mar-
kets have consistently outperformed advanced economies and have demonstrated 
successful economic performance over the past several decades.

Over the past several decades, the world has witnessed remarkable shifts in the 
composition of global economic performance (see Fig.  1). In the early 1980 s, 
emerging markets accounted for approximately 16–17% of global GDP. Since then, 
the share of emerging markets in global economy has grown rapidly. By 2022, these 
markets contribute 36% to the global gross domestic product. In contrast, the most 
advanced economies (G7)1 now constitute only 44% of global output, a significant 
decrease from their average share of around 64% in the early 1980 s. This conver-
gence in the global GDP composition is clearly depicted in Fig. 1, illustrating that 
emerging markets have consistently outperformed most advanced economies.

The data undeniably shows that emerging market economies are becom-
ing increasingly vital to the global economy. These economies have consistently 
achieved a high degree of economic growth, emerging as significant contributors to 
global economy and becoming one of the most important actors in the global trade 
and finance. Furthermore, this trend is accompanied by substantial financial returns, 
resulting from high degree of corporate income growth (Ballester et al., 2019).

The late 1980 s and 1990 s marked a milestone for emerging market economies. 
A majority of these countries underwent significant structural changes during this 
era (Al Nasser & Hajilee, 2016). Since the late 1980 s, with the increasing force of 
globalization and the emergence of unipolar world system, these economies adopted 
neoliberal policies. They embarked on financial liberalization and began integrat-
ing into international markets (Nazlioglu et al., 2022). One of the primary structural 
changes in emerging markets was the opening of domestic financial markets to for-
eign investors and institutions (Lucey & Zhang, 2011), by decreasing the degree of 
government intervention in finance and banking industries (Al Nasser & Hajilee, 
2016). The liberal transformation, along with the reshaped financial and institutional 
structures and changing macroeconomic dynamics and trade policies in emerging 
markets, has made international investors view these markets as attractive options 

1  G7 refers to the Group of Seven, an intergovernmental political forum that includes the seven largest 
advanced economies in the world: the United States, Germany, the United Kingdom, France, Japan, Italy, 
and Canada, along with the European Union as an additional, non-numbered member.



The Multifractal Nature of Cross‑Correlations between Emerging… 3609

Fig. 1   World GDP Composition. (Note: Author’s own calculation based on the data obtained from IMF 
and classification of MSCI’s emerging markets) (The definition covers 24 emerging market economies, 
namely Brazil, Chile, China, Czech Republic, Egypt, Greece, Hungary, India, South Korea, Kuwait, 
Malaysia, Mexico, Peru, Philippines, Poland, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, South Africa, Taiwan, Thailand, Tür-
kiye, United Arab Emirates.)

for diversifying their portfolios, driven by the potential for higher profitability 
(Bekaert & Harvey, 2003; Bekaert et al., 2002, 2011; Nazlioglu et al., 2022).

Emerging market economies are recognized as significant contributors to global 
growth and present as an investment option for international investors (Brzeszczyński 
et  al., 2015; Donadelli & Persha, 2014; Koesrindartoto et  al., 2020; Rajan & Zin-
gales, 2003). These investors are drawn to emerging stock markets due to the high 
level of financial returns, which can be attributed to key characteristics of emerging 
markets such as swift economic growth, young and growing workforce, and rich nat-
ural reserves (Khan et al., 2023). However, there is no gain without corresponding 
risks. While emerging market equities offer high returns, they are riskier than equities 
from developed countries and are exposed to numerous challenges including politi-
cal instability, volatile local currencies, sensitivity to capital flows from advanced 
economies, political and geopolitical conflicts, corporate governance issues, forms 
of government, and inadequate asset pricing by domestic investors (Balcilar et  al., 
2022; Khan et al., 2023; Li et al., 2022; Roszkowska & Langer, 2019), among other 
factors. In the finance literature, it is well-documented that emerging markets exhibit 
higher return and volatility compared to advanced economies (Bekaert & Harvey, 
1995; Claessens et al., 1995; De Santis & İmrohoroğlu, 1997). The reasons for this 
phenomenon can be attributed to the aforementioned factors.

Given the framework outlined above, a critical question emerges: To what extent 
and with which assets can we effectively hedge risks and manage return volatil-
ity in emerging market equities? This question is of significant importance to both 
practitioners and academics. Answering the question depends on understanding 
how emerging market equities are interconnected with alternative assets. The issue 
extends beyond international investors; domestic investors are also interested in 
hedging risks in emerging markets due to the limited options available for hedg-
ing, as short selling is often not allowed or is extremely restricted in these markets 



	3610 T. Acikgoz 

(Jobst, 2008; Lin et al., 2022; Maggi & Fantazzini, 2012; Saxena & Villar, 2008). 
Consequently, this study aims to explore the interconnectedness between emerging 
market equities and other financial assets, and to evaluate whether emerging market 
equities can be hedged with other financial assets, such as (i) bonds, (ii) commodi-
ties, (iii) energy commodities, (iv) cryptocurrencies, and (v) global equities.

The literature on the relationship between emerging market equities and other 
financial assets is quite limited. For instance, Sadorsky (2014) provides insights 
into the volatility dynamics between emerging stock markets and commodities such 
as copper, oil and wheat. He uses VARMA-GARCH and DCC-AGARCH models 
to generate dynamic conditional correlations and evaluates hedging performances. 
The results show significant comovements between emerging market equities and 
commodities after the global financial crisis of 2008. Basher and Sadorsky (2016) 
conduct a similar study to Sadorsky (2014) using different multivariate GARCH 
models. They evaluate volatility spillovers between emerging market equities, oil, 
gold and bond prices. The authors conclude that oil is the best hedging alterna-
tive for emerging market equities. Mizerka et  al. (2020) examine the relationship 
between Bitcoin and developed/emerging stock markets with users graph method 
and GARCH models. They document no significant relationship between Bitcoin 
and stock markets. Bhatia and Basu (2021) analyze the asymmetric effect of energy 
commodities shocks on emerging stock markets from a sectoral perspective. The 
authors use a non-parametric causality-in-quantiles approach and document that 
crude oil shocks have a strong impact on emerging stock markets. In their study, 
Wang et  al. (2021) investigate whether Bitcoin has a comparative advantage over 
conventional assets (crude oil, gold, commodities, U.S. Dollar index) in terms of 
hedging ability against stock markets (developed and emerging markets, US, China). 
They provide evidence from time and frequency domain connectedness analysis and 
exhibit that for emerging market equities, gold and USD are the best hedging alter-
natives among all. By using time and frequency connectedness approach, Balcilar 
et al. (2022) analyze interconnectedness between 27 emerging markets and crypto-
currencies. The results exhibit that cryptocurrencies cannot be utilized for hedging 
emerging market equities. Zghal et  al. (2022) investigate the association between 
various regional equity markets and commodities. The authors use different multi-
variate GARCH approaches to evaluate the findings. They conclude that commodi-
ties cannot diversify international emerging equity portfolios successfully. Jena et al. 
(2023) examine the interconnectedness of emerging markets with global financial 
markets such as US equities, crude oil and dollar index using wavelet denoised vola-
tility spillovers. Their findings show that emerging market equities are highly con-
nected to global financial markets in the long run.

The abovementioned studies are invaluable for understanding the correlation 
and spillover dynamics between emerging stock markets and other financial assets. 
However, they lack two important points. The first one is that the previous literature 
does not present a comprehensive study on how emerging market equities and other 
assets are interconnected. They only examine relationships from a low-dimensional 
perspective, mostly considering bivariate relationships. This paper fills this gap in 
the literature and documents a comprehensive guide on the nexus. Secondly, most 
of these studies have addressed the issue using linear approaches, predominantly 



The Multifractal Nature of Cross‑Correlations between Emerging… 3611

relying on the fundamental theory of finance, called Efficient Market Hypothesis 
(EMH). On the other hand, financial markets are complex systems that cannot be 
fully explained completely by traditional econometric models, which are mostly 
based on linear approaches (Niu & Wang, 2014; Fu et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2022). 
The literature has shown that financial markets are not efficient as EMH claims 
(Telli & Chen, 2021). The EMH asserts that (i) asset prices reflect all information 
that has been publicly disclosed, (ii) all market participants have equal access to the 
information and (iii) prices are formed by rational investors (Fama, 1970). Under 
the EMH, there should not exist any fractal properties in the market (Telli & Chen, 
2021). In contrast to EMH of Fama (1970), the empirical literature in econophysics 
has shown many times that most financial markets exhibit multifractal features.

As an alternative perspective to the EMH, the Fractal Market Hypothesis (FMH) 
emerged. For a long time, the literature has discussed that FMH can explain and 
describe financial markets better than EMH (Matia et al., 2003; Ali & Gupta, 2011). 
This is because that FMH approaches capital markets as complex systems charac-
terized by nonlinear dynamics, with interactive and adaptive features (Guo et  al., 
2021). Unlike the strict and unrealistic assumptions of the EMH, FMH provides a 
more practical and realistic way for understanding the real world (Pan et al., 2022).

In line with the EMH perspective, researchers maintain the view that the market 
operates in a state of random walk, where past events have no influence on future 
trends, making short-term market predictions impractical (Huang et al., 2023). On 
the other side, according to the FMH, markets exhibit fractal patterns, and histori-
cal events do influence future market trends, thus enabling the use of historical 
data for short-term predictions. Peters (1993) offered the FMH as an alternative to 
EMH, applying Hurst exponents and fractal Brownian motion to financial markets. 
The EMH has limitations in its ability to explain economic phenomena, whereas 
the FMH offers a more realistic explanation for the examination of economic occur-
rences (Huang et al., 2023). Fractal theory and fractal Brownian motions were pri-
marily suggested by Mandelbrot (1963) and Mandelbrot and Van Ness (1968). Sub-
sequently, Peters (1991, 1993) innovatively integrated chaos and fractal theories and 
employed them in the analysis of financial markets. The FMH takes into account 
the anomalies in the financial market, eliminates many assumptions of EMH, and 
employs nonlinear approaches to reflect the real dynamics of financial markets 
(Moradi et  al., 2019). Moreover, multifractal theory can provide detailed insights 
into various degrees of fluctuations in asset prices across different time scales (Man-
delbrot, 1999). Hence, when contrasted with monofractal theory, multifractal theory 
offers a superior understanding of the complex nonlinear dynamics within financial 
markets (Guo et al., 2021).

Statistical approaches that incorporate multifractality have demonstrated supe-
rior performance compared to traditional econometric models (Aslam et al., 2022), 
because they point out key features of asset prices such as fat tails (Gopikrishnan 
et al., 2001), long-term correlations (Alvarez-Ramirez et al., 2008), volatility clus-
tering (Kim & Eom, 2008), as well as chaotic behavior (Adrangi et al., 2001). More-
over, the standard correlation measures such as Pearson’s correlation coefficient or 
cross-correlation operate under the strict assumption of stationarity of the series, 
which is often problematic in many financial time series. Therefore, multifractal 



	3612 T. Acikgoz 

correlation measures provide a better understanding under these limitations (Kwap-
ien et  al., 2015). The literature also highlights similar characteristics in emerging 
markets as well. It has been shown many times that financial data from emerging 
markets do not follow a normal distribution and exhibit both large positive and nega-
tive returns (skewness) as well as fat-tailed distributions (see among others, Bekaert 
et al., 1998; Frankel & Poonawala, 2010; Conover, 2011; Atilgan et al., 2015; Nazli-
oglu et al., 2022). Thus, multifractal approaches are the best-suited tools for under-
standing emerging market equities.

Based on fractal theory, various methods have been developed to capture multi-
fractality and complex structures. Peng et al. (1994) introduced detrended fluctua-
tion analysis (DFA) to catch the long-range autocorrelation in non-stationary time 
series. Following this, with their pioneering work, Kantelhardt et al. (2002) offered 
multifractal detrended fluctuation analysis (MFDFA), the first method to reveal the 
multifractal features of non-stationary time series at different time scales. However, 
these studies only examine the multifractal dynamics of a univariate time series. 
Subsequently, Podobnik and Stanley (2008) proposed detrended cross-correlation 
analysis (DCCA) to measure long-range cross-correlations between two non-station-
ary series. Further, Zhou (2008) developed multifractal detrended cross-correlation 
analysis (MFDCCA), successfully combining the MFDFA and DCCA methods 
to analyze the multifractal features of two non-stationary time series. Building on 
Zhou’s work, further studies have emerged. For instance, Jiang and Zhou (2011) 
developed multifractal detrending moving-average cross-correlation (MFXDMA), 
which enhances Zhou’s method by using moving average windows for detrending 
process, while Oswiecimka et al. (2014) modified the detrended covariance defini-
tion of MFDCCA and proposed multifractal cross-correlation analysis (MF-CCA). 
Additional models have also been proposed in the literature, though they are not as 
widely recognized as MFXDMA and MF-CCA, to examine complex relationships 
(see, among others; Qian et al., 2015, 2024; Wei et al., 2017; Qian & Zhou, 2024). 
In this study, the fundamental method, MFDCCA, is chosen because it is more 
widely accepted by the general literature, is the most commonly used approach, and 
has been repeatedly shown to be robust.

Since Zhou (2008) proposed MFDCCA, it has been extensively used by research-
ers to examine multifractal cross-correlations in financial markets. MFDCCA has 
been employed to explore long-range nonlinear cross-correlations in the time series 
data of stock market (Li & Su, 2023; Pan et  al., 2022; Ruan et  al., 2023; Zhu & 
Fang, 2023), precious metals (Doğangün et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023), crude oil 
(Fernandes et al., 2022a, 2022b; Gaio & Capitani, 2023; Shao et al., 2023), crypto-
currencies (Aslam et al., 2023; Wątorek et al., 2022; Yan et al., 2022; Ruan et al., 
2021), green bonds (Fernandes et al., 2023), index futures (Jin et al., 2023), com-
modities (Liu et  al., 2022), agricultural commodities (Feng & Cao, 2022; Feng 
et al., 2022), energy markets (Fu et al., 2022; Ali et al., 2021), inflation (Fernandes 
et al., 2022a, 2022b), bonds (Yang et al., 2021), carbon market (Zhu et al., 2021) and 
economy policy uncertainty (Zhao & Dai, 2021).

This study contributes to the existing literature in two significant ways. First, it 
addresses a gap in previous research by offering a comprehensive perspective on the 
relationships and interactions between emerging market equities and other financial 



The Multifractal Nature of Cross‑Correlations between Emerging… 3613

assets. Unlike prior studies that focused solely on bivariate relationships, this study 
provides a more holistic view of these dynamics. Second, previous research has pri-
marily investigated the relationships between emerging market equities and other 
financial assets using linear and conventional econometric techniques, such as spill-
over indices or stochastic volatility models. However, it is widely acknowledged that 
financial markets exhibit complex behaviors characterized by nonlinear and multi-
fractal dynamics. These markets do not conform to the Efficient Market Hypothesis, 
instead, they exhibit fractal structures. This study employs multifractal approaches 
to investigate the nexus among emerging market equities and financial assets. The 
study also offers many practical implications. Investors in emerging equity markets 
or international investors who hold positions in these markets can use our findings 
for portfolio diversification, hedging, and making investment decisions.

The remainder of this paper organized into three chapters. The methodology sec-
tion introduces the research variables, their descriptive statistics, and the research 
models. The third chapter, titled “Empirical Findings” presents the research findings 
and discusses the multifractal cross-correlations between emerging market equities 
and financial markets. The final chapter contains the conclusion, which includes 
concluding remarks, practical implications, and suggestions for future studies.

2  Methodology

2.1  Data

The dataset comprises six financial time series, which are detailed in Table 1. Finan-
cial assets are chosen according to their essential role in global financial markets 
and their wide recognition in the literature. For emerging market equities, this study 
utilizes data from Morgan Stanley Capital International (MSCI) Emerging Market 
Index as a benchmark for emerging markets as a whole. This index includes mid 
and large-cap companies from 24 emerging economies and is widely recognized as 
a proxy for emerging market equities. The MSCI Emerging Markets Index is the 
globally recognized benchmark index for emerging market equities, representing 
both academic research and industry applications (see Basher & Sadorsky, 2016; 
Sadorsky, 2014; Uddin et al., 2018; Singh et al.,; 2019; Kristjanpoller et al., 2020;

Developed Aggregate Ex-Collateralized Bond Index. It is widely regarded to be

financial interconnectedness. To capture the dynamics of commodities, we use the 
S&P Goldman Sachs Commodity Index, a globally recognized benchmark for meas-

mid-cap stocks in 23 developed markets, which may be relevant when considering 
the state of global equity market integration research (Arif et al., 2022; Mroua et al., 
2024; Martins, 2024; Zhao & Park, 2024). Finally, to represent the cryptocurrency 
market, we include the Cryptocurrency Index 30, which tracks the 30 largest crypto-
currencies by market capitalization. The CCi30 has been used in recent studies that 
explore cryptocurrency market behavior and its relationship with traditional assets 
(Livieris et  al., 2022; Manahov, 2024; Neslihanoglu, 2021). We select these basic 
financial asset classes-equities, bonds, commodities, energy commodities, and cryp-
tocurrencies-to conduct a comprehensive analysis of the spillover between emerging 
market equities and other major financial markets. These asset classes are the most 
traded and represent core segments of financial markets; hence, they are of the most 
relevance for assessing risk management and diversification strategies.

Since this study aims to explore the multifractal features of cross-correlations 
between emerging market equities and financial assets, it is beneficial to investigate 
the interconnectedness from various perspectives. Thus, relationships in both first 
and second moments are examined.

lized in the analysis. Firstly, the return series are calculated as shown in Eq. 1. In

After constructing the return and volatility series for each variable, descriptive 
statistics for the return series are presented in Table 2, while graphical representa-
tion of data is displayed in Fig. 2.

The characteristics of the return series indicate that the means are approximately 
zero across all series. The median results also confirm that return series have a zero 
expected value. The sample space reveals extremely large positive and negative fluc-
tuations, with notably strong negative shocks in most of the series. For instance, the 
cryptocurrency market lost 48.4% of its value in just one day. Similarly, the energy 
commodity market experienced a −30.2% loss in a single trading day. In contrast, 
the equities and bond markets show relatively stable minimum and maximum values 
compared to others. When considering standard deviations, cryptocurrencies, com-
modities and emerging market equities exhibit relatively large values on average. 
The kurtosis and skewness values confirm that variables do not follow normal distri-
bution. The graphs in Fig. 2 illustrate an increasing trend in the level data. However, 
bond market has been experiencing a bearish market for a long time. The level data 
display a non-constant mean, with various local-means observable across different 
time scales. Return series reveal multiple volatility clusters and tail risks (several 
positive and negative fluctuations) throughout the research period. Volatility series 
show several extreme jumps, especially during the COVID-19 pandemic. To con-
clude, these features suggest that the markets should be evaluated using nonlinear 
and multifractal methodologies rather than linear approaches.

Step 6. For each value of q, determine the slope of log–log plot of Fxy(q, s) 
versus s. The slope gives generalized Hurst exponent for the corresponding q 
values. If there exists long-range cross-correlation between the two series, the 
fluctuation function Fxy(q, s) will exhibit a power-law dependency on segment 
size s which can be represented as follows:

Fxy(q, s) ∼ shxy(q) (11)

In order to obtain generalized Hurst exponents, Eq. 11 follows the estimation 
below:

( )

Here, C is a constant, and hxy(q) is known as the generalized Hurst exponent. 
The multifractal behavior between two series is determined by the slope of the 
log–log plots of Fxy(q, s) versus s. The generalized Hurst exponent is bounded by 
−∞ < hxy(q) < ∞ . If hxy(q) changes with different q values, then there exists mul-
tifractal cross-correlations behavior two non-stationary time series. Otherwise, if 
hxy(q) remains constant for all values of q, then we say that cross-correlations 
between the two series are monofractal.

Specifically, when the Hurst exponent hxy(2) (where q = 2) is higher than 0.5, 
the series exhibit persistent (positive) cross-correlation. In this case, cross-cor-
relations between two series exhibit long-term memory. Conversely, when anti-
persistent (negative) cross-correlations exist, the Hurst exponent is hxy(2) < 0.5 . 
Here, an increase (decrease) in one series is typically followed by a decrease 
(increase) in the other. Lastly, when hxy(2) = 0.5 , the two-time series do not dis-
play multifractal behavior in their cross-correlations, indicating that the series 
follows a random walk behavior.

to display the multifractal features. Renyi exponent can be calculated as fol-
lows:
