Figure 2 depicts the graphical representation of EWS analysis for each pair of mar-
ket with the Hong Kong’s Hang Seng index during the GFC period. The red line shows 
the real correlation paths based on Dynamic Conditional Correlation method, while the 
blue line indicates the correlations based on LSTM predictions. The absolute value of 
sigma parameter ranges between 1.5 and 3 according to the empirical finance literature 
(Tarantino & Cernauskas, 2009) where it represents a heuristic value to improve the 
signal performance. The threshold values are based on the various sigma levels where 
absolute values of higher sigma levels indicate expected persistence of potential volatil-
ity spillovers. Based on obtained results, the proposed model is able to generate sig-
nals well before the actual contagion began, except for the Hong Kong and Japan case 
where the first signal was detected only a few months ago. The prediction capability of 
the LSTM for information transmission channels is also strong and close to the actual 
path in most cases, except for the later stages in Singapore and China. In some cases, 
such as the US and Japan, the model signals several times within the 12-month period 
before the crisis occurs which is highlighting the potential risk of financial contagion 
between markets.

The picture is slightly different during the COVID-19 crisis period as presented in 
the Fig. 3. The test results of the model are stronger compared to the GFC period, thus 
making the risk contagion predictions highly accurate. As we can see in the blue lines, 
the LSTM model predicted most of the significant correlations and triggered alert well 
before the crisis occurs. Although, we focus on the COVID-19 crisis, one thing that 
should also be mentioned here is the trade war between China and the US in 2018 
which caused a rapid decline in major stock market indices all around the world in early 
2018. Specifically, in February 2018, the S&P 500 wiped out $2.8 trillion, while global 
indices had lost more than $5 trillion. The huge jumps in risk contagion during that 
time can be seen in the figure below, especially in the correlations with China, Tai-
wan, Malaysia and Indonesia. The models were able to predict the unexpected shock 
transmission in advance and signalled potential contagion effect. In some cases, multi-
ple signals were detected such as Hong Kong and Japan, and Hong Kong and Taiwan 
cases. When it comes to the COVID-19 crisis period, the proposed model identified 
financial distress among market pairs and signalled for the potential crisis event. How-
ever, the EWS system did not signal within the last 12-month period before the crisis 
occurred, which might be due to the unidirectional volatility spillovers from China to 
Hong Kong as revealed by Ahmed et al. (2021). Apart from that, we obtain strong evi-
dence supporting the high degree of efficacy and generalization capacity of the pro-
posed deep learning system.

Finally, the predictions are tested by using the RMSE and MSE criteria for each cri-
sis period as shown in Table 21. Based on the given empirical results, it can be clearly 
said that the proposed model provides extreme accuracy regarding volatility contagion 
effects between selected pairs. Specifically, the estimated correlations with Korea and 
the Philippines stock markets have smallest values for MSE criterion during the GFC 
period, followed by Malaysia with 0.7%. On the other hand, the prediction results 
are more superior for China and Korea during the COVID-19 crisis period based on 
the MSE loss function. Moreover, the highest error rate among all selected markets 
is found in the correlation series with Taiwan Stock Market based on MSE in both 
periods. Although the general failure rate is slightly higher in RMSE series, similar 

1 3



	2484 M. Sahiner 

results are found. When two crisis periods are compared in terms of model accuracy, 
the results draw a more complicated framework as it is hard to evaluate the clear supe-
riority. It should be noted that the accuracy of the predictions is highly dependent on 
the architecture of the deep learning model and training process. According to the train 
scores, there are no distinct differences for the predicted series except for Indonesia 
during the GFC period and Taiwan during the COVID-19 crisis period. In these two 
series, the model provides the largest error rates which may lead a bias for the testing 
period. Yet, the test scores are less affected, confirming the predictive accuracy of the 
proposed model.

6  Conclusion

Increased incidence of financial crises in the last few decades has reignited inter-
est in the role of financial linkages and crisis prediction models. Moreover, the 
pace of globalisation in the international financial markets has raised the question 
of whether interconnectedness between markets, a source for volatility transmis-
sion and possible contagion risk, can provide an early warning signal for crises. 
This paper examines volatility transmission channels across ten Asian markets 
and the US market for three different crisis periods and two calm periods by 
applying DCC, GARCH-BEKK, and Diebold-Yilmaz spillover index. In addition, 
we developed an early warning system to predict financial crises using the LSTM 
algorithm based on deep learning approach.

The empirical results indicate that the climb in external shock transmissions 
has long lasting impacts in domestic markets due to the contagion effect during 
the crisis periods, leading a more permanent surge in volatility spillovers across 
markets. Compared to the calm periods, all selected equity markets exposed 
intensified volatility spillovers during the crisis periods, confirming the findings 
of Suleman et al. (2017). However, it is revealed that the degree of volatility spill-
overs among advanced and emerging equity markets is less compared to the pure 
spillovers between advanced markets or emerging markets, offering a window of 
opportunity for international market participants in terms of portfolio diversifica-
tion and risk management. Thus, the outcome of the present study is not only rel-
evant to academics, but also to a wide range of investors. On the other hand, the 
proposed EWS system identified intensifying volatility transfers and generated 
signals within the last 12-month period before crises occur, suggesting important 
implications for policy makers since they need to take economic decisions during 
the crises times to prevent irreversible impacts on the broad economy due to the 
financial contagion. Of equal importance are the implications for risk and asset 
management practitioners, due to the fact that diversification advantages may 
continue to exist in turbulent periods.

The contribution of this paper to the field of empirical finance and existing lit-
erature is three-fold. First and foremost, this study explores all key relevant crises 

1 3



Volatility Spillovers and Contagion During Major Crises:… 2485

periods in the last three decades, including the recent COVID-19 crisis where there 
are still huge gaps due to the ongoing impacts. Therefore, the present study con-
tributes to the literature by providing comparison of interdependencies and chang-
ing intensity of contagion channels between markets for different periods. Second, 
the magnitudes and directions of volatility spillovers are verified for each selected 
calm and turbulent episodes, which offer key information for investors and financial 
regulators in terms of diversification benefits and macroeconomic stability. Third, 
instead of following earlier studies, we developed a novel EWS system and success-
fully predicted correlations and transmission channels with high accuracy, providing 
supplementary information that contributes the decision-making process of practi-
tioners, as well as offering indicative evidences that facilitate the assessment of mar-
ket vulnerability to policy-makers. Finally, the effectiveness and reliability of the 
LSTM model is confirmed with two different loss function to avoid false signals.

In a nutshell, the framework introduced here improves our ability to empiri-
cally evaluate as well as quantify volatility spillover and contagion channels in 
terms of financial market perspective. Furthermore, the proposed deep learning 
method in the present paper, allows us to identify and predict financial conta-
gion risk across selected countries. Consequently, the model provides signifi-
cant implications, not only for government related institutions, but also for mar-
ket participants in terms of possible contagion risks between selected markets. 
Thus, through the provided analysis in this study, policymakers can concentrate 
volatility transmission channels and make use of the model to maintain the finan-
cial stability, while market participants can benefit for managing their portfolio 
allocations and limit their risk exposure. Although the present study adopts wide 
range of Asian markets with a large dataset, the methodology here can be applied 
to EMEA region or different financial instruments; such as energy, bonds, cur-
rencies or cryptos after appropriate modifications. The main limitation of the 
study was accessing older data specifically for the emerging markets of Asia, and 
non-synchronous holidays in different markets which required special attention. 
Therefore, a further direction can be drawn by extending the data and parameters 
to propose an adaptive or coactive network based hybrid models. The value of 
such novel developments remains to be examined in future research endeavours.

﻿Anomalies, Roll’s Critique, and Proxy Error

Jaffe Greenwald∗

November 18, 2023

Abstract

Anomalies generate alphas. Roll (1977) notes that alphas contain two parts: the CAPM alpha

and a bias resulting from the assets that are omitted from the equity market proxy. However, the

size of the bias is not well understood. I develop a formal test that uses no arbitrage conditions

to quantify the bias. I find that 12 of 99 documented anomalies have statistically significant

bias, which range from .6% to 1.5%, annualized. I show that adding an anomaly as an additional

factor, to make a new proxy, reduces the biases across anomalies only when the added anomaly

had a significant bias. My test highlights that Roll’s Critique has sizable implications for asset

pricing. In addition, the test can help classify whether an anomaly has substantial exposure to

assets omitted from the equity market proxy. The test also provides a new proxy that may be

closer to the CAPM market.

∗Jaffe Greenwald is affiliated with University of Arizona; email: jaffegreenwald@arizona.edu. I thank Chris Lam-

oureux, Scott Cederburg, David Brown, Hidehiko Ichimura, Hui-Ju Tsai (discussant), and conference participants at

FMA 2023 for their comments and suggestions. All errors are mine alone.

Electronic copy available at: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4558057



1 Introduction

Should I invest in fund X and if so, how much? A precise answer to this age old question remains

elusive. Jensen (1968) attempts to fill this gap by examining whether a portfolio generates proxy

alpha – alpha with respect to the aggregate portfolio of equities (the proxy). Gibbons, Ross, and

Shanken (1989) shows that a portfolio’s alpha with respect to a benchmark answers this question if

the investor holds the benchmark. However, Roll (1977) highlights that the average investor holds

the aggregate portfolio of all risky assets (the market), which is unobserved. Using the proxy as a

benchmark will yield a proxy alpha, using the market as a benchmark will yield a market alpha,

and these may differ. If the difference between the proxy alpha and the market alpha are small

then the average investor could use the proxy alpha in lieu of the preferred but unobserved market

alpha. However, whether the difference in the alphas is large is an open question.

I provide evidence that the difference between proxy alphas and market alphas – proxy error

– can be significant and economically meaningful. I measure the difference in the alphas for an

anomaly by looking at the inner product of the vector of proxy alphas and the vector of proxy

betas from the anomaly’s ten characteristic portfolios.1 The intuition for the test stems from the

fact that a bias in an asset’s proxy beta will result in a bias in the asset’s proxy alpha. Namely,

bias will create an inverse relation between proxy betas and proxy alphas. The inner product of

the vector of proxy alphas and the vector of proxy betas is a weighted sum of proxy alphas where

the weights are the proxy betas. If the sum of the proxy alphas of the decile portfolios is roughly

zero, the inner product will be different from zero only when a relation exists between proxy betas

and proxy alphas. For example, given this inverse relation between proxy betas and proxy alphas,

the positive proxy alphas will receive less weight (smaller proxy betas) than the negative proxy

alphas (larger proxy betas) making the inner product negative. Therefore, the inner product is a

signal for bias in the characteristic portfolios of the anomaly.2 To evaluate the size of the inner

product, I split the anomaly’s sample history into 1-year non-overlapping sub-periods, calculate the

inner product of estimated proxy alphas and estimated proxy betas in each sub-period, and form

a t-score using the sample of inner products. If the t-score is large in magnitude, the anomaly has

significant proxy error.

Specifically, I study the differences in alphas in the many documented anomalies. I examine 99
1The inner product of the vector of proxy alphas and the vector of proxy betas is equal to the proxy alpha of the

proxy beta weighted portfolio of the anomaly’s characteristic portfolios.
2For more discussion on the geometric intuition see appendix section B.1.4

1

Electronic copy available at: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4558057



anomalies originating from three different sets of authors. Most anomalies (87 out of 99) do not have

significant proxy error but a non-trivial number do (12 out of 99). The anomalies with significant

proxy errors are robust across the multiple author groups and sub-period length specifications. The

corresponding time-series average difference in annualized alphas range from .6% to 1.5%.

In addition, my measure for proxy error is useful for selecting additional factors. The difference

in the alphas is the manifestation of an omitted variable. The omitted variables bias results from

using the proxy in lieu of the market, which differ by the omitted returns. The omitted returns are

the result of the omitted assets which are in the market but not the proxy. Therefore, portfolios

with exceptionally large differences in alphas likely have exposure to the omitted assets and their

inclusion as an additional factor should alleviate the omitted variables bias. I show that including

an anomaly with significant proxy error as an additional factor removes the proxy error across

anomalies. As the significance of the added anomaly’s proxy error declines, more anomalies continue

to have significant proxy error and more anomalies that did not have significant proxy error gain

significant proxy error. Proxy error not only helps to fix the proxy but also provides a way to

justify additional factors and classify the anomalies. All anomalies generate a large proxy alpha

which has two components – market alpha (pricing error) and proxy error. However, only some

anomalies generate large proxy errors (see section 8).

To corroborate this, I also provide evidence that proxy errors are likely driven by the anomalies’

covariance with the omitted returns. Specifically, the heterogeneity in proxy errors across anomalies

is most likely driven by differential exposure to the omitted returns. Similarly, simulations reveal

that an anomaly’s covariance with the omitted returns seems to best explain the data (see section

6).

Formally, my paper seeks to understand whether the impact of Roll’s (1977) Critique on tests of

alpha is significant. I test this by forming my null hypothesis so that the Roll (1977) Critique does

not affect estimated intercepts and residuals. If the tests assets’ proxy betas and market betas are

all non-zero then the estimated intercepts and residuals are unaffected if and only if the proxy and

market returns are proportional (see appendix section B.2 for details). Since proportional returns

imply no difference in alphas, proportional returns imply no proxy errors. Therefore, the existence

of proxy error implies that the returns are not proportional, which implies that the Roll Critique

affects tests of alpha. In addition, proportional returns imply that the market betas and the proxy

betas are proportional. This makes the inner product of proxy alphas and proxy betas proportional

to the inner product of market alphas and market betas. I show that the no-arbitrage framework of

2

Electronic copy available at: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4558057



Ross (1976) and a simple neutral model of arbitrageurs both motivate the identification condition

that the inner product of market alphas and market betas is zero. Under the joint hypothesis of

the null and the identification condition, the inner product of proxy alphas and proxy betas is zero.

Therefore, a large inner product of proxy alphas and proxy betas would reject the joint hypothesis.

I reject the joint hypothesis for several anomalies. Either the null hypothesis that the proxy can

be used in lieu of the market is rejected or the identification assumption of no-arbitrage is rejected.

Either case presents a challenge to asset pricing. If arbitrage trades exist, the identification of a

significant alpha with respect to a model may not be informative about the model’s performance.

This case is more troubling than a rejection of the null and may necessitate alternative methods

to assess a model’s performance. If the null hypothesis is rejected, correcting the proxy for omit-

ted returns is of fundamental importance for understanding the economic content of documented

anomalies.

Understanding the composition of proxy alpha in terms of market alpha and proxy error is

important as it will affect our inferences and potentially guide how the proxy alpha gets resolved. If

an anomaly generates proxy error, inclusion of the anomaly as an additional factor could be justified

under Roll (1977), while maintaining the current model. If an anomaly did not generate proxy error,

it must generate pricing error, which may highlight shortcomings of the model. If an anomaly

generates pricing error, including the anomaly as an additional factor may not resolve the anomaly

theoretically. Researchers may be left wondering how investors are valuing assets to generate this

anomaly in the first place (Fama, 1991). Without the test of this paper, researchers may have been

unsure of whether the proxy alphas that they document were due to the model (pricing error) or

the proxy (proxy error) and attempted to provide a justification in both circumstances (Fama and

French, 2015, pg 3). This paper can help researchers better interpret anomalies.

In addition, if average investors had the market alphas, they could use them as a guide to

determine the precise composition of the portfolio that they should hold. If an anomaly has a

positive market alpha and I am holding the market, I should hold some of the anomaly and the

level of the market alpha tells me how much to hold. However, even if there exists a combination

of my portfolio and the anomaly that is superior to my current portfolio, many combinations could

be inferior. Using proxy alphas in lieu of market alphas to build a portfolio could potentially make

me worse off. Therefore, getting proxy alphas closer to market alphas is important for helping the

average investor construct better portfolios.

This paper contributes to seven strands of literature. The first builds off of the Roll (1977)

3

Electronic copy available at: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4558057



Critique to improve the proxy. Cederburg and O’Doherty (2019) expands the market proxy – by

including debt and real estate – to study the ICAPM. Stambaugh (1982) performs pricing tests

of the CAPM under various formulations for the proxy – including stocks, bonds, real estate, and

consumer durables. In my paper, I examine whether an anomaly can be used to replicate the

portfolio of omitted risky assets. Cederburg and O’Doherty (2019) and Stambaugh (1982) try to

explicitly make a better proxy and then test. I let the data inform me through my test on how to

improve the proxy.

Second, my paper contributes to the long standing debate of whether anomalies should be risky

– having a large return variance.3,4 Kozak, Nagel, and Santosh (2018) show that risk alone can

not reveal whether alphas are due to rational compensation for risk or due to persistent irrational

mispricing along a coincidentally risky dimension. In the latter case, the irrational investors may

be mispricing the risky dimension because they believe this dimension should bear risk premium

and that the dimension is priced properly to reflect that risk premium. In doing so, the irrational

investors have created a risk premium but in the opposite direction. In both cases, there is a

dimension of risk that is difficult to diversify and exposure to the risk has an associated risk

premium. In this way, the rational and irrational risky factors are both risk factors. Knowing

whether an anomaly is a risk factor is crucial for deciding whether it should be added to factor

models, which relate priced risk exposure to expected returns. If an anomaly does not bear large

persistent cross-sectional variance, the anomaly’s alphas should be traded away (Kozak, Nagel, and

Santosh, 2018). Therefore, exposure to an anomaly that is an arbitrage trade, having small risk,

may not yield large risk premium and may not be a productive addition to a factor model.

However, in my paper, anomalies do not need to bear a lot of risk. Instead of the anomaly’s

ability to capture cross-sectional variance in equities, the focus is on whether the anomaly covaries

with the omitted returns. Even if the anomaly bears little risk, if it is correlated with the omitted

returns, a linear combination of the proxy and the anomaly could better represent the market than

the proxy alone. Therefore, even without bearing much risk, an anomaly could be added as an

additional regressor in a factor model. Moreover, these additions to the factor model do not alter

current model. For example, if the Value anomaly captured proxy error then – under the CAPM

– Value stocks could earn a higher return than implied by the proxy. Since the proxy error is not
3Cross-sectional anomalies are partitions of stocks on features of firms (characteristics) that capture large spreads

in proxy alphas.
4Harvey, Liu, and Zhu (2016); Kozak, Nagel, and Santosh (2018); Holcblat, Lioui, and Weber (2022); Linnainmaa

and Roberts (2018); Daniel and Titman (1997); and McLean and Pontiff (2016) to name a few.

4

Electronic copy available at: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4558057



an abnormal return, but an estimation bias, I would not expect it to get traded away. Therefore,

proxy errors are persistent not because they bear priced risk but because they correct an omitted

variables problem. Classically, anomalies are persistent either because they capture a risk factor

or because financing costs make the anomalies too expensive to trade away. Proxy error is another

possible explanation for why anomalies may be persistent in the data.

Third, by finding an additional factor that mimicks the omitted returns, my paper relates to

the literature proposing new factor models (Fama and French, 2015; Pastor and Stambaugh, 2003;

Stambaugh and Yuan, 2017; and Hou, Mo, Xue, and Zhang, 2021 to name a few). Generally, prior

literature identifies factor models that are closer to the in-sample pricing kernel. My paper also

seeks to better understand expected returns. However, these models are not focused on whether

the pricing improvement is due to a reduction in market alpha (pricing error) or proxy error. My

goal is not to better understand expected returns in general but instead to understand how the

market describes the expected returns.

Adding additional factors is not without danger. Whether proxy alpha comes from pricing error

or proxy error, including an anomaly in the factor model would improve in-sample pricing (Gibbons,

Ross, and Shanken, 1989; Barillas and Shanken, 2017). However, the in-sample pricing kernel –

the ex-post optimal portfolio (Gibbons, Ross, and Shanken, 1989) – generally has ludicrous weights

and terrible out-of-sample performance (DeMiguel, Garlappi, and Uppal, 2009). Given the zoo

of anomalies, a natural concern of incorporating many anomalies is exactly that the proxy would

approach the in-sample pricing kernel. To avoid this natural convergence it would be desirable to

include only anomalies that are robust out-of-sample. A potential solution is to search for anomalies

with substantial economy wide risk as these should be more persistent (Kozak, Nagel, and Santosh,

2018). I take an alternative approach and identify anomalies that appear related to the omitted

returns.

Fourth, my paper fits in with the growing literature on the economic content of the anomalies’

proxy alphas (Stambaugh, Yu, and Yuan, 2012; Baker and Wurgler, 2007, McLean and Pontiff,

2016; Engelberg, Reed, and Ringgenberg, 2018; and Novy-Marx and Velikov, 2016). Stambaugh,

Yu, and Yuan (2012) and Baker and Wurgler (2007) examine how anomalies’ proxy alphas vary

with sentiment, documenting that sentiment is an important component of the anomalies’ proxy

alphas. McLean and Pontiff (2016) show that many of the anomalies’ proxy alphas appear to

have been spurious or traded away after publication of the anomaly. This suggests that some

of the documented anomalies were lucky or near-arbitrage opportunities, instead of being driven

5

Electronic copy available at: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4558057



by persistent risk factors. If the anomaly was a near-arbitrage opportunity, the arbitrage profits

were an important component of the anomaly’s proxy alpha. Engelberg, Reed, and Ringgenberg

(2018) study whether short selling risk is an important component of proxy alphas. Novy-Marx and

Velikov (2016) seek to understand how much transactions costs prevent the removal of anomalies’

proxy alphas. After accounting for transactions costs, they find that the low transactions cost

anomalies still generate proxy alpha whereas most of the high transactions cost anomalies are no

longer profitable. This means that transactions costs can be an important component of anomalies’

proxy alphas. I examine whether proxy error is an important component of anomalies’ proxy alphas.

Fifth, my paper is related to the literature that constructs factor portfolios based on data driven

analyses of the covariance structure (Connor and Korajczyk, 1986; Kozak, Nagel, and Santosh,

2018, 2020; Kelly, Pruitt, and Su, 2019; Kim, Korajczyk, and Neuhierl, 2021; and Lettau and

Pelger, 2020). My construction is based on the covariance of each anomaly with the proxy, whereas

the others use the covariance structure between the anomalies. For example, Kozak, Nagel, and

Santosh (2018) explicitly remove their proxy for the market factor before calculating their PCA

factors. If their proxy was a PCA factor then the other PCA factors of the test assets are unchanged

by removing the proxy. In addition, the proxy betas, by definition, would be proportional to the

corresponding eigenvector of the covariance matrix. A proxy beta weighted portfolio would then

be proportional to the returns of the proxy. In this context, my proxy beta weighted portfolio is

“orthogonal” to the other PCA factors used in Kozak, Nagel, and Santosh (2018).

Sixth, my paper is related to the literature on evaluating factor models (Gibbons, Ross, and

Shanken, 1989 and Barillas and Shanken, 2017, 2018). Gibbons, Ross, and Shanken (1989) (GRS)

evaluate the absolute pricing ability of a factor model. Barillas and Shanken (2017, 2018) evaluate

the relative pricing ability of two factor models. I do not directly examine the pricing ability

of factor models. Instead, my paper measures whether pricing an anomaly using the proxy is

informative about the pricing relation of the anomaly with respect to the market. However, my

finding that the Roll Critique is not negligible has implications for tests that seek to determine an

asset’s market alpha using the proxy (see Appendix section B.7 for more details).

The seventh literature explores the importance of the Roll (1977) critique in regards to efficiency

tests of the CAPM (Shanken, 1987 and Kandel and Stambaugh, 1987). The primary result of

Kandel and Stambaugh (1987) and Shanken (1987) is that the rejection of market efficiency using

a proxy should be robust to concerns about the proxy. Specifically, Kandel and Stambaugh (1987)

show that provided the proxy is at least 70% correlated with the market, the evidence with respect

6

Electronic copy available at: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4558057



to the proxy supports a rejection of market efficiency. However, we do not know whether the proxy

is sufficiently correlated with the market. While my test does not address efficiency it provides

evidence for whether the market and proxy would yield alphas that are significantly different.

While my test can show that the alphas may differ, the market alphas may still be large enough to

reject the CAPM.5 Nevertheless, knowing the market alpha is important for factor selection and

portfolio construction. Therefore, knowing when the proxy alpha differs from the market alpha can

be useful.

The remainder of the paper continues as follows. Section 2 motivates and provides an example.

Section 3 describes the testing procedure. In section 4, I describe the sets of test assets and market

proxy used in this study. Section 5 presents the tests results. Section 6 examines the cause of

proxy error and finds evidence that proxy error is predominately a signal that the anomaly is

correlated with the omitted returns. Section 7 examines the small sample distribution of the test

statistic under the null and alternatives. Section 8 demonstrates that incorporating anomalies with

significant proxy error seems to alleviate proxy error. Section 9 shows that my method is robust to

outlier sub-periods. Section 10 concludes.

2 Proxy error motivation and example

The basic idea behind the test is to identify the component of proxy alpha that arises from the

discrepancies between the proxy and the market. In the context of a stochastic discount factor

(SDF), the expected value of the product of the pricing kernel and a test asset’s excess return

is zero. However, this may not hold with the market, which is not the pricing kernel and may

admit market alphas. In addition, the market’s excess return can be separated into the sum of

the proxy’s excess return and the omitted return. If I price securities based only on the proxy and

omit the omitted return, the mispricing associated with the omitted return gets combined with the

mispricing of the market. Therefore, the mispricing of the proxy contains both the mispricing of

the market (pricing error) and the mispricing of the omitted returns (proxy error).6

5Formally, the Kandel and Stambaugh test, a GRS test of the CAPM, and my test differ in important ways. The

Kandel and Stambaugh test and a GRS test of the CAPM both assume in their null hypothesis that the market is

efficient (the market is a levered version of the pricing kernel). I do not make this assumption. Instead, I assume

in my null hypothesis that the proxy is a levered version of the market, which is also assumed in a GRS test of the

CAPM. However, this is not assumed in the Kandel and Stambaugh test.
6See section B.5 and appendix section B.1.1 and B.1.2 for details.

7

Electronic copy available at: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4558057



As an example, let the proxy be the value weighted equity market (VWEM). Let Sharpe’s

market factor – the market – be the optimal combination of the proxy and the Return on Equity

factor (ROE). Let the optimal combination of the market and the Value factor (HML) be the

pricing kernel. In this case, the ROE factor is an omitted asset and the Value factor is a priced factor

that is omitted from the market (omitted factor). The mispricing of the proxy has two sources:

the ROE factor, which generates proxy error and the Value factor, which generates pricing error.

This distinction is crucial. If this example was true, investors could use the ROE factor to better

understand the return implications of Sharpe’s CAPM and can better incorporate anomalies into

their portfolios. However, in this example, the ROE factor would not yield “free” returns – market

alpha. The proxy alpha of the ROE factor would be due to a bad proxy, not due to mispricing

or risk factors omitted from Sharpe’s model. On the other hand, the Value factor would capture

mispricing or risk factors omitted from Sharpe’s model. However, without a model to inform an

investor whether the risk premium of the Value factor is persistent, it is up to the investor to

determine whether they should expect these returns in the future and if the risk premium is indeed

compensation for risk.

While the Value sorted portfolios generate market alphas, a market beta weighted portfolio

of the Value sorted portfolios does not generate a market alpha under the no-arbitrage based

identification condition of my paper. To form a market beta weighted portfolio, I determine the

vector of market betas of the Value sorted portfolios and use that vector as portfolio weights. The

no-arbitrage based identification condition is discussed in detail in section B.4 and the model is

discussed in detail in section B.3.

3 Testing Framework

In this section I motivate and describe my testing procedure. Proxy alphas are the sum of market

alphas and proxy errors. An anomaly has 10 decile portfolios, each of which has a proxy alpha, a

market alpha, and a proxy error. My identification strategy to isolate the proxy error is to form a

portfolio of the decile portfolios that should theoretically have a zero market alpha. In this case the

portfolio’s proxy alpha is also the portfolio’s proxy error. Knowing the proxy error of the portfolio

tells us something about the proxy errors in the original decile portfolios of the anomaly.

I use the no-arbitrage conditions of Ross’s APT (1976); Kozak, Nagel, and Santosh (2018);

and Hansen and Jagannathan (1991) to show that the market beta weighted portfolio of decile

8

Electronic copy available at: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4558057



portfolios has the smallest market alpha (section B.4). A simple neutral model on how arbitrageurs

classify stocks and how arbitrage capital is distributed provides an example for when the market

beta weighted portfolio has a zero market alpha (section B.3). The market beta weighted portfolio

having a zero market alpha is my identification condition.

To determine whether the proxy errors (Roll bias) in an anomaly are significant I want to

understand whether the proxy errors have a significant impact on asset pricing tests. To do this I

form a null hypothesis, which assumes that asset pricing tests are unaffected by using the proxy in

lieu of the market. I then check an implication of the null hypothesis in the data, as is standard. If

the data deviates largely from the implication of the null hypothesis I can reject the null hypothesis

and assert that proxy errors likely have a significant impact on asset pricing tests.

For asset pricing tests to be unaffected, I require that the estimated residuals and estimated

proxy alphas be unaffected by using the proxy in lieu of the market. In the section B.2, I show that

this condition is equivalent to the proxy being a levered version of the market – given that all betas

are non-zero. Therefore, my null hypothesis is that the proxy is a levered version of the market.7

Notice that in this case, the market alpha and proxy alpha are equal, making the proxy error zero.

An implication of the null hypothesis is that the proxy betas are proportional to the market betas.

The proxy betas are the vector of 10 betas obtained by regressing each decile portfolio on the proxy.

Likewise the market betas are the vector of 10 betas obtained by regressing each decile portfolio on

the market. Since the proxy alphas are the market alphas under the null, the null implies that the

proxy alpha of the proxy beta weighted portfolio is proportional to the market alpha of the market

beta weighted portfolio. Thus under the null hypothesis and my identification condition, the proxy

alpha of the proxy beta weighted portfolio is zero (see appendix section B.4 and B.5 for details).

This is the condition that I test in the data.

To evaluate this condition, I build an estimator for the proxy alpha of the proxy beta weighted

portfolio in each sub-period and form a t-score from the sample of estimators. If the t-score is large,

the anomaly has significant proxy error. The testing procedure is described in detail in section 3.1.

The connection between the no-arbitrage conditions of Ross (1976); Kozak, Nagel, and Santosh

If arbitrageurs classify all stocks into either the long end or the short end of the anomaly with

the long end and short end having the same market capitalization then the long arbitrageurs’ dollar

position in the long portfolio is the same size as the dollar position of the short arbitrageurs in the

short portfolio. This is because for someone to hold the long end, someone else must hold the short

end since all the stocks must aggregate to the equity market portfolio. If arbitrageurs further refine

their classification of anomaly exposure to match the decile portfolios then decile portfolios k + 1

to 10 are on the long end and decile portfolios 1 to k are on the short end, for some number k.9

If each arbitrageur tilts to only one decile portfolio, an arbitrageur tilting toward the i-th decile

portfolio invests wi percent of their portfolio in the i-th decile portfolio. This arbitrageur’s optimal

dollar tilt to the i-th decile portfolio is their total capital times wi. The sum of the optimal dollar

tilts on the long end make up the aggregate dollar position in the long portfolio and the sum of the

optimal dollar tilts on the short end make up the aggregate dollar position in the short portfolio.

3.1 Testing procedure

My procedure for testing whether the anomalies have proxy errors involves calculating a t-score of

independent estimates that under my joint hypothesis are unbiased and mean zero. I obtain inde-

pendent estimates by breaking up the full sample period into smaller non-overlapping sub-periods

and determining the estimate for each sub-period. Since the returns are assumed to be independent

over time, the non-overlapping samples are independent, making the estimates independent. With

these independent estimates, I determine the t-score – the sample mean of the estimates over their

sample standard deviation times the square root of the number of estimates. Since the estimates

are independent, the t-score is asymptotically standard normal in the number of sub-periods under

mild regularity conditions (see appendix section B.12 for details).10

I perform the procedure separately on each anomaly, using the anomaly’s set of characteristic

portfolios (predominately decile sorted portfolios).

First, I split the data into sub-periods. For the main results a sub-period of one year was taken

and the results are robust to alternative sub-period lengths (2 years, 3 years, 4 years, and 5 years).

The sub-periods are always January to December, inclusive.

Second, for each sub-period, s, I regress the excess returns of each of the anomaly’s characteristic

portfolios on the excess returns of the proxy with an intercept following

i∼idr(t) = αe,s + βe,srp(t) + υ(t) , υ(t) N(0N ,Υs)
10The use of independent sub-periods to form a t-score is reminiscent of the Fama-MacBeth (1973) procedure.

However, the sub-period estimates of my paper are unbiased under the null, which precludes any biasing problems

that are associated with the Fama-MacBeth procedure. In addition, Fama-MacBeth regresses expected returns on

beta to obtain an estimate for the risk premium of the proxy. By using alphas instead of expected returns I estimate

the expected return delivered by the beta exposure that is not captured by the proxy. This is the proxy error.

4 Data

For data on the proxy, I used the value weighted returns net of the risk free rate, obtained through

Ken French’s website.12 For my set of documented anomalies, I collect the anomalies used by three

sets of authors, with intentional redundancies. The redundancies across authors provides a check for

the method’s robustness to author variability in anomaly construction. The test assets associated

with each anomaly are the sorted decile portfolios based on the characteristic defining the anomaly.

The factors are long-short portfolios of the highest and lowest decile portfolio, respectively. The

three sets of authors are Fama and French [FF ],13 Novy-Marx and Velikov [NMV ],14 and Giglio,

Haddad, Kelly, Kozak, and Santosh [GHKKS].15 All returns are monthly returns. From the

characteristic decile portfolios, I subtract the risk free rate taken from Ken French’s website. For

the list of the Fama and French set of anomalies that I use see Table 1. From the NMV and

GHKKS set of anomalies, I use all the anomalies for which they provide data on their websites

as of December 2022.16 For each set of decile portfolios associated with an anomaly, I drop the

months that have a missing return for any decile portfolio. Effectively, this drops all anomalies

that are lacking all data in at least one decile portfolio over the whole sample.17 For each anomaly,

any sub-periods with incomplete data (missing months) are dropped. Sub-periods range from 1−5

5 Results

I follow the procedure outlined in section 3.1 using the data described in section 4. I find that

many anomalies have significant proxy error, that proxy error is likely driven by the anomaly’s

covariance with the omitted return, and that including an anomaly with significant proxy error

seems to remove the proxy error in the other anomalies.

I perform the test for each anomaly, to measure the anomaly’s proxy error. For each sub-

period, for each decile portfolio, I run a time-series regression with respect to the proxy and obtain

estimates of the proxy alpha and proxy beta. For each sub-period s, I use the 10 estimated proxy

alphas and proxy betas from the time series regressions to calculate the inner product of the vector

of proxy alphas and the vector of proxy betas, m̂s. Next, I add the bias correction term as described

in section 3.1 to obtain unbiased sub-period estimates of proxy error, m̂adj
s . Then, I compute the

sample mean and sample standard deviation of the sub-period estimates and determine the standard

t-statistic as described in section 3.1. These t-statistics are asymptotically standard normal under

the null hypothesis (see appendix section B.12 for proof).

The resulting p-values are shown in figure 1 for 1 − 5 year sub-periods. Each histogram has

ninety-nine counts which correspond to the ninety-nine anomalies. In all sub-period length spec-

ifications, the number of anomalies with p-values lower than 5% is large – between 24 and 35

portfolios. The number of anomalies with p-values less than 5% corresponds to the height of the

leftmost bar in the histogram. If all of the test asset sets followed the null hypothesis, we would

expect to see around 5 sets below the 5% threshold. Overall, I obtain between 5-6 times this

benchmark. The large number of rejections is also consistent across author groups. With 1-year

sub-periods, the Fama and French sample rejected more than 17% (3/17), the Novy-Marx and Ve-

likov sample rejected 25% (8/32), and the GHKKS sample rejected more than 24% (12/50). Given

the number of rejections at the individual testing threshold of 5% and the size of the p-values that

correspond to individual rejection, it seems unlikely that these multiple testing results are entirely

driven by sampling error. Under the null hypothesis an individual p-value being below 5% occurs

5% of the time. If the tests are independent, the probability of yielding at least the number of

15

Electronic copy available at: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4558057



rejections reached for each author group is 5% or less. For GHKKS, obtaining 12 rejections out of

50 occurs with 5E−4% of the time. For NMV , obtaining 8 out of 32 rejections occurs .014% of the

time. For FF , obtaining 3 out of 17 rejections occurs 5% of the time. Taken together, the author

level results occur with frequency at or below individual rejection levels – warranting a rejection

of the null hypothesis over the multiple tests. Therefore, multiple testing can not explain the large

number of rejections if the anomalies’ test statistics are independent.

The large number of rejections is robust to correlations between the anomalies’ test statistics.

To examine whether the large number of rejections is driven by correlations between the tests, I

perform a multivariate Hotelling’s T 2 test (Hotelling, 1931). The null hypothesis of this test is

that all the anomalies considered jointly have no proxy error. This test is analogous to a GRS

test (Gibbons, Ross, and Shanken, 1989) that all the alphas are zero. Specifically, I run the T 2

statistic on the panel of the anomalies’ proxy errors, madj
s . To perform this test, I need the number

of anomalies to be smaller than the number of sub-periods. Increasing the number of time periods

and decreasing the number of anomalies should also reduce the standard errors of the estimators and

increase the test’s power. To get a balanced panel with many time periods, I study each authors’

anomalies separately and keep only the anomalies with the longest series. For FF , the maximum

sample period length is 95 sub-periods, between 1927− 2021, in which 5 of the 17 anomalies have

complete data and the resulting p-value is .3 basis points. For NMV , the maximum sample period

length is 50 sub-periods between 1964− 2013, in which 24 of the 32 anomalies have complete data

and the resulting p-value is .3 basis points. For GHKKS, the maximum sample period length is

56 sub-periods between 1964− 2019, in which 40 of the 50 anomalies have complete data and the

resulting p-value is 3.7 basis points. The p-values for the T 2 tests on a subset of the anomalies

in an author group are small enough to be rejected at standard levels. Therefore, for each author

group, I reject the null hypothesis that none of the anomalies in the subset have proxy error. If at

least one of the anomalies in the subset has proxy error, at least one of the anomalies in the whole

set have proxy error.

The subset of anomalies is representative of full set unless there is a relation between either

the anomaly’s time series length and proxy error or the time in history and proxy error. Since the

proxy – the value weighted equity market – had a larger scope of equities after December 1972

when it included NASDAQ and AMEX, it seems plausible that more recent proxy returns could be

more informative of the market than older proxy returns. However, using all 17 anomalies of the

FF sample, the balanced panel has 47 sub-periods, between 1975 − 2021, and a resulting p-value

16

Electronic copy available at: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4558057



of 12 basis points. At least in this instance, where I can use the full sample of anomalies and have

a balanced panel with a reasonable number of degrees of freedom, I still reject. This provides some

evidence that while the time in history may play a role, the null is still rejected in the more recent

period.18

An assumption of the Hotelling’s T 2 test is normally distributed estimators, madj
s . While this

does not hold theoretically, the estimates in the data do appear to be normally distributed. To

test the normality of the estimators I run a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test on the empirical distribution

of each anomaly’s time series of estimators. Generally, I fail to reject at standard levels that the

estimators are normally distributed. At the 5% threshold, none of the 40 GHKKS anomalies tested

are rejected, 1 of the 24 NMV anomalies tested are rejected, and 3 of the 5 FF anomalies tested

are rejected. In the test using all 17 of the FF anomalies, only 1 anomaly rejects the normally

assumption.

A Benjamini and Hochberg (1995) test and Bonferroni test applied to these p-values identifies

sufficient evidence against the null at the 5% level. These two tests allow for more general correlation

structures and distributional assumptions. Table 2 shows the result of the Benjamini and Hochberg

(1995) test for the 1-year sub-period specification. This test identifies the anomalies with significant

evidence against the null controlling for the false discovery rate. The Bonferroni threshold is equal

to the threshold of the top ranked p-value. Since the top ranked p-value is less than the Benjamini

and Hochberg (1995) threshold, I also reject the null in the Bonferroni approach, controlling for the

family-wise error rate. The other sub-period specifications have similar results. At the individual

level, 24% to 35% of anomalies would capture proxy error at standard thresholds. Once I control

for multiple testing, the number of significant anomalies is between to 13% and 24%.

In addition to the number of anomalies, the sets of the anomalies with p-values below 5% and 1%

is also robust across the sub-period length specification and across author groups. The histogram

of the one year sub-period specification is broken out in a scatter plot of the anomalies’ p-values

in figure 2. The p-value scatter plots for the other sub-period length specifications are available

in the appendix (figures 36, 37, 38, and 39). The overlap in anomalies with p-values less than 5%

across the author groups demonstrates the robustness of the method to author level variation in

anomaly construction. This provides some confidence that these results are not driven by specific
18On the other hand, if I use the most anomalies possible, which results in the smallest time period, the NMV and

GHKKS sets fail to reject – though this may just be due to too little power. The NMV set can use all 32 anomalies

and have 39 time periods. The GHKKS set can at most have 43 of the 50 anomalies resulting in 47 time periods.

17

Electronic copy available at: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4558057



construction methodologies. The overlap can be seen by the appearance of similar anomalies with

different author prefixes below the 5% threshold in figure 2. Across all sub-period specifications

there are 12 anomalies whose p-values are always less than 5%. Therefore, the number of significant

anomalies and the anomalies themselves are robust to sub-period length, author implementation,

and multiple testing.

Another interesting pattern is that these test asset sets seem to generally capture features of

firm fundamental performance such as Value, Profitability, ROE, ROA, Momentum (Novy-Marx,

2015), as well as intra-industry market performance. This pattern is even stronger at the 1% cutoff.

the beta weighted portfolios should have small market alphas. Alternatively, the dispersion in

estimated alphas could be due problems with the proxy (proxy error). Therefore, the dispersion in

the economic magnitudes must be due to dispersion in exposures to the proxy, βe, or dispersion in

exposure to the omitted returns, βo. The source of the dispersion in the beta portfolio alphas is

explored in the next sections.

6 Sources of differential power between anomalies

In this section I show that the anomalies’ dispersion in proxy error is most likely due to dispersion

in the anomalies’ exposure to the omitted returns. If there were no omitted returns but the proxy

could be mispriced, I would not expect the anomalies to yield such a large variety of outcomes. In

this case,

Alternatively, if these differences are driven by violations of the minimum pricing condition this

there are no arbitrage strategies, then it must be that the proxy has random omitted returns.

Specifically, the different anomalies have different loadings on the omitted returns and these

provide differential effects on the population statistics. The differences in these loadings is exactly

what I want to capture. The Roll (1977) critique can be alleviated by adding an anomaly that

loads on the omitted returns as an additional factor.

A potential concern with the above analysis is that the estimates of proxy alphas, α̂e, and

the estimates of proxy betas, β̂e, have sampling errors. Another potential concern is in how the

covariance between the residuals enters the equation. To address these concerns, I show how the

covariance between residuals enters and perform a simulation study to see whether sampling error

alone can explain the results I see in the data or whether a covariance between the residuals is

necessary. In particular, I show this by comparing a second stage regression using the original data

with the same second stage regression using simulated data. The only way to replicate the results

between the distributions of second stage intercepts.

In the second stage regression, the first stage betas differ between the data and simulation.

The simulation would have returns based on estimated betas from the data and compute estimated

first stage betas from the simulated returns. This makes the first stage betas from the simulation

slightly larger than the estimated betas from the data as a result of the extra sampling error. This

is shown in Figure 7. For simulations with large residual variances, using estimated betas from the

data as first stage betas for the simulation helps to bridge the gap between second stage intercepts

from the original data of the simulation. However, there is still a sizable gap. This is seen in Figure

Unsurprisingly, this gap is removed when data alphas are used in simulating the data to generate

average characteristic portfolio returns in addition to using the betas from the data. In this case,

the inputs for the second stage regression for the data and the simulations will be extremely similar

by construction. This is seen in Figure 9. Importantly, this demonstrates that the existence of

alphas in the data can explain the gap second stage intercepts.

However, from equation (24) these second stage intercepts can be explained by a covariance

between residuals without alpha. This is seen in Figure 10 and 11. In these figures the simulated

returns have no alpha, but the residuals are correlated with the proxy. While relevant measure

as shown in (24), is the covariance, I parameterize the simulation using correlations because it is

more intuitive. However, the optimal amount of correlation for each panel will vary as the standard

deviation of the residuals are different. For Figure 10 the correlation is 50% and the panel with

a residual standard deviation of 3% fits well. For Figure 11 the correlation is 99% and the panel

with a residual standard deviation of 1% fits well.

This simulation experiment shows that sampling error alone is insufficient to explain the second

stage intercepts in the data. In addition, it highlights that either the proxy beta weighted portfolios

have market alphas or that there are non-zero covariances between the market residuals of the proxy

beta weighted portfolios and the omitted returns (the proxy’s market residuals). Since this gap is

quite large it seems unlikely that the covariance between market residuals is small as this would

imply the existence of large market alphas on relatively easy to form portfolios. The next section

highlights that even with the existence of covariance between residuals, the measure of proxy error

(βT
e αe) in this paper seems to capture true proxy error (||αe||22 − ||α||22).

6.1 Test performance under plausible alternatives

In this section, I construct plausible alternative environments to show that true proxy error – the

difference between proxy and market alphas – can be large and that my proxy error estimator –

the inner product of proxy betas and proxy alphas – captures true proxy error. An important

characteristic of the data appears to be that anomalies are correlated with the omitted returns.

Therefore, to replicate the effect of the omitted return, I need a portfolio of securities that explains

the characteristic portfolios’ returns even after controlling for the proxy. Each anomaly has 10

characteristic portfolios, predominately decile sorted portfolios along the anomaly’s characteristic.

24

Electronic copy available at: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4558057



However, finance researchers have discovered a zoo of portfolios that explain the characteristic

portfolios’ returns after controlling for the proxy. These portfolios are the characteristic portfolios

themselves.

Therefore, I use the anomalies’ characteristic portfolios as omitted portfolios. Specifically, for

each anomaly, a market return is constructed as the value weighted return of all 10 of the anomaly’s

characteristic portfolios. This is equal to the equity market proxy up to data filtering related to the

anomaly’s characteristic. For each characteristic portfolio of the anomaly, a proxy is constructed

where that characteristic portfolio is omitted. The proxy return is the value weighted return of

these remaining 9 portfolios. The difference between the market and the proxy is the omitted

return. For this simulation experiment, I use only the GHKKS dataset as they provide weights

and have the most extensive sample of anomalies considered here.

Using a market and a proxy, I regress the returns of the proxy on the market to obtain values

of e, b, V ar(η),E[rm], V ar(rm), and the residuals ({ηt}Tt=1). Using the same market, I regress

each characteristic portfolio, i, on the market to obtain market residuals ({ϵi,t}Tt=1), market alpha

(α), and market beta (β). There are 500 characteristic portfolios = 50 anomalies × 10 portfolios

per anomaly. For each characteristic portfolio, I compute the covariances between {ϵi,t}Tt=1 and

{ηt}Tt=1 to capture the covariance between the proxy residuals and test assets’ market residuals. In

addition, I regress each anomaly portfolio’s returns on the proxy to obtain the proxy alphas (αe)

and the proxy betas (βe). For each triple – (anomaly, proxy, and market) – all regressions use the

full time-series of data for which all twelve series have non-missing returns. Each anomaly has 10

return series. The proxy and market both have one return series.

There are 500 alternative environments described by the 500 characteristic portfolios, which

is the omitted return in that environment. Each environment is characterized by a market and

a proxy. In each alternative environments, the market and proxy alphas and betas are obtained

for all 500 characteristic portfolios. With these estimates I can compute the true proxy error in

each alternative. The true proxy error is the difference between the proxy alphas and the market

alphas. This is shown in Figure 12, Figure 13, and Table 3. From these figures true proxy error

can be large depending on the specific alternative – as large as 2%, annualized. As the interior

anomaly portfolios (2-9) are dropped the true proxy error becomes much less concentrated. This

highlights that omitted returns with greater potential to explain characteristic portfolio returns,

such as the High and Low portfolios, can generate larger true proxy error. Since a minority of

anomalies captured significant proxy error under the null, it may be unsurprising that the number

25

Electronic copy available at: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4558057



of large increases in alpha is small. Figure 14 shows that the proxy error estimator, βT
e αe, captures

true proxy error, ||αe||22 − ||α||22, under these alternatives.

Using the returns from this simulation, I run my test using 1-year non-overlapping sub-periods

to construct the t-scores. For each combination of model parameters, I run the simulation 10, 000

times to obtain 10, 000 t-scores. For each set of model parameters, I plot the distribution of t-scores.

There are four potential ways that the proxy could differ from the market and the effects of these

deviations on the distribution of the test statistic are explored in turn. The possible deviations are

a constant shift, a constant multiple, a white noise term, or an omitted factor that is informative

about test asset returns.

The first type of deviation is a constant shift in returns, e ̸= 0. I simulate 10, 000 t-scores

for each value of e = k × r̄p for k ∈ {−1,−.5,−.1, 0, .1, .5, 1}, where r̄p is the full sample average

monthly return of the proxy. In each of these simulations b = 1, V ar(η) = 0, and Corr(η, ϵ) = 0.

This is shown in Figure 15. When e = 0, the null hypothesis is true and the number of statistics

rejected at the 5% level is 5%, which alleviates concerns of small sample bias. In addition, as e

increases we can see the inverse relation between e and the t-score. Small changes in e can have

large impacts on the distribution of the statistic. Even if the proxy had a 64 basis point annual

market alpha, corresponding to k = .1, the 5% rejection rate increases from 5% to more than 20%.

With the proxy generating a 3.2 percent annual market alpha, corresponding to k = .5, the 5%

rejection rate is 100%.

The second type of deviations is a constant multiple, b ̸= 1. I simulate 10, 000 t-scores for each

value of b ∈ {.1, .5, 1, 2, 10}. The other parameters are e = 0, V ar(η) = 0, and Corr(η, ϵ) = 0. This

is shown in Figure 16. This corroborates the results that b does not effect the test statistic (see

appendix B.6).

The third type of deviation is due to a white noise term, which is uncorrelated with test asset

returns (pure measurement error). In this case, V ar(η) ̸= 0 and Corr(η, ϵ) = 0. The other

parameters are b = 1 and e = 0. I simulate 10, 000 t-scores for each value of V ar(η) = k× V ar(rp)

for k ∈ {0, .1, .5, .9}. This is seen in Figure 17. The null hypothesis holds in the sub-plot “V ar(η) =

0× V ar(proxy)”, where k = 0. From equation (21) and (22) and the above parameters, the inner

correlation the terms combine yielding a monotone increase in the center of the distribution as the

correlation increased.

Kandel and Stambaugh (1987) found that with a correlation between the proxy and the market

greater than .7, CAPM efficiency can be rejected. A correlation between the market and the proxy

larger than .7 corresponds to a value of ℓ less than .51. A large value of ℓ, would yield many

29

Electronic copy available at: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4558057



more rejections than I observe for the anomalies, unless the correlation between residuals is close

to negative one. The correlation between residuals would be close to negative one if the omitted

returns, r⊥o , were extremely informative of the anomalies’ residual returns (see appendix B.1.1). If

the omitted returns are less than nearly perfectly correlated with anomaly residuals, the data would

suggest that ℓ is much smaller than .51 and closer to .1. An ℓ = .1 corresponds to a correlation

between the proxy and market of .81. If the market is efficient, e = 0 and thus in the Kandel and

Stambaugh (1987) framework, my results show that the correlation between the market and proxy

is larger than Kandel and Stambaugh’s required threshold. This bolsters their conditional rejection

of the CAPM.

8 Proxy error with anomalies as additional factors

In this section I show how adding anomalies with low p-values as additional factors affects the

proxy errors and proxy alphas in the set of anomalies. I find that when the added anomaly had a

low p-value: proxy alphas get bigger, the angles between proxy alphas and proxy betas get more

volatile, and the proxy errors vanish. These effects are much more muted when the added anomaly

has a high p-value.

To add in an anomaly as an additional factor, I use the proxy beta weighted portfolio of the

anomaly’s characteristic portfolios (the βe-factor) as the additional factor. This differs from other

studies which traditionally use the High minus Low combination as the factor. I use the proxy

beta weighted portfolio because that is the combination that I test and is the combination that

may capture omitted returns. My two factor model contains the proxy and the βe-factor of the

added anomaly. For the returns of the two factor model, I use the returns of the ex-post optimal

combination of the two factors. This differs from the traditional procedure which includes both

factors as regressors. However, my procedure guarantees that the benchmark has the highest

squared Sharpe ratio of all possible combinations of the two factors. In addition, this procedures

yields a single factor, which I need to run my test. Using the single factor improved by the added

anomaly, I rerun my test and examine the proxy errors and proxy alphas. The effect of adding

anomalies with low p-values is shown in Figure 19 and Figure 20, which is Figure 19 zoomed in

toward the anomalies with lower p-values. The x-axis is the p-value of the anomaly using the proxy

as a benchmark. Each anomaly has two points on the graph: one black and one orange. Both

of these points sit at the x-value corresponding to the p-value of the anomaly. When an anomaly

30

Electronic copy available at: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4558057



is added as an additional factor, some anomalies that had significant proxy error under the proxy

become insignificant. The percent of anomalies that switch from significant to insignificant is y-

value of the black point. The percent of anomalies that switch from insignificant to significant is

the y-value of the orange point. Significance is determined by a p-value less than 5%. Since there

are 99 anomalies there are 198 = 2× 99 points on Figure 19. A successful additional factor has the

black points toward the top at 1 and the orange points toward the bottom at 0. We can see that

this separation is cleanest at the leftmost end where the p-values are smallest. As the anomaly’s

p-value with respect to the proxy increases – lower proxy error – the success of the anomaly as an

additional factor declines.

I find that the low p-value anomalies reduce proxy error by increasing the variance in the angle

between proxy betas and proxy alphas – weakening the systematic connection between the vectors.

Estimation problems resulting from the proxy having deviations from the market is a source of this

systematic connection. Therefore, the weakening of this connection is suggestive that the estimation

problems have been alleviated – making the proxy closer to the market. To separate between low

and high p-value anomalies I use the 1% p-value with respect to the proxy as the cutoff. I dig

deeper into the source of proxy error reduction by looking at several measures across these two

groups – low p-value and high p-value anomalies. Since the ability of an anomaly to remove proxy

error is based on p-values, the source of the reduction should also be based on p-values. For each

measure that contributes to proxy error, I examine how the measure changes when the anomaly is

added as an additional factor and how this behavior differs across the low and high p-value groups.

If a measure has large changes when a low p-value anomaly is added and small changes when a

high p-value anomaly is added, that measure is likely the source of the pattern in proxy errors.

Since proxy error is the t-score of the sub-period inner products of proxy alphas and proxy

betas, I first examine the times-series average of the inner products and the times-series standard

deviation of the inner products in Figures 21 and 22, respectively. The left column is for the low

p-value anomalies. The right column is for the high p-value anomalies. The top row shows the

measure – such as the time-series average of the inner products – under the proxy (in black) and

under the proxy with an added anomaly (in orange). The orange points are the average of the

measure using each anomaly in the group. For example, in the left column and top row, a black

point at x-value i corresponds to i-th anomaly with respect to the proxy. For each anomaly i and

j, I determine the measure of anomaly i with respect to the proxy and anomaly j. The average

of the measures of anomaly i over the j anomalies is the y-value of the orange point at x-value i.

31

Electronic copy available at: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4558057



The orange point at x-value i in the left column and top row characterizes the expected measure

of anomaly i with respect to the combination of the proxy and an arbitrary low p-value anomaly.

The orange point at x-value i in the right column and top row characterizes the expected measure

of anomaly i with respect to the combination of the proxy and an arbitrary high p-value anomaly.

The plot in the left column and bottom row looks at the differences between anomaly i’s measure

with respect to the proxy and anomaly i’s measure with respect the combination of the proxy

and anomaly j, for anomaly j in the low p-value group. For each anomaly i, this is a sample of

differences. The mean to standard deviation ratio of this sample of differences for anomaly i is

the y-value for the point at x-value i. The mean to standard deviation ratio corresponds to the

t-score associated with an arbitrarily chosen low p-value anomaly. If the measure differences where

independent Gaussians, a t-score larger than two in magnitude would suggest a rejection of the null

that the difference between the measures is zero at a five percent level. While the measures are

likely not perfectly Gaussian or independent the t-score can still characterize how significant the

differences in the measures are, controlling for the variability in the differences. The same applies

to the right column and bottom row but anomaly j belongs to the high p-value group. Looking at

Figures 21 and 22 the time-series means of the inner products decreases more for the low p-value

group and the time-series standard deviations of inner products increases more for the low p-value

group. Both are consistent with the low p-value group reducing proxy errors. The differences in

the time-series standard deviations seem more significant than the time-series means. However

neither are extremely significant so I dig deeper into both. The inner product is a product of the

magnitude of proxy alphas, the magnitude of proxy betas, and the cosine of the angle between

the vectors. For the case of the time-series mean, I look at the time-series mean of the magnitude

of proxy alphas, the magnitude of proxy betas, and the angle in between the vectors (theta) in

Figures 23, 24, and 25, respectively. For the case of the time-series standard deviation, I look at

the time-series standard deviation of the magnitude of proxy alphas, the magnitude of proxy betas,

and the angle in between the vectors in Figures 26, 27, and 28, respectively.

For the time-series means, the thetas increase slightly, the magnitude of the proxy alphas

increase and the magnitude of the proxy betas decrease. The t-scores of the proxy alphas and proxy

betas are around traditional significance levels of 3 and 2, respectively. However, the significance

is not extreme. These effects are more muted for the high p-value anomalies. The size of proxy

betas declining is not very surprising as using the proxy constrains the weighted average of proxy

betas to 1. Including assets that are different from equities in the benchmark should also reduce

32

Electronic copy available at: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4558057



the covariance of the asset with the benchmark. The reduction in proxy betas is consistent with the

anomaly making the proxy closer to the market. The increase in the size of alphas corresponds to a

decrease in the characteristic portfolio alphas (Figure 29), which reveals that the proxy errors tend

to be positive and market alphas tend to be negative. The market alphas being mostly negative is

consistent with limited arbitrage or the proxy being overpriced compared to the market. In Figure

29, I show in the top plot that the distribution of average estimated alphas shift to the left when a

Low p-value anomaly is incorporated with the proxy (orange). In addition, the average estimated

alphas do not change very much when a High p-value anomaly is incorporated into the proxy (grey).

For reference the distribution of average proxy alphas over the characteristic portfolios is in black.

There are 99 anomalies each with 10 characteristic (decile) portfolio yielding 990 portfolios each

with one time-series average proxy alpha. The proxy alphas are calculated using 1-year sub-periods.

The middle plot compares the changes in average estimated alpha between using an arbitrary Low

p-value anomaly (blue) and an arbitrary High p-value anomaly in (black). These are computed

by taking the average change in estimated alphas over all the anomalies in the p-value group.

We can see that Low p-value anomalies almost uniformly decrease alphas more than High p-value

anomalies. The bottom plot looks at the significance of this change via the average change over the

anomalies in the p-value group divided by the standard deviation of the change over the anomalies

in the p-value group. This represents a t-score for an arbitrarily chosen anomaly from a p-value

group. While the changes are uniform across anomalies and between High and Low p-value groups,

the changes are not very significant.

However, while the average magnitudes of the proxy alphas increase and the alphas of the char-

acteristic portfolios decrease, the average High minus Low factor alphas (Figure 30) and the average

proxy beta weighted portfolio alphas (Figure 31) do not change substantially. Also, in Figure 32 I

measure, for each anomaly i, the percent of sub-periods that have GRS p-values (Gibbons, Ross,

and Shanken, 1989) that are below 5%. While the percent of GRS rejections (Figure 32) are less

extreme, there does not appear to be a pattern between high and low p-value anomalies.

For the time-series standard deviations, the thetas, magnitudes of proxy alphas, and magnitudes

of proxy betas all increase. These increases are more muted for the high p-value anomaly. The

t-score for the difference in the time-series variability in the magnitudes of proxy alphas and proxy

betas is significant at traditional levels – between 2 and 3. However, the t-score for the difference

in the time-series variability of the thetas is around 8 – more than double the t-score of the other

measures. In addition, the difference between using low p-value and high p-value anomalies is the

33

Electronic copy available at: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4558057



largest for this measure. For most measures, the t-score of using low p-value anomalies is less than

twice that of the t-score from using high p-value anomalies. For the time-series average of the size

of proxy alphas the t-scores using low p-value anomalies are three times that of the high p-value

anomalies. For the time-series variability in theta the t-scores using low p-value anomalies is four

times the t-score using high p-value anomalies. The data suggests that the most important source

for alleviating proxy error is in weakening the systematic relationship between proxy alphas and

proxy betas. This corroborates the intuition in the introduction that since proxy deviations affect

theta over all sub-periods, an increase in the variability of theta is consistent with a reduction in

proxy deviations from the market.

9 Robustness to outlying sub-periods

The estimates of the proxy error for each factor is an average of the sub-period estimates, scaled

by the standard deviation and number of sub-periods. The sub-period average will approach the

expected proxy error. However, the sample proxy error being an average could be largely driven by a

single sub-period. While the estimate may indicate significant evidence against an error-less proxy,

the result may feel less credible if the mispricings exist only in single sub-period. The anomalies

generally, and especially in this context, are believed to capture priced risks in the economy that

are omitted from the proxy. However, there is a notion that if a risk is priced into securities, the

risk should be sufficiently persistent to worry investors. If the risks occur very infrequently, say

once in the available history of data, it may be outside of some investor’s experiences and be under

compensated (Malmendier 2021). If investors do not substantially price in the risk, the risk will

largely only appear in returns during the realization of the risk. This could make the risk appear

priced, via the average, even though the risk is not priced. This will make a few sub-periods appear

as outliers. However, priced risks can also have large tails and have sub-periods that appear as

outliers. The Momentum (Daniel, and Moskowitz (2016)) strategy, for example, has large crashes

but generates large return spreads. Therefore, anomalies with large tails and near zero medians may

be indicative of risks that are not highly priced in the economy due to their infrequency. However,

these weakly priced anomalies may still yield significantly large test statistics. To examine the

sensitivity of the test to extreme sub-periods I plot the distribution of the sub-period components
